en: Salutations to Śiva and Śivā. In the midst of the illustrious assembly of clouds, [I praise] the one who is eternally... [endowed with] joy... [the one] who is worshipped by the Lord of the Earth... [I praise] the illustrious Nandikeśvara, the highly renowned and beloved Lord; [this is from] the Svāyambhuva [Purāṇa].
Satisfaction for the most excellent qualified person arises through the word;
satisfaction for the middling qualified person arises through an illustration; and satisfaction for the lowest qualified person arises through a single example.

Ajita, (–) (third line), Kaṇva, Māyāvāda, Pāñcarātra—these six are equal. (...... Pāśupata, Vāma, Bhairava, Mahāvrata, and that which is known as Kālāmukha—thus ends the group of six internal systems.
In the Bhīmasaṃhitā: "There may be a breach of the rule regarding the calf; Śiva is said to be like milk.
One who dwells in the stage of life dedicated to Śiva should constantly worship Śiva, who is all-pervading and tranquil."
O Ajitā, he who is the Lord of stainless nature, free from beginning, middle, and end,
is to be known as the omniscient, perfect, and auspicious one in the Śiva-āgama.

The Guru, who is full and the bestower of the true path, should out of compassion initiate with the initiation of higher knowledge a disciple who has already been prepared by the previously mentioned initiation into the universe of the conceivable. (5th line)
That initiation which exists through the mere activity of the mind, according to the sequence, is indeed the initiation of knowledge;
it is also known as the initiation of higher realization (vijñāna).
Elsewhere— in the region of the heart, at the place between the eyebrows, and especially at the location of the head—
having meditated upon one’s own Guru as Śiva, one should awaken the knowledge of one's own Self.
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"He who instructs the disciple according to their aptitude through Sanskrit or Prakrit sentences, and by means of the local dialect and other such methods, is known as a Guru. (7th line)
O Lord, to those who are attached to Pauṣkara and others, and who desire [liberation] through incidental association,
the Lord grants a station that corresponds to their disposition.

Thus it has been said by the Teachers: "Those who desire the enjoyment arising from the manifestation of the worlds worship you through various modes of sacrifice; having bestowed [the fruits of those rites] upon them, you grant enjoyment to those practitioners of the Supreme Lord, and [finally] liberation."

"O Lord, even the gods beginning with Brahmā and Acyuta, as well as the Vedas, though they have reflected upon it, are not able to praise Your Self, which is consciousness and bliss"— thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa,
in the Pauṣkara section.
Now, O Treasure of Compassion, we wish to hear about the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Listen, if you have the curiosity to hear these unsurpassed [teachings].
In the Siddhatantra,
the means of valid cognition regarding the three categories are established as tenfold:
one should know that perception is the first, and inference is the second.
The third is said to be the treatise (śāstra); the fourth is non-existence (abhāva);
the fifth is the attainment of the object (arthasaṃprāpti), and the sixth is likewise the same.

The seventh is the circumambient (*pariveṣya*), and the eighth is indeed the state (*bhāva*). The ninth is declared to be tradition (*aitihya*), while the tenth is intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaka*). Even in the treatise (*śāstra*), ten [categories] are reached, ending with perception (*darśana*) and inference (*anumāna*).
In the *Siddhitantra*,
the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is to be understood as "well-seen" (*sudarśana*), free from conceptual differentiation, division, and doubt;
in detail, it is the existing object established by the reason known as "inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*).
And inference (*anumāna*) is that which is called scripture; one should perceive the object through inference.
In the *Suprabheda*, it is said: "That which is perceived by means of the senses and other instruments is here called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)."
The cognition of the possessor of a mark through the mark itself is known as inference.
This verbal [cognition] is declared to be cognizable through the words of a reliable person (*āpta*).
In the *Pauṣkara*, it is stated:
"Doubt based on two [contradictory] objects is a cognition arising from the perception of a common form."
Error is knowledge otherwise, not established in the true nature of the object.
Perception is that which is perceived by means of the sense organs, such as the eyes, and it is of two kinds: non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*),
which is the grasping of the mere nature of an object,
and conceptual (*savikalpaka*), which is accompanied by the mental construction of names, universals, and so forth.
Likewise, in the *Siddhatantra*, it is said:
"Others [hold that] those two, the seen object and the non-dual [subject], are previously subject to doubt;
it is determined that there is a distinction because that very [non-dual] exists for the sake of another."
Name, genus, quality, action, and substance—these five types of conceptual constructions [are absent];
indeed, it is only in non-conceptual [perception] that [the object] is truly apprehended.
In the Siddhatantra, however, in the [system of] Darśana, the measure of the four yogas consists of sensory perception (*indriyavedanā*),
inference (*anumāna*) [and so forth], and [the remaining means of knowledge]. (9th line)
Scripture (*āgama*) is of three kinds, [namely] Tantra... [and] Yukti. That which is composed of both is to be known as the middle [type], for it possesses two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) has been declared to be of three kinds; elsewhere, direct perception... [is described].
...intolerance... due to the power of [wrong] views.

Nevertheless, it is held to be threefold: [perception] dependent on the external sense-faculties (*bāhyendriya*), likewise [dependent on the internal sense-faculties], and dependent on the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Thus, in some cases, there is one side [of the argument].
In the *Siddhatantra*, it is stated: "The middle [nature] should be known as the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), yet it is indeed characterized by two measures.
That which has transcended its own genus is called the primordial nature."
One should avoid [the term] "other genus" (*anyajāti*), which is designated as being equal to its own middle genus (*madhyasvajāti*).
In this way, one should carve out half [of the term], and the whole is thereby determined.
The faculties of the sense organs, as well as form and the rest associated with the self,
should be known as being devoid of conceptual construction and the like, while maintaining the perception of the senses.
The varieties of knowledge and forbearance are to be understood through their objects, such as sound and so forth;
that knowledge which is defiled and obstructed is the view of the self and what belongs to the self.
In the Pauṣkara [Tantra],
another [method] is described which depends on the senses for the sake of removing the veil,
whereas [this method] depends on the internal organ through the conquest of the external senses.
In the *Siddhitantra*, it is stated that the connection with the object of meditation depends on the mental faculty (*antaḥkaraṇa*);
through self-knowledge, one experiences pleasure, pain, and so forth, along with passion and other such states.

For this is called internal: it may consist of feeling or vision. Having set aside the dharma of meditative concentration, the practitioners of yoga should understand the manifestation [of the truth] as occurring in another place, either once or seven times.
In that very context,
each of the three aspects and the three reasons shall be of three kinds. I shall now describe this twofold excellent inference.

"O Vāsava, that which brings about knowledge of oneself and others is called 'for one's own sake' (svārtha) and 'for the sake of others' (parārtha); likewise, the withdrawal of oneself is declared as such, while the other is called 'becoming' (bhava)."
This [inference] is of two kinds, known as the positive-negative (*anvayavyatirekin*) and likewise,
as stated in the *Pauṣkara*,
the purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*).
It is observed sequentially in the form of pure positive concomitance alone.
In the *Siddhatantra*, one's own position (*svapakṣa*), the similar position (*sapakṣa*), and even the opposing position (*parapakṣa*) arise.
One's own [position] should be...; the similar position (*sapakṣa*) should be seen as a *saṃpuṭī*.
In this context, the "opposing side" (*parapakṣa*) is said to be that which leads to a non-accepted object;
likewise, in the *Pauṣkara*, it is stated:
"The thesis (*pakṣa*) is endowed with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*); the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is endowed with the property [of being established]."
That which arises from the exhaustion of its opposite or from the limit of its measure is of that kind.
I shall first explain the reason (*hetu*), which possesses distinctions according to its different stages;

the second is said to be the effect (*kārya*), and the third is that which consists of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). The wise know that "possessing distinctions according to its different stages" refers to the progression through the various opportunities [for proof].
The effect is the production of smoke, and fire is the means of perception.
The absence of cold should be known as the absence of frost, which is established through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
In the *Pauṣkara*,
that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is to be known as twofold, consisting of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) and positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
In the *Siddhatantra*, it is stated that fire follows from smoke, as in the case of a kitchen; this is called positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
On the other hand, it is said that there is no smoke in water where a lotus grows.
[The syllogism] of others is considered to have three [members], while for some it is held to be fivefold;
in the Pauṣkara [treatise], that [syllogism] here consists of five members: the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*), and so forth.
The example, the application, and the conclusion as the fifth.
The statement of the meaning here is the proposition (*pratijñā*); the reason (*hetu*) is its pervasion (*vyāpti*).
In the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the reason is stated as being of that same kind; one should examine it as such.
(5th line) The application (*upanaya*) is the pervasion between the example and the subject (*pakṣa*).
Furthermore, the restriction of the thesis must be accompanied by a reason.
Furthermore, in the *Siddhatantra*, it is said:
"That inference is again declared to be of three kinds, just as [one perceives] a flower by its distant scent through prior observation and inference. (6th line)
The knowledge of the sentence, like inference, arises from inference upon inference;
it should be understood as yielding results such as the past and so forth, through scripture, just like inference.
The word of a reliable person (*āptokti*) is also a means of establishing supersensible objects (*parokṣārtha*),
provided that the object has been well-ascertained through either direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*).
He who speaks is inferior to the authoritative source; therefore, Śiva is more authoritative than him.
In the *Siddhatantra*, this aforementioned threefold scripture has been fully explained here.
The scriptures were spoken by Śiva, who is eternally pure and omniscient.
One should resolve any contradictions between earlier and later [statements] through the art of the Tantra;
having made the mind and so forth steady, one should perform the worship without agitation.
In the *Śuddhatantra*, there is the instruction on the awakening to the state of Brahman, which is devoid of beginning and end;
[therein] the absence of positions consists of four [and] twenty-one.
That period (daśā) is known as the period of suppression (nigraha), characterized by the loss of one's state and the destruction of one's eightfold [prosperity].
These appearances have been declared in the teaching of Śiva as being stable;
in the *Niśvāsakārikā*,
having indicated [them] with a needle, [there is] the threading [of the needle].
By that, all [of this] has been established in the Sūtra through [logical] reasoning.
In the *Pārāśarīya*, it is said:
"Those who know the Sūtras recognize a Sūtra as being concise, free from ambiguity, substantial, comprehensive in its scope, not meager, and faultless."
O Brahmin, in the illustrious Svāyambhuva [Purāṇa], it is stated that the entire world— consisting of female, male, and neuter— is born from the seed of the Lord,
and its maintenance and destruction are always preceded by an agent.
He is liberated from beginningless time, whose nature is consciousness, the agent of action, the destroyer, and the Lord; likewise, according to the awakening of supreme knowledge,
because the world consists of female, male, neuter, and so forth, its causal nature is observed.
There exists a creator; together with this [world], the Lord Hara creates from it.
In the *Svāyambhuva*, the Lord is said to be the eternal creator, sustainer, and destroyer of the world. (4th line) [The answer:
"uttaram" (the answer).
In this case, neither inference nor scripture establishes the possibility of such an effect;
rather, the destruction and arising of all beings is observed to occur just as it is seen [in ordinary experience].
Likewise, in the presentation of all [other] views: "For when an object is established by direct perception, inference does not operate;
if it were to be established by inference, it would follow that the ultimate reality is something other [than what is perceived]."
"Intrinsic nature" refers to the creation and dissolution of the elements; however, in the subsequent [section] called Parā,
the intrinsic nature of even the four elements is not perceived at all.
Therefore, where it trembles, heat is seen somewhere;
fire reaches extinction, and the wind moves upward in some places.
For such is the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) among the elements—how much more so when an effect is produced?
Because it is connected here with the states of creation, maintenance, end, and destruction as its effects,
and because it is insentient, this world is therefore entirely preceded by an agent.

In the tradition known as *parākhyā*, it is said that the fourfold being (*caturbhūta*) himself performs all actions; therefore, it is declared to be the bestower of fruit. Do not, however, imagine yourself to be the agent.
The four elements are said to be eternal, characterized by persistence, origination, and dissolution. This God, devoid of beginning and end, acts from every side.
In that very context, the intention (*āśaya*) of beings is especially [determined]; [otherwise] it would not come to pass. It is said that without this, there is no agent of actions here.
The wise say that the cause of these two is *māyā*.
In that very context,
the production of effects such as pots and cloths occurs through the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
And likewise, because this [world] is also an effect, they say that its creator must exist.
Likewise, in the northwest (–),
whatever is fit to become in whatever manner, that shall become so of its own accord;
without [the need for] meditative cultivation, the agent would be independent in every respect.
In the *Niśvāsottara*,
it is said: "If one were to say that existence and non-existence themselves are a state of non-belief [in the real], and that there is no single entity,
then it would be exactly so."
How could there be any movement for him, arising from your grace?
There exists a creator of this [universe], for its effects are observed to be such; otherwise,
how could the production of bodies and dissolution, as well as insentience, be conceivable?
O Pārvatī, you wish to hear the answer regarding the origin of all things; listen. From space arises wind, and from wind, fire is said to arise.
From fire comes water, from water comes earth; such is the sequence of the elements (bhūta). The union of all these elements is held to constitute the world.
Otherwise, these dissolutions occur in such a sequence; and that has been taught as occurring after a period of time.
O Pārvatī, listen further: if there is no destruction anywhere, then hear this.
Just as a sprout is seen after a year [of rain], so too is the world [seen] after its great sleep; thus one should reflect.
Since time is the cause, the world arises through time; for time alone is indeed the agent.
Furthermore, by means of arising through appropriation and also by means of destruction, [the self] would become insentient.
Moreover—
It has been stated that the creation of the phenomenal world occurs simultaneously;
therefore, Maheśa alone must be its protector, just as he is the master of time. Furthermore, from him arises the manifestation of all atoms and their respective karmas.
Furthermore, it has already been stated previously that action would also be insentient,
just as clay is observed to be the material cause of a jar. (7th line)
In this context, it has been stated that *māyā* is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).
They declare *māyā* alone to be the cause of atoms, because their effects are observed.

In the case of the cause of the world, that which is known as the cause and exists in the form of atoms is said to be the "effect," because it is perceived in the form of the constituent parts of the effect, just like a jar or similar objects.

Whatever is perceived is subject to destruction, having *māyā* as its material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). For the wise, creation, maintenance, and dissolution within that cause are the effects of *māyā*.
And how so? For [a thing] supported by the earth, such as a seed or a branch...
(9th line)... that entity arises like an illusory form (*māyeyā kalā*).
O Maheśvara, you have said that arising and destruction are illusory phenomena (*māyeya dharma*).
In the *Kiraṇatantra* (P7b4a, first line): "The power called action (*kriyā*), which produces that effect, belongs to that which has a subtle form;
for it is subtle [even when] gross... like the seed of a *nyagrodha* tree."
The cause of the world, known as Māyā, is never separate from the Supreme.
Since the world is born from Māyā, it is not produced like the horn of a hare. Therefore, it is not as if leaves arise later on trees that were previously without them.
Even when its effect has perished, that cause would still persist; however, [in reality] there is no further cause for it.
In this cause, by means of the effect of that cause, this world called "beginningless" exists eternally;
because it is the first manifestation, one should therefore say that its creator is the agent of the act of creation.
In the *Parākhyatantra*, it is stated: "How can Māyā alone be called the agent of the universal cause? Thus ends the question.
Therefore, there exists some intelligent Lord who is eternally established;

one may assert that He is the creator of the primordial world-phenomenon based on the evidence of the act of creation. This is established here through inference from the perceived effects which have been accomplished by Him.
Or else, by the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (anyathānupapatti), it is likewise beginningless.
The distressed and the virtuous should go there, adorned with various forms and garments;
he is the Lord of the universe, the measurer, distinct from both the individual soul and its bonds.
In that very case,
since these two— the individual soul (*paśu*) and the bond (*pāśa*)— are insentient and ignorant, how could there be the creation of this universe in their absence?
Whatever is insentient, such as primordial matter (*pradhāna*), atoms (*paramāṇu*),
and so forth, is endowed with an intelligent cause in order to produce and perceive itself.
The world is dependent upon an agent because it is an effect consisting of parts;

therefore, the agency of the effect belongs to the Lord, and not to the bound soul (*paśu*) or the fetter (*pāśa*). In the *Parā* [Tantra], that which is called the Lord is the efficient cause (*nimitta*), observed as the cause of dissolution.
And that subtle grasping which is present in all activities.
The Lord, together with his power, is like Māyā; it is like clay [is to] a potter and his wheel.
Thus, in the Niśvāsa [Tantra], it is said: "Just as in the world a jar and other vessels are [produced] from clay by a potter..."
He brings about the entire world, known as the effect, by means of the cause.
The Supreme Lord, known as Action, creates the entire universe;
by means of the three causes, every effect is inferred from Him.
(From the *Niśvāsottara*)
The unmanifest (avyakta) consists of the bindu and māyā; therein, what is called the "feet" are its four modes of speech (vṛtti) in the form of words, beginning with vaikharī.
Vaikharī, Madhyamā, another, Paśyantī, and that which is known as Sūkṣmā;
and in the Pauṣkara [Tantra], these are Kalā, Vidyā, Rāga, Kāla, and Niyati.
And these five principles, O best of the twice-born, are illusory.
In the *Mṛgendra*,
[the deities] beginning with Mātṛbhūta have their eyes fixed on pride for their qualities and wisdom;
[in the] *Pauṣkara*...
O Brahmins, the [lineage] is said to be twofold, consisting of millions of *saṃkalpas*;
those eight who preceded Andu were, as before, superior in qualities.
Others are equal to Śiva and imitate his activities.
The path of principles (tattvādhvan), the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan), the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), and the path of words (padādhvan) in succession— (3rd line)—
the path of mantras (mantrādhvan) pervades them, and the path of kalās (kalādhvan) is likewise supported by them.
For those by whom that which is produced from the substrate of the bindu is called "baindava."
Among those [three],

that *vaikharī* speech which is perceivable by the ear and denotes meaning occurs when the eight places of articulation are held by the breath (*vāyu*) and there is the grasping of phonemes (*varṇa*).
The speech of speakers is for the most part dependent on the vital breath;
it follows the sequence of phonemes solely through the operation of the intellect.
In that very state, [the speech] in the form of internal discourse does not approach the lineage (*gotra*); rather,
it proceeds by means of the *madhyamā*, having transcended the activity of the vital breath (*prāṇavṛtti*).
In that very state,
where the sequence of phonemes has been entirely withdrawn without distinction,
she is the self-luminous Paśyantī, resembling the fluid within a cosmic egg.
In each of those places,
there exists within the very light of one's own nature a subtle, non-departing speech;
when that [speech] has been perceived in its true form, one’s qualification [for ritual action] ceases.
In the person consisting of sixteen parts, they call that [sixteenth part] by the name "Immortal.
Who is he?
He enters into them; he neither rises nor sets, he is not weary, and he is free from modification.
In that very context,
this fourfold activity, based on the digits (*kalā*) such as cessation (*nivṛtti*) and the rest,
is further divided fivefold; those digits are joined with the point (*bindu*).
The existence of the *bindu* is merely like that of a fringe on a cloth;
for it is stated in the Śruti: "The Supreme Self is the essence of speech," and "Speech is the Self."
Vaikharī is perceived in the cognition born of the ear; Madhyamā, in conceptual [cognition];
and Paśyantī, in the efforts toward the production of Madhyamā.
When the activity residing in the mind has entirely dissolved—
Then, through discernment, consciousness alone shines forth as subtle and pure.
In the *Nādakārikā*:
"The wise one who is proficient in the Brahman of Speech attains Brahman by means of that [which they describe];
through the knowledge of Nāda, there is supreme perfection and liberation, whereas ritual action is fruitless."
She is Nāda, the supremely auspicious Mālinī, Mahāmāyā, Samanā, Anāhata,
Bindu, Aghoṣā, Vāgbrahma, and Kuṇḍalinī.
Thus, in their respective scriptures, it is described by various such terms as "Reality" (*tattva*) and "Knowledge" (*vidyā*).
In that very context,
in some [traditions], because it is not yet completely purified, it is said to be distinct even from Māyā and situated above it.
The pure *vidyātattva* bestows enjoyment upon the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśas*);
it is the world-sphere (*bhuvana*) prescribed within the path by others, and it is always for my supreme welfare.
Thus, [it is] the cause within the Three Jewels.
The Lord Ananta, whose body is knowledge, through the desire to cause agitation, [emerged] from Māyā; and he is called by the learned "the Bindu."

The path of the principles (*tattvādhvan*), the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*), and the path of words (*padādhvan*)— in their respective order— are the eternal material causes for the multitude of principles beginning with Sadāśiva.
The pervasive path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*) belongs to them, while the path of the energies (*kalādhvan*) rests upon the *bindu*.
For those by whom that which is produced from the grasping of the *bindu* is called "the *bindu*-born" (*baindava*).
Right there,
the Sun, whose essence is the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman), moves within all beings;
having pierced through him with the sword of awakening, those who are free from doubt remain beyond suspicion.
Those who know the Self call that very speech "the subtle";
these functions, fixed within each individual self, are of the nature of bondage.
Indeed, individuals do not perceive the self as distinct from these;
in the *Pauṣkara*,
there are four modes of conduct by which the three channels are pervaded.
There is no bondage higher than these, and there is no liberation other than these.
Since the power of vision and action (*dṛkkriyā*) is inseparable from that cessation [of the world],
so it is said in the *Niśvāsottara*:
"The entire universe proceeds by means of the functions of sound."
For there is never any cognition for a person apart from words.
When, by the grace of Śiva, knowledge arises for one who seeks liberation,
[it is said in the] Kālottara:
"Even cowherds, women, and barbarians speak in the vernacular."
Even those beings dwelling within the water always speak by means of them. The meaning of this [verse] has been explained at length in that commentary (*vṛtti*).
Regarding the Three Jewels:
whatever object arises is like an illusion, just as [the forms of] artistic skills [appear in a mirror].
Maheśvara declares that arising and destruction are both forms of illusion.
For the transformation of things consists in the attainment of another state by means of the relinquishing of the previous state,
as in the case of milk [becoming] curd.
And from curd comes buttermilk; therein the state of buttermilk is examined.
For in your view, it is neither the prior state of the curd nor that of the milk.
In that state, there is one underlying substance: first milk, then curd, and afterwards buttermilk; likewise... [the rest of the verse].
In the *Viśvasārottara*, it is said that although the Lord (*īśvara*) is the material cause (*upādāna*) of entities consisting of reality and its objects,
even though he arises in various forms, he remains changeless despite being subject to transformation.
In that which is changeless and formless, as in heaven, and among the four elements, it is born.
Like lightning, smoke, a rainbow, clouds, thunderbolts, and sounds; just as in the world, jars and other objects are produced by a potter through his agency—
so too does He bring about the entire world, known as an effect, by means of His status as the agent.
[Regarding] the question:
Where does he, who is indivisible and complete, abide? And what does he do for you? [The answer is: In the breath (*niśvāsa*).
Time, though formless, brings about the gathering of flowers upon the trees,
as well as the ripening and falling of fruits in their respective directions.
Likewise, Śambhu, though formless, is the agent of creation and destruction;
as it is said in the *Kiraṇa*:
"Just as time, although entirely formless, is seen to be the bringer of results."
In this way, Śiva, though formless, accomplishes his work by his own will.
In the *Śrīviśvasārottara*, the meaning of the term "practice" (*abhyāsa*) regarding the Self is explained: even that which has arisen and passed away remains.
Thus, that agent is the true being; for him, no "play" (līlā) exists.
In the Śrī-Cintyaviśva,
Śambhu and Vanas, out of compassion, beholding the afflictions of those who are the souls of all, [performed] their birth and likewise their death.
Having created [them] as before for the sake of preserving the *karmas*,
he remains asleep in the Lord of Beasts (*mṛgendra*), awakening those worthy of awakening, uplifting the Romans, binding the actions of the *karmika*s.
Making the power of illusion (māyā-śakti) fit for manifestation, he perceives every category of entity exactly as it is.
In the *Viśvasārottara*,
it is said that Śiva, remaining changeless, performs the threefold task:
[the formation of] a lotus baked by fire within the form of a stone, and the depletion of the essence upon the earth.
Just as [the world] is seen by Āditya, so too by Īśvara;
in the Viśvasārottara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā are the deities of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
If it is argued that Śiva alone is said to be the possessor of the attainment of the task in the beginning, listen.
Brahmā, having indeed worshipped that auspicious linga made of stone with devotion,
attained supreme Brahman-hood solely through the worship of that linga.
Janārdana, likewise, having worshipped a linga made of sapphire...
Because he attained Viṣṇu, he is therefore the wondrous and unique Eternal One.

From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, Śiva is remembered as the source of the world of moving and non-moving beings, and as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of all creatures, both mobile and immobile. Thus,
in the northwest [is the mantra].
Endowed with supreme sovereignty and permeated by the Supreme Lord,
they are eternally presided over by His power and are capable of performing His work.
Having created the entire universe at the beginning of the Svāyambhuva [Manvantara], he, the Protector, withdrew within himself;
at that time, Rudra was alone, and there was no second being whatsoever.
Indeed, countless [kalpas] have passed for Brahmā, who has Hara as his deity;
according to the Skanda Purāṇa,
they are so called because they remove the suffering of dissolution and because they remove the phenomenal world.
The name "Hara" has been proclaimed for you because of your primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
When the dissolution of primordial nature occurs and all things, both mobile and immobile,
are consumed, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and all the gods go to their destruction, except for Śiva.
In the *Svāyambhuva*,
this activity known as "the diversion through the supreme reality" is asserted by those who maintain the doctrine of non-duality;
for what reason has this been proclaimed?
The subsequent [teaching] concerning the union of the body with the sacrificial animals is said to be for the sake of enjoyment and liberation;
nevertheless, the virtuous say that it is the releaser from beginningless impurity.
In that very place, it is said that for bound souls (paśus), there is a "passage" (hāra); one should lead them to rest upon the plane.
Having created [the world] through the bond of impurity (mala), the so-called "emission" (sṛṣṭi) has reached its respective karmic impurity.
From this [power] comes the maintenance, acquisition, and restraint [of things]; "action" (karman) refers to the ego-sense (ahaṃkṛti).
One should know that for bound souls (paśu), the bestowal of knowledge constitutes grace (anugraha) when there is a desire to speak.
Likewise, elsewhere [it is said]:
"Because of his compassion for the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world, he is of the nature of Śiva. Elsewhere [it is said]: [—]

[Question: Regarding the Śiva-āgama, which speaks of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the world out of compassion, and which describes both the formed (*rūpa*) and the formless (*arūpa*): among those [teachings], which one possesses the nature of an author? [Answer:
(The answer follows:)
Thus this triad has been declared, and its nature has been illustrated;
likewise, in the *Suprabheda*, that body should be known as threefold: the partless (*niṣkala*), the both-part-and-partless (*sakalaniṣkala*), and [the part-possessing].
And the entire [object] should likewise be known as threefold in its specific distinctions. In the *Mṛgendra*,
it is stated that the forms of the deities are never like the bodies of those such as ourselves.
In the *Kiraṇa*,
it is held that for him [the Lord], desire alone is the cause, just as it is for a yogin;
exactly as a yogin is considered [the cause] in both the seizing and the releasing [of objects].
In that very same way, O All-pervading Lord, one should understand grasping and liberation;
that body is illusory in nature, caused by the remnants of past karma.
In the *Uttara* and the *Mṛgendra*, because [the transmission] beginning with the Root (*mūla*) is impossible, Śakti is incomplete (*apūrṇa*).
Since he alone is liberated from bonds (*pāśa*), by whom can his knowledge be obstructed? (2nd line)
In Mataṅga,
if Śakti is indeed the essential nature, then transformation is observed;
if it is the nature of eternal bliss, then the path of the sixfold way is the Vāgbhava.
In that very [context],
all things (*viśva*), even though they consist of both form and formlessness, do not arise from yoga.
Even Śiva, among all things, likewise remains one once again.
In that very context,
the categories of bondage and liberation do not exist even as something devoid of another state;
I shall not speak of them to you in such a way, for their existence is nowhere determined.
Inconceivable, free from affliction, without support, devoid of color and form;
omniscient, all-pervading, peaceful, the self of all, facing every direction.
He who is the witness of all things— of pleasures and pains— in this world,
he alone is the Blessed One, all-pervading, immeasurable, and incomparable. (In the Pauṣkara...)
Since his mere will brings forth a form consisting of his own power as its cause,
he is remembered as Sadyomūrti (the One whose Form is Immediate).
In the Vātulottara,
having assumed a form out of compassion, it is told from the oceans of the Āgamas:
[if] this were not so, there would be no one who holds the lineage of the succession of Gurus.
Thus it is said in the *Kiraṇa*:
"As long as one does not act in this way, the lineage of the Guru is not [established];
the Lord bestows grace upon all embodied beings. (7th line)
However, because he performs the act of instruction, that Śiva is the "hand" (the means);
for if this lineage of gurus were complete in every respect,
yet lacked instruction, it would likewise be fruitless.
If this were not so, then the lineage of the gurus would not exist.
For the sake of bestowing grace upon men, even the Supreme has assumed a non-supreme state;
having fashioned a body consisting of mantra, he speaks the tantras in manifold ways. (8th line) {15}
Due to the relationship between the object to be known and the knower, the systems based on individual manifestation are manifold.
As stated in the *Vātulottara* (line 9): "That which is His form is compassion; likewise, [His] creation of Śiva and so forth."
Together with its limbs and sub-limbs, this [text] bestows enjoyment and liberation upon the Lord, the Sovereign.
Thus it is stated in the *Kāraṇa*:
"The eyes, the tip of the nose, the ears, the hands, the soles of the feet, and the fingers—
along with the matted hair and the crown— are proclaimed to constitute the [deity] with its limbs (*sāṅga*)."
Clothing, sacred thread, and garlands, as well as weapons and ornaments;
likewise Gaṅgā, Candana, Apasmāra, the Nāga, and indeed the Kūrma.
All [elements] beginning with the seat (*āsana*) are proclaimed as the *upāṅga*.
In the work titled *Vātulaśuddha*, it is stated: "The *aṅga*, *pratyaṅga*, *sāṅga*, and *upāṅga* constitute the fourfold [classification]."
In the *Suprabheda*, there are eleven Rudras preceded by [the first], joined with twelve Ādityas;
and the Vasus joined with the Aśvins— these are the thirty-three deities.
In the Skanda [Purāṇa]: "Other deities, such as Brahmā and the rest, are certainly not the liberators from saṃsāra;
it is exactly so for living beings wandering in the great cycle of existence."
The liberator from saṃsāra, the manifest omniscient Lord Śiva,
who assumes various forms and is endowed with manifold enjoyments, resides in the [city] called Śuddhā.
Hara is endowed with various marks and assumes various playful forms.
One should know Maheśa as the manifest one, whose nature consists of creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
likewise [in the northwest],
his various wondrous deeds and secret movements.
Difficult to comprehend, they bewilder even the minds of those who are indifferent.
In the *Vīratantra*: first indeed Somāskanda, then Sukhāsana,
Kalyāṇasundara, and Candraśekhara.
Gaṅgādhara—these five are declared to be forms of creation;
likewise Vṛṣabhāvahana and Ardhanārī.
Kirāta, Vīreśa, Bhikṣā, Naṭana,
and Eva— these indeed constitute the five forms, which are declared to be the Sthiti-mūrti (the form of maintenance).
And likewise, the dance of the Enemy of Kāma, the Enemy of Time, and Hara;
the slaying of the elephant, the destruction of Tripura, and the killing of Jalandhara.
The sixth [chapter] proclaims the distinction of forms among the deities of withdrawal;
in the *Śaiva Ekādaśarudrasaṃhitā*, [it is said that] once, being pleased in private, [he addressed] one who was subject to his own command.
The innocent woman, knowing him to be her lover, approached him respectfully from behind.
Out of curiosity, wondering "What might happen? she playfully covered the eyes of Śambhu, the teacher of the world, with her two lotus-like hands.
A fierce darkness arose, terrifying for a long time; yet in the mere twinkling of the god's eye, millions of years passed away.
(................................... arising from his playful sport, that destruction of the world occurred;
the universe was filled on all sides by a boundless darkness.
Thus the wise ones remained, bowing with devotion and praising Śambhu.
Having heard these words of theirs, [he who is] the soul of his devotees...
With his blossomed eye, he destroys the darkness pervading all directions;
he is the witness of the universe, Gaurī, the embodiment of compassion, and the knower of all flaws.
And that goddess removed the covering of the eye of Hara;
the great world, consisting of the forms of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire, began to shine forth. (From the Mahāliṅga Purāṇa)
Having then gone to that hermitage of Śambhu together with Rati,
he set his mind on fighting the god, with Vasanta as his companion.
Then, beholding Madana, the three-eyed God smiled and looked at him with his third eye with contempt. Thereupon,
the fire born from his eye [consumed] Madana, who was standing nearby.
At that very moment, the ocean of compassion burned [the sin] and lamented.
For the stability of the stages of life and for the welfare of all beings,
the Blessed Lord Bhava then married the goddess Haimavatī according to the prescribed rites.
[Cintye]
In that very [scripture] where emission, maintenance, and withdrawal are proclaimed,
likewise in the Kāmika:
"The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, sages, and human races..."
"From the species of ants and so forth, including all those that are mobile and immobile—
they are declared in the scripture to be worthy of grace; they are considered worthy of grace in many ways," as stated in the *Vātulaśuddha*.
For the sake of the emanation of all principles (*tattva*), the cause of the world's origin,
he assumes a body by his own will for the benefit of yogins.
(In that very place).
Śiva, Sadāśiva, and Maheśa are remembered as the threefold [forms];
however, the Niṣkala (partless) Śivatattva is highly extolled.
The Sakala, the Niṣkala, and that which is called Sādākhya—
these are indeed known as the threefold Maheśas.
In the *Suprabheda*, it is said: "That which is partless (*niṣkala*) and devoid of parts (*kalāhīna*) becomes possessed of parts (*sakala*) through the parts;
that which is a mixture of the whole and the partless is therefore called the 'part-and-whole' (*sakalaniṣkala*)."
The supreme is said to be partless (*niṣkala*), while the inferior is remembered as having parts (*sakala*).
Likewise, the intermediate is declared to be both with parts and without parts.
In the *Vātulottara*, it is asked: "O Lord, how is the Supreme Lord known as Adhvamūrti? The reply is: [as follows].
And by that which is eternal, pervasive, full, and consisting of the light of consciousness,
the formless path (*adhvāmūrti*) is described here in the Vedas, Āgamas, and Śāstras.
This has been stated by the venerable Brahmaśambhu:
"The *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*) is the head; peace (*śānti*) is the lotus-face;
knowledge (*vidyā*) is the expansive chest; and establishment (*pratiṣṭhā*) is the secret circle."
The path of the worlds consists of the knees and shanks as its cessation;
the body hairs, colors, and skin; the mantra, blood, and feet; and it is composed of flesh and veins.
The elements of the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*)—skin, bone, marrow, semen, and so forth—are Sadāśiva, who consists of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvā*). His abode is known as Śiva.
Thus it is stated in the *Svāyambhuva*.
Reality, the state, the mantra, the phoneme, the world, and the digit—
these are declared to be the paths because Śiva is all-pervasive.
Just as the path is conceived, so too is the reality of the Tathāgata pervasive.
In the *Vātulottara*, for what reason is the path of mantra said to be the body of the God?
One who possesses the power of the mind of grasping becomes deluded by the drops of [subtle] energy.
That which is devoid of thought is proclaimed as the Supreme;
it is the source of mantra, the Great Māyā, which revolves through the appropriation [of all things].
(From the *Kālottara*)

In that [reality] the mantra is born, and in that very place it dissolves. In the *Vātulottara*, it is proclaimed that for those presided over by Śakti, the path of mantras (*mantrādhvan*) is Śiva himself.
Mantras, when worshipped in the sacrifice to Śiva, bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
According to the sacred tradition (śruti), Śiva is the mantra for the sake of favoring the world;
that power which favors the elements has here attained the state of being mantra.
In that very [context], among the mantras, the fifth mantra situated therein will be explained in the aforementioned tantras. (7th line) The subsequent [section]. (–)
For the sake of one's own benefit, the body of five mantras is taught;
the glorious Sakala is recited [therein].
In Mataṅga,
the first is Īśāna, then Brahmā, which consists of Tatpuruṣa;
the third is called Aghora, and likewise that which consists of Vāmadeva.
The fifth is said to be "Sadya," which accomplishes all the goals of Brahman;
for these sciences and mantras abide as preeminent and are most excellent to bestow.
Īśānī, Pūraṇī, Hārdī, Vāmā, and Mūrti— thus [the power] is fivefold.
Presided over by these supreme powers of the Lord (Parameśāna),
so it is stated in the Pauṣkara.
Thus, these five mantras have Śiva as their body bound together by them;
yet in reality they are not distinct, because [Śiva] is not dependent on anything else.
In the northwest (–) (P12a, 1st line),
even Brahmā and the others are the causes of the creation, maintenance, and end of the worlds;
Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā are the deities of creation, maintenance, and end, respectively.

In the beginning, Śiva himself was declared to be the one who has attained his task; he is remembered as such. Then, by means of the nectar-like splendor of Śiva, the god of gods, there arose the power that bestows grace upon all, endowed with supreme strength.
This activity, which does not abide in the distinction between one and many by the will of Śiva, is to be known as threefold: Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī.
In the *Niśvāsottara*,
it is said: "Just as for many beings beginning with the practitioner and even for a king there are various distinctions of power (*śakti*),
so too is Śiva one alone, yet his power is manifold due to the diversity of effects."
Therefore, the power whose essence is Śiva, by the will of Śiva regarding enjoyment and liberation,
manifests as the form of power within the object of contemplation; for who can say that it is anything other than supreme consciousness itself?
And action arises from desire; listen to that [explanation] regarding knowledge, O Pārvatī, without [further] delay.
As far as knowledge, action, and will are concerned, therefore there is a triad of powers.
In the *Svāyambhuva*,
it is stated that when power (*śakti*) possesses these aforementioned qualities, its capacity for dharma is threefold.
The power of knowledge, the power of action, and the will—knowledge, action, and will are thus threefold.
This very will of all living beings is thus declared to be compassion;
through the power of knowledge it understands, and through its activity it acts upon the world. (From the *Parākhyatantra*)
The nature of the Self is consciousness, characterized by the qualities of vision and action;
even for that which abides in the form of knowledge, its essential nature consists of vision and action.

In the context of liberation, however, it is heard that [the Lord] has faces on all sides; yet, because that [state] is not manifest, it is perceived as being withdrawn [into the heart]. This is stated in the Pauṣkara.
"Only pure knowledge indeed, and that alone is established as Śiva.
In that very state,
when the knower remains with his active nature withdrawn—
For this reality is indeed the Ālaya, and that very reality is the Śiva-tattva.
In the Cintyaviśva [Tantra],
it is said that Śakti is indeed liberation for the sake of bestowing grace upon the conscious and the unconscious.
For the sake of the non-differentiation of the food and the beings, and for the sake of the fire-eaters.

Knowledge is the power of cognition (*jñāna-śakti*) and action is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*); all this [is] my... (9th line). That reality (*tattva*) called Sadāśiva may be both with parts (*sakala*) and without parts (*niṣkala*).

The predominance of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) and the diminution of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*)— that state of clarity therein is what is called "Lordship" (*īśvara*). [Even] for the purpose of seizing [something], it is grasped even by a thief.
This deed has been performed in sequence, and its results, such as pleasure and pain, are now being experienced.
Therefore, for the bound soul (paśu), at all times and in every respect, it is solely due to what was done previously that there arises—
in the state known as the "Other" (parākhye)—
destruction, pleasure, suffering, old age, and likewise death.
Thus has been declared this hexad, which is the definitive determination regarding the conception of the embryo.
Thus, having reached that very place where previously performed karma, knowledge, and death— which constitute the sixfold group— bring about happiness, one then enters the womb.
In the *Cintya*, it is said:
"Action performed by the body alone is likewise performed by the body;
therein [it is resolved]."
Even for those who have attained liberation, there is no destruction of the subtle body;
by means of the karma already set in motion (prārabdha-karma), the physical body is brought forth once again.
Elsewhere,
it is eternally joined with [it] in mutual dependence, like the seed of a banyan tree.
Likewise, in the Parākhya [Tantra]:
"Just as those who have attained perfection through the Self and so forth remain dependent upon their past actions,
this beginninglessness of the stream is uninterrupted in birth after birth."
Except for the seed from which the tree arises, and the seed that originates from the tree— herein lies the law regarding the birth in a previous life.
In some cases, O fair-faced one, it extends for a yojana behind regarding what is beneficial and what is harmful.
In the same way, if this [mind] were to exist previously, it would arise again in succession;
however, when considered, it is like grain that has been consumed and [the digestion] initiated, which does not [re-emerge] like a seed.
For in this very same way, living beings are born according to their past karma.
In that very state, without action, the activities of embodied beings are not possible;
for those activities consist of merit and demerit, arising as the sprouts of fruits in future births. (7th line)
This is indeed to be known as the precursor for one who is about to enter existence;
merit and demerit arise from the actions of mind, speech, and body.

When this has been said, one should know that which is joined by the command of the Creator for all beings abides in manifestation (*ābhoga*), and it is opposed to the two-fold fruit. Then the Person (*puruṣa*) sustains all these worlds and experiences joy.
That is called "dharma" by those who know it; "adharma" is its opposite.
In the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā (9th line):
Even the diversity of beginningless karma does not reside in the self nor is it of the nature of the self;
indeed, even karma must be brought about by the Lord.
O Lord, you who are supremely compassionate and auspicious contemplate great sufferings and evils; why then do you [behave] toward the bound souls (*paśu*) in such a way? Tell me that.
The answer is: This is the activity of the all-pervading Śiva, for it is His very compassion for Himself;
He effects both restraint and grace toward those whose natures are characterized by merit and demerit.
In the north-western direction, they say Śiva is the benefactor of all (*sarvānugrāhaka*).
[If] he restrains the gods (*devān*), how can he be the benefactor of all? (2nd line)
The old man, in the form of a Śarabha, violently tore apart the gods many times, including the five heads of Brahmā and even the man-lion form of Viṣṇu.
Having entered the state of differentiation (*vibhedapaktyām*) by means of the harsh [energies] of the heart, Śiva bestows grace upon all; he does not exercise any restraint whatsoever.
That which is called "restraint" is merely the cessation of those very [powers], due to their non-manifestation.
Furthermore, whatever punishments have been prescribed for Brahmā and the others, [they apply].
These [punishments] were also created by the form of Śrīkaṇṭha solely for the benefit of the world;
for in reality, the infliction of restraint upon the agent is indeed an act of compassion.
In this world, the child, the mother, and the father are like those who must be instructed.
In the presentation of all [these] views:
from the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites, an unprecedented merit (*apūrva*) is produced;
of that which has the form of a fruit such as heaven, the deity is indeed the deity. (5th line)
The proponents of the Mīmāṃsā of Action have thus declared their own defining characteristic:
[as stated] in the Kāmika,
that sacrificial rites and the like indeed bestow fruits upon living beings.
And the application of medicinal herbs and so forth achieves its result just as [the results of] visible [means do].
But apart from this, what is the purpose of their agency in the *Kāmika* [Tantra], which sets forth all philosophical systems?
Likewise, if that effect is seen— namely, what is stated regarding the fruit of sacrificial rites,
as well as what is stated regarding the subsequent purpose— the eater of oblations remains free from impurity.
O Sage, if one performs the act of giving material objects even without [physical] substances— as in the case of water, a vessel, or fire— then from that [act] comes the fruit.
It exists in this world and it exists in the next world;
right there,
having performed the action oneself and being conscious of it oneself, one experiences it according to that knowledge.
Does it perform coming and going upon the earth, in the hells, and in the heavens?
This has not been stated anywhere else here as being mutually [contradictory].
In that very place, everything here reaches destruction; yet the visible fruit would arise again.
O Great Lord, he is the one who applies the medicines and other remedies like a physician.
In the Kāmika [Tantra], the worlds arise from the body, its objects, and the instruments; from these, Time and Necessity come into being.
Furthermore, [the world] is characterized by the predominance of the power of action and the power of knowledge.
The arising of the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) exists as something accessible through cognition;
indeed, will, knowledge, and action are eternally established in Śiva.

Each performs its own specific function for the sake of bestowing grace upon all. In the *Kiraṇa*, it is said that because [the Lord] acts through the grace of His will, He possesses the authority over dissolution (*laya*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and sovereignty (*adhikāra*).
It is shown to be threefold according to the distinction of its functions and according to the distinction of its names.
In the *Mṛgendra*, the agent is held to be threefold: [the agent as] potential (*śakta*), the agent as striving (*udyukta*), and the agent as acting (*pravartamāna*).
The distinction between these is based on the differentiation of the effort directed toward that potential, though it is designated [as such] only figuratively.
In the Kālottara [Tantra]: Śiva, Śakti, Sādākhya, Īśvara, and immediately after that Śuddhavidyā— these five are proclaimed as the pure principles (śuddhatattva).
In Mataṅga,
it was previously stated that the "pure body" is the embodiment of eternal sovereignty;
there is no sequential process of expansion without the distinction between prior and posterior actions.
Just as the many forms of food and drink belong to Śiva alone who possesses a single form,
so too the existence of all things does not [arise] by way of its own inherent nature (*svabhāvataḥ*).
Nor is Śiva’s power anything other [than him], just as hardness is not other than the tree.
Just as a crystal or a sapphire [appears different] due to contact with gold, blue objects, and so forth.
Even Śiva is divided by Śakti; likewise, if it were inherent, then even the division of Śiva from Śakti would not abandon that very nature.
(From the Mataṅga-tantra)
In the process of manifestation, the powers are established; Śiva is the cause of those powers.
In this Pārameśvara Tantra, Śiva is declared to be without a cause.
Women, men, and the entire primordial universe consist of Śakti and Śiva;
likewise, the sequence of the Liṅgas and Pīṭhas is taught for the sake of bestowing grace upon all.
In the northwest is Śaṅkara and Puṣan; all women are Maheśvarī.
Therefore, all men and women are indeed the manifestations of those two alone.
In the *Suprabheda* (8th line): "Masculinity is marked by the *liṅga*, while femininity is indeed marked by the *yoni*.
The *liṅga* is said to consist of Īśa, and the *yoni* consists of Śakti."
Therefore, this entire world of moving and non-moving things is indeed Śiva-Śakti.
Śambhu has arisen in the Liṅga, and he is also known by the name Sadāśiva. Śakti has arisen in the Pīṭha, and she is also known by the name Manonmanī.
In the *Makuṭa*, the *Liṅga*, and the *Pīṭhikā*, [it is taught that] Śiva and Śakti arise together;
likewise in the *Mataṅga*.
Form does not belong to it, nor does formlessness and so forth; yet it performs its function.
There is no union with heat and the like, nor is there enjoyment; neither consciousness nor unconsciousness exists—therefore, it is Śiva.
For all [beings], this may indeed be so, even though they are not absorbed in that [state].
(Second line) In the *Śivajñānabodha*.
Another, though distinct, is not different [from Him]; as the agent according to his karma, he brings about the cycle of worldly existence for men by means of the combined command [of the Lord].
That which all living beings act upon through its mere presence,
and by whose existence all the scriptures are said to proceed— [that is the object of meditation]. (3rd line)
That which is the witness of all things—of pleasure and pain—in this world;
subtler than the subtle and greater than the great; that which is beyond the highest.
In that very context, [the question is:
since it is said in the Vedāntas that there is only one [Brahman], how can there be an injunction regarding Brahman? The answer is:
Among them, it is established from the perspective of ultimate reality that there is only one agent; as stated in the *Vātulottara*:
"Śiva resides within all living beings, just as the letter 'a' resides within all syllables."
Likewise, in the [text] called Śuddha,
the *kalā* is known as the individual soul (*jīva*), while the *sakala* is said to be the body.
Thus it is stated in the Kiraṇa.
Śiva alone is said to be the vital breath of all beings, both moving and unmoving.

Without him, [the phonemes] are like the letter 'A' among the imperishables (*akṣara*) even before [their manifestation]. Thus, the imperishables are [situated] in that which is called the Pure (*śuddha*).
That which is known as *kalājīva* is called the *vikalā*, and it is said to be the body;
both *kalā* and *vikalā* are traditionally understood as the embodied self (*dehī*) and the body (*deha*).
In the Parākhyatantra it is said: "The union of the body with the all-pervading Maheśvara occurs through karma;
because he is not [limited] by himself, he lacks the capacity for the application of karma. (7th line)
In the *Siddhāntasaṃgraha*, [it is said]:
"By others here, merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are called pleasure and pain;
by their very nature, one is happy or miserable, and for that reason, they are the cause."
In the Parākhyatantra it is said: "Is its nature as water, heat, skin, and smell anything other than that which is experienced by all?

One should know the partless within the partless, and likewise the part-possessing within the part-possessing.
In the crown, the part-possessing is declared to be the partless, and the partless is the part-possessing; now hear that from me.

In the Vātulottara:
"Therefore, by that sequence, one's own power (*svaśakti*) and the will of Śiva (*śivecchā*) likewise abide in a state of non-dependence (*avaśe*).

In the *Vātulottara*,
it is said that from Śiva alone arises Śakti, and from that, the arising of Śakti and Śiva;

In the [tantra] called Vātulaśuddha, for the sake of the emanation of all principles (*tattva*) and as the cause of the world's origin, [the Lord],

Within that Śiva, the Supreme Power (Parā-śakti) arises as a thousandth part;

From a thousandth part of that power arises the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
These indeed are proclaimed as the five powers that are partless (*niṣkala*).
This is declared to be the creation of Śiva; now the creation of the powers is described.
For the purpose of meditation and worship for all, it should be simple and partless.
In the tenth part of Parāśakti, indeed, arises Śivasādākhya;

According to the method of the Liṅga and the Pīṭha, the Karmasādākhya is described.
In the *Vātulottara*,
the Blessed One, the celibate practitioner (*brahmacārin*) [is described], and his power (*śakti*) is declared. By the wise man, this state is known through this sequence of names.

From that [state], there arises the impurity called "beginningless" (*anādi*) and karma;

In that regard,
if the soul (*ātman*), residing in one part of the body, were to undergo dissolution (*laya*) through that [part],
then it should be understood as being like a lamp's light; for it has been declared that [the soul] is situated in one place.
Just as the touch of a lamp burns the body, so too does the touch of [the fire of knowledge] burn [the self].
If everything were to occur simultaneously, and whatever [is perceived],
if the body were to be cut [and yet remain], and if [the self] were situated within the letters, how could there be sleep?
O Sage, if consciousness were to arise simultaneously with the sense faculties, then—
For even if one has awakened within the body alone, at the end of the body, one dissolves once and for all.
Abiding therein, one abides everywhere; like a pervasive space, one has transcended the states of coming and going.
O Kīrti, that knowledge has been described as being perceived individually by each of the senses;
when the expansion of the body is withdrawn, what then remains as the abiding Self?
In the *Svāyambhuva*, [it is said]:
"If there is no impurity in the person (*pums*), why were the powers (*śakti*) created for enjoyment?
O wise one, such enjoyment is possible only when the seat (*pīṭha*) is pure."
In the *Mṛgendra*, [it is said]: "That [power] which consists of vision and action always resides within the Supreme Self;
for it is heard that in liberation, He has faces everywhere and is omnipresent."
Because that too does not appear, it is offered as ceased;
for one whose power is obscured by the subjugated state, that very [offering] is [the cause of] liberation.
In the absence of bonds, what basis could there be for speaking of dependence?
If it were inherent, then the term "liberated" would be precluded even in the case of those who are liberated.
In the Parākhyatantra: How can the Supreme [Lord] lead that which is insentient and corporeal?
For its fruit resides in a different location, while [the Lord], being all-pervasive, is adorned by his lack of body.
Otherwise,

wherever there may be the manifestation (*vyañjana*)— that is, wherever his body may be— there it exists for the sake of experience; by this, its pervasiveness through the manifestation of qualities is understood.
In Mataṅga,
all whose powers were obstructed, impelled by the rays of Śiva’s sun,
cause the lotuses of individual souls to blossom within the expansive lake of Māyā. (4th line)
In the Pauṣkara [Tantra], it is said:
"At that time, the animal is obstructed by its state of animality, and the expansion of its vision and action [is likewise blocked].
In the Siddhātantra [it is said]: [—]
The Self, situated within the belly of Māyā, exists by its own nature as the consciousness of time and the other [categories]. This is the activity of the Knower (*jña*).
Due to the connection with the three *guṇas* and so forth, it is experienced even amidst worldly enjoyments.
Therein,
having existed as a bound soul within the subtle body, and subsequently endowed with the nature of the gross body,
he remains as an enjoyer of the fruits of his karma through states associated with waking and the other conditions.
In the *Kālottara*,
[it is said that] through union with the *puryaṣṭaka*, [the breath] bestows [the state] situated above and below; in the *Cintya* [Tantra], it is likewise stated.

Food, vital breath, mind, knowledge, and the fivefold blissful essence— O Goddess, food is the primordial constituent, and these exist in mutual subtle form. United with the Self, they are not the material cause of form, which is [rather] like an illusion.
Among those, he stands both within and without, formless like the five sheaths.
As it is stated in the *Sarvasiddhāntasaṃgraha*:
"Deluded by [the notion of] selfhood elsewhere within the five sheaths—
namely, the sheaths consisting of food (*anna*), vital breath (*prāṇa*), mind (*manas*), intellect (*vijñāna*), and bliss (*ānanda*)— one is led astray from that true Self."
And the sheath consisting of bliss; thus the five sheaths have been described.
The wise know that even when there is a modification of the mind, [the self] is not benefited;
indeed, the materialist grasps the self as consisting of food, [identifying it with] the body.
The wise know that the *prāṇamaya* [self], which has evolved within the body, has attained the state of being worthy [of realization].
The followers of the Buddha grasp the *vijñānamaya* self, and no other.
Some Vedic scholars have declared the *ānandamaya* self to be the [ultimate] self.
But one who maintains the doctrine of a self consisting of egoism generally says that [the self] is composed of mind.
In the Skanda [Purāṇa],
it is said that he effortlessly causes machines strung with threads to dance,
just as a skilled actor displays forms fashioned from leather.

Likewise, in that which is to be contemplated— some [being], like a leather-worker, performs a dance of forms, while another, fashioned from wood, pervades the chariot; then, like one possessing many forms, [he manifests] his manifold nature.
They say that the carpenter is like the self, and so too are the body and the senses;
[in this] section concerning the body and the senses, the knowledges have been forgotten even at the end.
Otherwise, their rising would be like that of a planet seizing an entire village.
Questions:
Otherwise, the body and the sense-faculties are perceived; [this] is to be reflected upon—[here follows] the answer.
Likewise, being free from the notion of the body as the self and from [the perception of] nails, hair, and so forth,
one should maintain the bearing of weapons there and not perform any action oneself.
From that, both the visible body and likewise the self are excluded.

In that case, O Lord of Devas, since the body and the self are distinct, how could the Vidyā be firm? And if that [Vidyā] is not like [the self], how could the Guru initiate [the disciple] according to the prescribed rule? (6th line)
The exhaustion of past karma is the agent; it is the conduct of all embodied beings.
In some cases, that which is called the mind is the intellect, and in other cases, that which is called the intellect is the mind.
In some places it is called *citta*, in some places the *jīva*; in some places it is known as wealth (*vittaka*), and in some places as the *jīva*.
In some places Śiva is proclaimed as the *ātman*, and in some places the *ātman* is said to be Śiva.
For all [beings], that which is called "awakened" is water; by the other, one contemplates the self.
Therein, how can the body and mind—which are for the sake of knowledge—be the self, since the self is conjoined with the non-self? (8th line)
Likewise, one should likewise contemplate that which resides within the lamp called the Great Light (mahāprakāśa).
The self exists as undivided, yet its state of division is entirely [imputed];
in the case of a profound distinction, there is the exhaustion of enjoyment; therefore, it is not seen therein during sleep, as it was while waking.
The self is awakened by awakening, or it is known as distinct from the body and entirely separate from everything else.
In that regard,
even though he is one who knows his own awakening, if the sense faculties and so forth are given away,
the self (*ātman*) is born obstructed by impurity; thus the self and the sense faculties become conjoined with ignorance.
Even though he is established in his true nature (*bhūta*), he should then perform the recitation of mantras and so forth like a king.
In that regard:
just as a king who circumambulates a village proceeds in order until finally [he reaches the end].
The Self, even when accompanied by Indra (and the other elements), likewise possesses five states;
thus it is stated in the *Śivajñānabodha*:
"Its five states consist of its own vision and action obstructed by impurity (*mala*)."
One should know that the waking state is in the mouth, while the dreaming state is within the heart.
Beginning from the heart and extending down to the navel is the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptika*).
Below that is the state of restraint (*niyatam*), and the subtle body (*liṅgaka*) is the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*).
It is joined with the thirty-five, twenty-five, three, two, and one established principles (*tattva*).
Thus, the very locus of waking and so forth is said here to be active.
The five [faculties] are indeed the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose;
and the five [objects] are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
Speech, feet, hands, anus, and the generative organ constitute the pentad;
their functions are speaking, grasping, locomotion, excretion, and sexual pleasure—this is the pentad of actions.
Prāṇa, apāna, udāna, vyāna, and samāna;
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya.

The mind, the intellect, the ego, the consciousness, and the knower of the field—these thirty-five function in the waking state; one should designate them as such. Sound and the rest, speech and the rest, the vital breaths and the rest, and the mind and the rest [are their respective domains].

These indeed move about in dream with illusory forms as if in the waking state; the experience of objects occurs in the waking state, while the appearance [of such experience] is just like in a dream. The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), through the mind and vital breaths, experiences deep sleep when devoid of the mind.
The fourth state, however, exists in that which transcends the fourth; it is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), devoid of all attributes.
The Self, which is situated between the eyebrows and awakened in the waking state,
is likewise to be known as this Person (puruṣa) in the forehead, established by the causes and so forth, in an inconceivable state throughout the universe.
The individual soul moves upward and downward together with the instruments of the waking state and the others.
Just as a ball of thread, when shaken, revolves incessantly,
so too do the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta).
Five states are to be known from the instruction of a true teacher;
one should contemplate them through the enumeration of the thirty-six principles during the waking state.

O Nandikeśvara, one should recollect the [result] born from the cognition of sound and so forth at that locus, the ear and so on; and one should meditate upon speech and so forth in the [locus of] speech and so on.
One should examine the twenty channels beginning with the *visaja* and the *dhamana*;

one should dismiss the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṅkāra*) there at the site of the *deśaka*. One should also dismiss passion (*rāga*), illusion (*māyā*), and limited agency (*kalā*) at the fourfold [site].
One should emit [the mantra] from the beginning of the purification of the Vidyā up to the end of the Kāla within that [mandala].
The supreme reality beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*) is that in which the mind undergoes dissolution;
and through the dissolution of the mind, O Cintyaviśve, you shall both attain supreme liberation simultaneously.
The states of waking and so forth are to be known as twofold, pertaining respectively to worldly existence and liberation.
Now, great liberation is said to reside in the place of the *svaṇu*, while the path of worldly existence is described [as follows].
The gross, the subtle, the very subtle, and likewise the extremely subtle, as well as the transcendent;
the gross is to be known as the waking state, while the subtle here is called the dreaming state.

Deep sleep is extremely subtle, while the fourth state (*turya*) is exceedingly subtle; that which is beyond it is the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*). Thus, [the practice] is traditionally held to be fivefold.
Through the gradual practice of yoga, it becomes manifest in the waking state.
The activity of the waking state is stilled by means of withdrawal (pratyāhāra).
Through *dhāraṇā* one should abandon the dream state; through *dhyāna* alone, the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*);
through *samādhi*, one should conquer the fourth state (*turya*); and the state beyond the fourth (*turyātīta*) is conquered by Śiva.
When it is perceived by Śiva, it is designated as the "Foremost of the All-Knowing.
One should demonstrate it in the waking state throughout the five states, beginning with waking.
By the grace of the True Guru’s instruction alone, it is accomplished.
One should cultivate practice through the yoga of knowledge and by way of the path of devotion.
In that very state,
having contemplated the auspicious reality— which transcends cognition, supreme, pure, with all limbs and facing in every direction—
one should thus meditate upon it within oneself.

Having meditated thus, the great yogi [attains] unbroken, great prosperity. Now, the self is to be known as existing in three states: bound with impurity, liberated again by initiation, and the pure one who is free from impurity; [the third is] the one with impurity.
In the *Svāyambhuva*, [it is said]:

"The Supreme (*para*) is insentient, all-pervading, eternal, devoid of qualities, inactive... [and] possesses the power of the portion of destruction; it is to be purified as the absolute (*kevala*)."
Likewise, in the *Kiraṇa*:
"The Lord is the eternal, formless knower, beyond purchase, and devoid of qualities.
In the *Svāyambhuva*: [same].
Then, from that [state], consciousness (caitanya), intensified by primordial matter (kalā), proceeds toward the objects of experience;
likewise, being colored by the qualities, it is joined with the instruments such as the intellect (buddhi).
Along the path of the self consisting of those elements, extending from the earth up to the realm of Māriṣa.
There, the man, whose sole delight is in enjoyment, partakes of stable pleasures.
In the realm of transmigratory existence, he is called the enjoyer, the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), and the embodied one (*śarīrin*);
thus, by the wise, he is termed the "entire" (*sakala*) bound self.
(*Suprabheda*)
Having entered eighty-four hundred thousand different wombs, the living self indeed remains there.
The state of being with parts (*sakalāvasthā*) has been explained; now hear from him about the state of purity (*śuddhāvasthā*).
As it is said in the *Kiraṇa*:
"When one is initiated by a Guru through the descent of the intense power (*tīvraśakti*)."
Just as Śiva is omniscient and entirely devoid of limited knowledge.
At that time, the transmigrating soul is no longer [merely] a possessor of the manifestation of Śiva-nature;
rather, as stated in the *Suprabheda*, this is called the state of purity (*śuddhāvasthā*), characterized by qualities such as omniscience and the rest.
The self, abiding in a state of purity, is remembered as being of the nature of Śiva.
Because the three states have been applied, rebirth no longer exists.
[The Fourth Sūtra is completed. (In the Śivajñānabodha...)
The senses perceive the objects of man, but not by themselves; even he [the soul] is awakened by Śambhu.
When Śiva is contemplated, He awakens the knowledge of all; what deficiency or excess could there be? (7th line)
The answer is:
Just as the steps of the sun proceed in sequence through its activity,
so it is in the case of Mataṅga.
All the hundred-fold channels, having ceased, are impelled by the rays of the auspicious sun;
they blossom like minute lotuses within the vast lake of illusion.
In the *Śivadharmottara* (8th line):
"Since he does not perform anything himself, but rather causes [everything] such as his own enjoyment to be done, he is a non-doer due to his lack of independence;
he is a 'doer of something' only like a puppet-master."

Nothing is to be felt; all that is known by him is the Person (puruṣa), who is like a beast. Because he is conditioned by the intellect (buddhi), he is called "one who knows something" due to his limited knowledge.
Thus it is stated in the Pauṣkara.
"O bulls among sages, since this ignorant living being is not its own master,
it too must be dependent for its own activity, like a jar or similar objects;
likewise in the case of breathing."
The self, though knowing only a little, is nevertheless the knower of everything; therefore, it is the awakener of that which is to be awakened.
From Śiva, the *kalā* comes into connection with that impure [self], as described in the *Kiraṇa*.
With his consciousness empowered by that [Prakṛti] and with the sphere of experience shown by Vidyā,

the bound soul (paśu) is further colored by Rāga; thus, through its connection with the manifold instruments beginning with the intellect (buddhi), which are essentially the constituents (guṇas) of Pradhāna, he is bound.
Thus, through the bond of necessity (*niyati*), one is constrained to what has been earned by oneself;

by time (*kāla*), and not deluded by the enjoyment of effects, [one experiences] the reckoning of time. In this way, bound by the categories of reality (*tattva-kalā*) and joined with a body, one is a possessor of limited knowledge (*kiñcij-jña*).
Embraced by the enjoyment of illusion, they are absorbed in that and veiled by the innate nature.

Then, by virtue of his own karma, he enjoys the entirety of experience, such as pleasure and so forth. In the *Niśvāsa*, it is said that the omniscient Śiva awakens the self from all sides; therefore, one should awaken the self as Śiva.
He is remembered as being the very form of the vital breath of all living beings, both moving and stationary.
In the Siddhatantra,
it is said that there is no connection between the insentient and the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), nor does [consciousness] arise with respect to an object for people;
rather, one should state that in the Vedas, [cognition] arises from awareness (*bodha*) in the very presence of the selves (*ātman*).
In that regard,
the entire world, the source, the body consisting of the limbs of Śiva,
the consciousness of the internal organ, and the fivefold duties are known.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"The one who eternally bestows upon me the fivefold acts—of him there is no doubt.
This alone is proclaimed as the supreme, divine Tāṇḍava."
In the Pauṣkara [Tantra],
the manifestation of the object occurs sequentially: first it consists of mere perception (*ālocanā*),
then it takes the form of doubt (*saṃdeha*), and after that, it consists of self-identification (*abhimāna*).
Subsequently, that which is of the nature of resolve is established in due order;
likewise, within the state called the "Equalization of the Thinkable," there is the birth and death of all souls.
Out of compassion, having perceived their affliction, Śambhu again acted in that manner.

O Nandikeśvara, having fashioned creation as before for the destruction of the bonds of karmas, may the Supreme Lord cause all those whose impurity is fully ripened to experience the entirety of their sufferings. (9th line) When the impurity is indeed fully matured, [the Supreme Lord acts] toward those who are ripe.
Assuming the form of the Teacher, he should certainly bestow [the fruit] through initiation.
In the *Niśvāsa*, [it is said]:
"In reality, there is only one stainless, supreme power belonging to Śiva;
she is inseparable from the Lord Śambhu, just as heat is inseparable from fire."
In that manner, the union of the Self and Śiva is for the sake of the awakening of Śiva.
Thus, in the Vātulottara:
"There is no Śakti without Śiva, nor is there a Śiva devoid of Śakti."
For, O Guha, by the power of Śiva, he dispels darkness like the sun.
[The fifth sūtra is completed.]
In the *Śivajñānabodha*:
