"If it were invisible, it would be non-existent; if it were a substance, it would be insentient. Therefore, the wise know that its form is to be known as distinct from Śambhu."
In the glorious Ajita, which is invisible, there is no mental cultivation; that which is devoid of the visible perishes.
How do yogins meditate upon Brahman, which is without color or sound?
Having made the heart pure and having contemplated the state free from affliction, one should perceive the supreme bliss, seeing: "I alone am all this."
Likewise, in the *Vātulottara*:
"Whether it be the knowable or the unknowable, or that which arises from the appropriate [state] together with the knowable;
or else, through the unknowable, one who abides by the commitment (*samaya*) is established in the pair."

In that regard, O Guha, even the creation, maintenance, and destruction seen in the fourfold manifestation of effects would be perceived through self-knowledge; otherwise, the world would be insentient.
In that regard, even the existence of those three worlds is the supreme abode of Brahmā and Viṣṇu;
it should be known as being like a mirage or a dream— real, yet devoid of purpose.
One who knows the nature of even the most trivial thing can dissolve it in an instant;
for through the power of the intellect, one can at will [perceive] the entire world, from the realm of Māyā down to the earth, as a mere magical illusion.
In that regard,
if [it is argued that] the object is indeed invisible and thus not purposeless—
[this is] the response.
Previously, knowledge was not seen, yet there was gain nonetheless;
by this aforementioned self-knowledge, both the existent and the non-existent have been rendered fruitless.
For the reality that transcends the movement of breath is remembered as the state of Śiva.
As stated in the *Vātulottara*:
"What purpose could there be for the Supreme Lord [if He were not so]? Nevertheless, [He exists] thus."
The supreme [state] possesses true enjoyment, transcends speech and mind, and is itself characterized by direct experience;
that alone is the enjoyment of Śiva, and that alone is the ultimate bliss.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Having abandoned all existence, one should always contemplate non-existence. Likewise in the *Niśvāsa*: [same].
Having relied upon existence within non-existence, and having rendered non-existence supportless,
one should make the mind abide in itself and not think of anything at all.
Relying on existence within non-existence, that which is to be manifested remains unhesitatingly dissolved;
there is no need for deliberation here regarding this inversion of the inner self.
How can there be existence for the partless Great Self, which is non-existence?
Even by means of non-mind, there is abiding; that is his state of nirvāṇa.
Therein,
one who is endowed with the contemplation of non-duality and is always established in the Self perceives that which is all-pervading and resides within all bodies; of this there is no doubt.
In Pauṣkara,
a person never attains liberation through his own power alone,
except by the grace of the god Śiva, the destroyer of the poison [of worldly existence]. (5th line)
Except through the vision of knowledge, the Supreme is to be reached, which is superior to both form and formlessness—
this is stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*.
By which it is known that, having known everything, one becomes Śiva.
(The sixth sūtra is completed.)
In the awakening of the knowledge of Śiva, it is not that the non-conscious and the conscious are absent in proximity to one another, nor are those two perceived as mutually distinct; rather,
he who perceives both the phenomenal world and Śiva is the Self, which is separate from them both.
One should perceive the auspicious phenomenal world, as well as the duality of what is to be known as existent and non-existent,
as being within oneself for the sake of attaining the Self, like a beautiful fragrance and flower within oneself.
One should transfer all one's own faults onto the Supreme Self,
even though the three categories of existence remain like the salt ocean.
In the *Kiraṇa* [Tantra] it is said: "Due to the connection with beginningless impurity (*anādimala*), the individual soul (*aṇu*) arises as one who knows only a little;
because he is liberated from that beginningless impurity, he is then all-knowing Śiva. (9th line)
In the northwest,
although this Śiva is himself engaged in the terrible ocean of saṃsāra from time immemorial,
he is traditionally known as the liberator from saṃsāra through his beneficial vehicle and other means.
[The seventh sūtra is completed.]
Having remained in the awakener of the knowledge of Śiva, together with the hunters that are the senses, he, being awakened, shall perceive you;
liberated from the bonds, that other fortunate one attains that state.
In the *Suprabheda*, it is stated that Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are born from the Pure [Source];
among them, the Ācāryas are to be recognized, and never those of other [castes].
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Who is a father equal to him who, with the hand of the knowledge of Śiva, lifts up a man submerged in the mire of saṃsāra?"

One who is joined with impurity and karma is called *sakala* (the conditioned). The support (*sādhārā*) of the *sakala* may be either with support (*sādhāra*) or without support (*nirādhārā*). Thus, initiation (*dīkṣā*) has been declared for these [categories].
By Śambhu, through his intense power, the teacher was rendered without oversight.
Whatever ritual action is performed is declared to be without a substratum;

yet, by assuming the form of the Guru, Śambhu performs it through a power (*śakti*) that varies in degrees such as mild, intense, and so forth. That initiation (*dīkṣā*) is the one that confers authority.
In the *Varuṇapaddhati*, it is stated:
"For those who have performed the [prescribed] rites, the initiation of grace (*anugrahadīkṣā*) from Śiva arises.
And that has been declared to be of many kinds; its detailed exposition is now being told."
The initiation of sight, the initiation of touch, the verbal initiation, the mental initiation,
the scriptural initiation, the initiation of yoga, the initiation of the *hautra* priest, and so forth are of many kinds.
The *hautrī* initiation of *Rajaḥ-kuṇḍavatī* is declared to be of two types in its entirety.
One [type of initiation] is known as "possessing knowledge" (*jñānavatī*), while the other is traditionally called "possessing action" (*kriyāvatī*).

The initiation possessing knowledge is said to arise from the correct awakening to reality, consisting merely of mental activity such as the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) and other rites for the sake of disciplining [the disciple].
But that [practice] which possesses sacrifice and fire, and arises from skill in ritual action—
Furthermore, that [initiation] is of many kinds, including the "with-ritual" (kriyāvatī) and the "seedless" (nirbījakā).
In the *Kālottara*, it is stated:
"The seedless initiation for children and others is devoid of the conduct of the observances (samayācāra)."
In the *Varuṇapaddhati*:

"Because of the authority over the *mātrās*, the *samayin* and then the *putraka* [receive] initiation; for the one without authority, it is indeed [only] occasional (*naimittika*), whereas for the one with authority, it is occasional."
In the *Viśvakārottara*,
it is stated that one who performs worship there is not entitled to the status of a *samayin*.
In the *Varuṇapaddhati*...
Now, the seedless initiation (*nirbījakā dīkṣā*) has been described; it is of two kinds:
one bestows liberation immediately, while the second [bestows it] upon the falling away of the body.
In the Siddhānta...
The web of karma—consisting of that which has begun to bear fruit (*prārabdha*), that which has been accumulated (*sañcita*), and that which is yet to come (*āgāmin*)—is purified;

for those who are utterly dispassionate, it bestows immediate liberation (*sadyo-nirvāṇa*). Just as she [the boat] carries one across while remaining within the realm of the *prārabdha* karma until liberation is attained.
Even fools and others likewise go [there], and it shall grant liberation according to one's own desire.
In the *Kiraṇa*,
it is said that upon the destruction of *prārabdha* karma, the body falls away of its own accord.
(4th line) [This is stated] in the *Kālottara*.
Those who possess the seed-mantras, who are empowered, and who are joined with the conduct of the observances (*samayācāra*),—
they, through effort, desire liberation and the attainment of supernatural powers (*siddhi*) by means of the *tetravālī* [mantra].
From the *Varuṇapaddhati*.
The initiation for both the *sādhaka* and the *ācārya* may also be "with seed" (*sabījā*).
In the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*, it is stated that there are three [types of] regular practice for the *ācārya*: the obligatory, the occasional, and the optional.
O Six-faced One, for the practitioner, there is the obligatory (*nitya*) and the optional (*kāmya*) rite as prescribed in one's own scripture.
Because of the qualification [to perform rites] everywhere, [the results apply] to both those with qualification and to those at the conclusion [of practice], according to the *Varuṇapaddhati*.
She is proclaimed for the practitioner through the consecration of the mantra to be accomplished;
through the consecration of all vidyās, she comes within the sphere of the ācārya.
[From the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*].

And initiation for nirvāṇa is twofold: that which follows worldly custom and that which follows the Śiva-dharma. That which is purified of mere unrighteousness is declared to be "worldly" (*lokadharmiṇī*). (From the *Vātula*)

For those who have been initiated according to the sequence of the guru’s instruction, there shall arise in due order the observance (*samaya*), the special [practice] (*viśeṣa*), liberation (*nirvāṇa*), and consecration (*abhiṣeka*). (From the *Varuṇapaddhati*, 9th line)
That initiation is considered by all to be effected either through ritual action or through power;
by means of initiation, the embodied soul is liberated from the threefold bondage of worldly existence.
Initiation by ritual action is for those who are awakened; initiation through knowledge is for the wise.
Through initiation through knowledge, one is liberated, with the release from the bonds of destruction occurring at its conclusion.
In the *Varuṇapaddhati*:
"And that initiation is the complete purification of the paths; and those paths are traditionally held to be sixfold.
Mantras, words, and phonemes pervade them here on all sides."
The castes are pervaded by the worlds; those worlds are pervaded by the principles (tattvas);
and those principles are here pervaded by the digits (kalās) in due order.
Having thus contemplated the path, and then having meditated upon the Supreme who pervades the six paths,
they shall reach the supreme state above that Śakti.
Upon cessation, the single royal reality consisting of the letter *kṣa* is to be contemplated;
there are one hundred and eight cities beginning with Kālāgni.
O Mahādeva, [this occurs] in reverse order from the final word up to the word "Mahādeva."
There are twenty-eight words pervading the sky, according to the supreme enumeration.
The two mantras Sadyojāta and Hṛdaya are proclaimed [as the first pair].
The qualities, beginning with smell and ending with sound, are the cause of the five Brahmans and the rest.
In the Pratiṣṭhā [kalā], twenty-three principles ending with Pratṛti are to be known from within one's own womb;
likewise, there are twenty-three syllables, starting from *bha* and ending with *ṭa*, in reverse order.
The fifty-six cities, beginning with Parameśa, are to be known.
The twenty-one words beginning with Maheśvara and ending with Arūpyānata constitute the head and the two mantras, Vāma and Śira; these four are known as the qualities.
From the sense objects such as taste up to the word itself, Viṣṇu is the cause here;
and within knowledge, there are seven principles in sequence, beginning with the Puruṣa.
The twenty-seven worlds, beginning with Vāma and ending with Dhyānahara, as well as those beginning with Vyāpin and others, are to be known.
The twenty words are established as the two mantras, Śikha and Ghora;
the seven letters beginning with *ña* and ending with *gha* are in reverse order.
Form, touch, and sound are the qualities, while Rudra is the cause.
In the state of Śānti, however, there are three principles: Vidyeśvara, Sadāśiva, and [Śiva].
The three Gakhakas, the two mantras, and the two Vāmatanucchadas;
the eighteen principal cities of the Left, by way of enumeration.

Beginning with "to the eternally united" (*nityayogine*) and ending with "to the all-pervading space" (*vyomavyāpine*), these eleven [names] have been stated here in reverse order. Furthermore, the quality (*guṇa*), touch (*sparśa*), sound (*śabda*), and the Lord of the two worlds (*dvīśvara*) are the cause.
But in the kalā beyond peace (śāntyatītā), the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) is established.
In this [system], there are fifteen puras, beginning with Nivṛtti;
the single-word mantra is "Oṃ"; and the three [deities] are Īśāna, Śiva, and Astra.
The sixteen phonemes, beginning with the Visarga and ending with the letter 'A', are proclaimed [to be these].
Sound possesses a single quality, while Sadāśiva is its cause;
when [the syllable] *cintye* is added, there are eleven mantras, which together constitute eighty-one words.
The syllables (*akṣara*) are fifty-one; the *kalās* are said to be two hundred and twenty-four, and indeed thirty-six *tattvas*, along with the group of five. Thus it is stated in the Mataṅga.
In this world, white and black karma are established;
all such actions as harming others constitute the black karma of those who perform deeds.
This [city] is proclaimed as white due to its ponds, wells, tanks, and so forth;
it is provided with two gates and is suitable for all living beings.
Having regard for the path of the Agniṣṭoma and other sacrifices as prescribed by Vedic injunctions.
Regarding this distinction between action and non-action, that which is white and black has indeed been explained.
These three types of action are not to be considered in this scripture concerning the arising of Śiva; rather,
action performed in a previous birth is purified through experience.
In this very life, once it has been attained, make it slack through knowledge.
Likewise, elsewhere it is said:
"Prārabdha [karma] perishes through experience; sañcita [karma] is destroyed by initiation;
and āgāmin [karma] is destroyed by meditation and worship—such is the certainty of the scripture. (8th line)
Born of yoga, the commitment (samaya) is of two kinds: gross and subtle;
it is inconceivable.
Lokāyata, then Bauddha, [Ārhata], and Mīmāṃsā;
Māyāvāda and Pāñcarātra—these six are the many systems (samayas).
Elsewhere [are mentioned]: Manu, Bṛhaspati, Dakṣa, Gautama, Yama, Aṅgiras,
the Lord of Yogins (Yājñavalkya), Pracetas, Śātātapa, and Parāśara.
Saṃvarta, Urvaśanas, and Likhita, as well as Atri,
Viṣṇu, Āpastaṃba, and Hārīta, were likewise the promulgators of the Dharmaśāstras.
In the *Suprabheda* (second line):

"The student (*brahmacārī*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the mendicant (*bhikṣuka*). The student is to be known as twofold: the temporary (*bhautika*) and likewise the lifelong (*naiṣṭhika*)."
In the *kūrma* [cakra], there is the indifferent (*udāsīna*) and the practitioner (*sādhaka*); the householder (*gṛhastha*) is of two kinds.
Dependent on the *kuśambhabharabhaṇa*, the *sāyaka* arises.
He who, having discharged the three debts and abandoned wife, wealth, and the like,
wanders alone and indifferent, is called an Udāsīna.

In the *Cintyaviśva*, the types of ascetics (*yatayaḥ*) are to be known as threefold: the practitioner of austerity (*tapasvin*), the scholar (*vidvas*), and likewise the one possessing realized knowledge (*vidvajjñānin*). These are declared to be threefold; their characteristics are now described.
Austerity such as the Cāndrāyaṇa and so forth,
as well as the sixty-four arts, the six duties,
all the treatises on Yoga, Vedānta, and Jyotiṣa— [all these are included] in the lineage.
Having understood the Sāṅkhya system and the path of the Siddhānta, the Teacher indeed spoke [as follows].
In the Śaiva Purāṇa:
the Brāhma, the Pādma, the Vaiṣṇava, the Śaiva, and likewise the Bhāgavata.
Then there will be the Nāradīya and, after that, the Mārkaṇḍeya.
The Āgneya, Brahmakaivarta, Laiṅga, and Varāha; the Skānda and Vāmana are proclaimed, as well as the Kaurma, Mātsya, and Gāruḍa.
And the Brahmāṇḍa— this is the meritorious sequence of the Purāṇas.
In the Suprabheda, the four Vedas— the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva— are proclaimed.
In the Devīkālottara,
ritual action and conduct are proclaimed for the purpose of generating knowledge; likewise in the Suprabheda.
Having acquired knowledge through yoga, one should always install the reality of knowledge;
for in the Śaiva tradition, liberation arises from knowledge alone, and not otherwise, even by means of ten million ritual acts.
O fair-faced one, liberation is described in various ways in the scriptures; otherwise, it would be manifold.
One shall obtain incomparable liberation from Śiva; this is now being stated by me.
In the Niśvāsa, regarding the Lokāyata school, the reality consists of the four elements.
Beyond the world of sugarcane, there is no other heaven nor any hell.
Worlds such as Śivaloka are imagined by other deceivers who are deluded;
for they falsely claim that the experience of heaven is like a sixteen-year-old maiden.
Fine garments, fragrances, and the enjoyment of red arsenic, sandalwood, and the like;
the experience of hell, and afflictions such as those caused by the Vedas, scriptures, and venomous serpents—these are [the fruits of karma].
Liberation, however, is death, the cessation of the vital breath known as *prāṇa*, and the withdrawal of the wind.
In the presentation of all these views: "Indeed, for these Vedic sentences, the deity is merely that which is beyond words;
some transcendental result (*apūrva*) is acquired through the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma."

The proponents of Karma-mīmāṃsā declare this as the defining characteristic of their own doctrine: that heaven and the like, being the nature of the fruit, are the primary [objects], but the deities are not.
In the *Mṛgendra*,
it is never shown that the form of a deity is like the bodies of those such as ourselves;
for this is not the case for one who possesses distinguished sovereignty.
Therefore, this jar [is non-eternal] because it is a word denoting something other [than its parts], like the word "Indra";
cognition is known as a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), even though it lacks both form and substance;
the meaning of the word "aggregate" (*samūha*) or "collection" (*skandha*) denotes that continuum.
In this context, the aggregate of consciousness is said to be precisely the continuum of cognition.
What is called the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is the continuity of the thread of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
It consists of cognitions whose nature is pleasure and pain, as well as those whose nature is equanimity (*upekṣā*).
What has been called the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha), that indeed is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha);
here, the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is the collection of the primary elements (bhūta).
(8th line) In the realm of thought,
the treatises and the observances are indeed mutually contradictory;
what liberation or gain is there in these, if you listen to the ultimate truth?
"O beloved, because the principle is the same, one person has said, 'This is not so.
However, when [the truth] is seen in some instance by all, this ultimate limit is established as supreme."
In the Vedas, Āgamas, and Śāstras, she is celebrated as the teacher of the Lord; likewise, in the Niśvāsa, [it says:
"She is the knower of Sāṃkhya, Purāṇa, Pāñcarātra, and Itihāsa."
And likewise, other yogins remained even within those situated in the wells.
Having deluded them with sophistry, they show their own bodies [as proof], saying:
"What other source of refuge could there be here?
[They argue that] the fault would lie in the movement of the wings, or else liberation would have to exist everywhere.
"O Lord, such is my doubt; tell me that which can be done."
In the *Śivadharmottara*,
this is an injunction (*vidhi*) belonging to Śiva, not a mere eulogy (*arthavāda*) concerning the nature of Śiva;
for it describes a thing exactly as it exists, according to its inherent qualities and defects.
And as for that merit and its fruit, the Omniscient One would speak of them;
[others], however, might speak falsely because they are seized by defects such as passion and ignorance.
If those [defects] do not exist in Īśvara, how could he speak otherwise—
that which has been cast away by Śiva, who is omniscient and free from all defects?
The scripture that has been proclaimed is stainless; it is authoritative, without a doubt. Therefore, the words of the Lord should be trusted by the wise. (From the *Makuṭa*)
This knowledge, consisting of the meaning of Vedānta, is the supreme and auspicious final doctrine;
it should be known as that which bestows the essential meaning of the Vedas and accomplishes all other noble purposes.

In the *Kāmika*, it is stated that because it is the essence of the Vedas, the Siddhānta is [the true path], whereas anything else is indeed external (*bahiṣṭha*). The conduct prescribed by the Siddhānta is called Vedic conduct.
Having assumed five faces, through those very five mouths,
the Lord brought forth the entire web of scriptures beginning with the Vedas.
(As stated in the Kāmika)
Therein, the mantra is divided into many kinds: the worldly, the Vedic, the spiritual (adhyātmika), and that which transcends the paths (atimārga).
The forms of Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Puruṣa, and Īśāna each possess five faces; by means of these, the worldly [rituals] and so forth are taught.
In the *Svāyambhuva*, Śiva-knowledge is proclaimed here through the various divisions of knowledge beginning with the Vedas;
like a wish-fulfilling gem, it stands here as the cause of everything. (9th line)
O Lord, that self-awareness which arises from the practice of the Dharma,
as well as the memory rooted therein, and likewise the cessation resulting from those two,
and similarly the state beyond [that]— [all these arise].
This fourfold [state] is liberation, and union (*sāyujya*) is the supreme among them.
In the *Kāmika*, Śiva is the creator of the path of servitude (*dāsamārga*), as well as the meditation, the linga, the image, the temple, and so forth.
O drummer, come and perform the dance, hymns, and songs for Śiva!
In the *Śivajñānabodhasaṃgraha*,
[it is said that one should be] concentrated in the temples of Maheśvara, which are the embodiments of His ritual action.
One should perform the sweeping slowly with a soft and fine broom.
The characteristics of that [mirror] are stated in the *Suprabheda*:
it should be polished with a network of woolen cloth to a measurement of twelve finger-breadths,
using the pith of coconut leaves combined with *bahula*.
At its base, there is a binding with a rope extending one *aratni* in length;
this is declared to be the twofold "sweeping" (*mārjanī*) regarding the rite of sweeping in the *Śivadharmottara*.

A cow that is weak from lack of food, one that has recently calved, one that is nursing, one that is exhausted, one afflicted by disease, or one that has just given birth— these should not be used for collecting cow dung intended for cooking ghee.
One should take cow dung situated on a clean spot, or that which has fallen in an auspicious place; it must be fresh, produced from a living cow, and free from anything above or below it.
He who performs the smearing [of the ground] with water filtered through a cloth,
and subsequently avoids [unworthy] company, shall obtain the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
(From the *Śivajñānabodhasaṃgraha*)
Having gathered flowers produced from the *rāma* plant for Śiva,
one who ties together the impurities (*mala*) and offers them to the Supreme Lord;
whoever performs this ritual procedure of the *rāma*-flower for Maheśa—
He who performs all acts such as hymns and songs follows the Dāsa path;
whereas in the Kāmika [Tantra], the Putra path is devoted to the worship of Śiva, recitation, and fire-offerings.
The Praveśaka, the Śivajñānin, and the Aupadeśika.
In the Vātula [Tantra], one should know Sadāśiva as the Mūrti, resembling pure crystal,
endowed with five faces and ten arms, possessing five mouths and [ten] eyes.
One should install Śambhu, endowed with his ten weapons and adorned with all ornaments, together with Unmanī, by means of the heart-mantra.

But when one understands all this, one should contemplate the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*); joined with the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), one should place it within the form. Having invoked Śiva above that, one attains Sadyojāta.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"But he who worships with devotion that which ends with the body—he is Śiva, the doer of all, self-controlled; he is called one liberated while living."
In the Kāmika [Tantra], it is stated: "One who has abandoned the path of worldly existence, who is pure and endowed with wisdom,
who is free from egoism, and who has undertaken the discipline of Śiva-yoga."
In the *Suprabheda*, it is stated: "Two finger-breadths above the anus and two finger-breadths below the penis—that is to be known as the *mūlādhāra*; thus it has been declared."
The support is said to be the quality; the self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna) is the linga.
The jewel (maṇi) is in the region of the navel, and the heart-lotus is thus described.
Purity is in the region of the ears, while the Command resides in the middle of the bow.
The support is said to be the seat, and that which is supported is Supreme Śiva.
O Supreme Goddess, listen to [the names] of the deities of the six supports (*ṣaḍādhāra*) and so forth on the crown:
Vighneśa, Bhairava, Kṣetrapāla, and Ṣaṇmukha.
Now hear concerning Svādhiṣṭhāna, whose presiding deity is Mūlādhāra;
it is the foundation in pure Gairika, within the path of the sages through meditative contemplation.
Seated upon a lotus, the Yoginī of the Lotus, she is the presiding deity of the Svādhiṣṭhāna;
she is the protector of the Kula, the one who has cast away the eyes [of worldly perception], the dweller on Kailāsa, and the one possessing the male form.
Upāṅgī, Uṣṇīṣā, Kaivāśinī, Triśaṅkarī, Tapanī, and Navanī are the deities of Maṇipūra.
This is declared to be Maṇipūra; now hear concerning Anāhata.
Kaśanī, Śātanī, Cāmuṇḍī, Virāṭī, Durgā, and Jyeṣṭhakā.
Araṇī and Svaraṇī are the deities presiding over the unstruck sound (anāhata);
this is declared to be the "unstruck" (anāhata). Now, listen to the description of Viśuddhi.
Sudandī, Ānandī, and Ājñā are the presiding deities;
this should be known as the six supports (ṣaḍādhāra) endowed with the presiding deities.
In the north-western direction (the ninth line),
through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one proceeds everywhere in the light of wisdom (*prajñāloka*);
that which appears as the mere object remains motionless, like curdled milk.
That which appears devoid of its own intrinsic nature is designated as *samādhi*.
[In the *Cintyaviśva*,] it is situated above the mandala of the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*) known as the *mūlādhāra*.
If they are the benefactors of all supports without exception...
Carrying the nectar of refined culture, she is the very embodiment of Śiva and Śakti;
she floods all places, bestowing both spiritual perfection and liberation.
Thus has Kuṇḍalinī been described, whose great arising is exceedingly pervasive. In the Kāmika [Tantra]:
"One who follows the true path, having abandoned worldly existence, and who is endowed with equanimity and purity..."

He has fulfilled his ascetic discipline through the yoga of Śiva by means of the thorough knowledge of the meaning of the *Tri-pāda*; he is a devotee of Śiva who regards all people as his sons and belongs to the lineage of the *Ācāryas*.
Thus...
That which is beneficial for those of pure soul and protects them from the ocean of existence is called "śāstra" because it is the vessel for that teaching (*tacchāsanasya*).
(Cintyaviśve)
The eternal, supreme state is bliss devoid of the fourth [state].
In the Skanda Purāṇa: For one engaged in concentration and meditation, samādhi certainly arises.

That state of equilibrium between these two— the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*)— is called *samādhi*, once all volitional thought (*saṃkalpa*) has been abandoned. When one has attained this *samādhi*, the self is free from all conceptualization.
In this manner, the object of knowledge, the knower, and knowledge itself— this very form— is dissolved;
as stated in the *Kāmika*, regarding the progressive excellence in each successive chapter.
In this context, excellence is also recognized as being established through the sequence beginning with the true path.
The path of the good, the path of the companion, and likewise the other, the path of the son;
among these four paths, each succeeding one is superior to the preceding when considered in reverse order.
In the *Śivadharmottara*, it is proclaimed that this fivefold sacrifice of knowledge (*jñānayajña*) consists of: study, teaching, exposition, listening, and reflection. (8th line)
The progressive superiority of all [the systems] has been proclaimed;
now, it exists through various distinctions such as worship, fire-rituals, and so forth.
That which is designated as the sacrifice of action (*karmayajña*) consists of austerities such as the *cāndrāyaṇa* and so forth;
and that which is declared to be the sacrifice of self-study (*svādhyāya*) is established in the recitation (*japa*) of the mantras known as those of Śiva.
The meditation sacrifice is defined as the repeated contemplation of Śiva.
Among the five sacrifices, the sacrifice of knowledge bestows liberation.
The sacrifice of austerity is ten times superior to the sacrifice of ritual action.
The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) should be known as being a hundred times superior to the sacrifice of austerity (tapoyajña).
Because he performed the *gomūga* sacrifice—which consists of meditation (*dhyāna*), internal [restraint], [the wheel of...
and the sacrificial rite—he was distinguished above all other sacrifices by innumerable great virtues;
therefore, he was pure and the bestower of the fruits of the five groups.
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"At the time of commencement, there is recitation; at the time of performance, there is contemplation;
through certainty, there is its realization; and at the time of completion, there is serenity."
In the *Cintyaviśvasādākhya*,
it is stated: "For as long as time as it takes for the knowledge of Śiva to become firm within him,
for that same duration, one must especially perform [the practices] such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth."
In the Śivadharmottara:
Knowledge that is full of conceptual constructions and defiled by passion and other afflictions is actually ignorance; it cannot serve the purpose of purification, just like turbid water. (5th line)
In that regard, he states the definition of knowledge and ignorance:
"When [the mind] is clear, one-pointed, and remains motionless like curdled milk, that is declared to be ignorance; ignorance is the dispeller of darkness."
Thus, that knowledge which is serene is the supreme state regarding all things;
it should be understood as being untainted by passion and the like, and as bestowing liberation.
When ignorance exists, there arise passion and the rest, and through their power, merit and demerit.
By the power of merit and demerit, a body is produced for persons;
since, when a body exists, one is joined with all its afflictions, therefore,
for the sake of removing those afflictions, one should desire [the absence of] a body once again.
Through the awakening to that world, ignorance is eliminated;
and with its destruction, one is no longer joined with a body.
Upon death, he shall go to the city of Śiva accompanied by twenty-one generations of his kin;
there he remains for a hundred times ten million divine kalpas, being served [by celestial beings].
At the end of that time, he shall dwell for that same duration in the world of Viṣṇu;
then, descending from the world of Viṣṇu, he reaches the abode of Brahmā and rejoices there.
For that duration of time, he enjoyed various subtle and unsurpassed pleasures,
in succession, within the worlds of Prajāpati, Indra, Gandharva, and Yakṣa.

Having exhausted various kinds of enjoyments on earth, he is born in due course, after a long time, among brahmins endowed with wisdom, virtuous conduct, and good qualities. Then, through his previously cultivated disposition, he attends upon a lord of yogins.
Through contact with him, having attained the knowledge of Śiva, he practices yoga.
One who is detached from yoga [and] from worldly existence attains the supreme state.
Regarding the preeminence of Dharma: vows, gifts, austerities, sacrifices, renunciation, pilgrimages, the stages of life, and the yoga of action—[all these are contained within it].
This is heavenly, auspicious, and unstable; yet through knowledge it becomes stable, peace-bestowing, and of great significance.
There may be sovereignty over one's own enjoyment; Śiva is the Lord of the entire universe.
In that regard, some say that there are men devoted to the yoga of knowledge.
Others, devoted to yoga, turn back again toward the funeral pyre;
therein, one should abandon attachment to enjoyments that have been severed from saṃsāra.
Being dispassionate, with a peaceful and pure self, one shall attain the knowledge of Śiva.
Whatever fruit has been acquired through acts such as giving and sacrifice during the exhalation (*niśvāsa*),
that too reaches complete exhaustion through his enjoyment.
From sacrifice comes the attainment of the fruit of heaven, but from its exhaustion, there is again a lack of progress;
for in other animalistic practices described in the *Suprabheda* and elsewhere, that fruit is indeed heaven alone.
For this indeed, within the Śiva scriptures, is the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having cast aside all other scriptures, one should apply oneself to the Śiva scriptures;
for therein, in the chapter on the ripening of fruits, [it is stated]:

Having enjoyed vast pleasures in the world of Śiva— which is now unattainable even for the gods and deities— when the dissolution of the universe has arrived, (*8th line*) [he shall attain liberation].
Having attained the yoga of knowledge, he is liberated right there;
for them, there is no return to the terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
They are all-knowing, all-pervading, pure, perfectly complete, and great lords.
The Siddhas, possessing strength equal to Śiva, have gone to the supreme city of Śiva.
Even a small gift given to one who knows the meaning of the Śiva-jñāna serves as the enjoyment for the giver until the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*).
In the *Mṛgendra*,
it is stated that the bliss found in the positions of Māyā, Kārya, Īśvara, and the Rudras is the lower [bliss];
one should know that the higher [bliss] is the state [found] in the levels beginning with Ananta.
In the *Dharmottara*, who can prevent your liberation from being manifold?
Therefore, in this context, liberation as a single entity is established by means of knowledge.
Through knowledge of the distinctions [of the elements], one attains that which is equal to them; there is no doubt in this regard. In the *Dharmottara*...
Because he is bound by the fetters of ignorance, the person is considered unliberated;
since liberation comes through knowledge, knowledge is therefore superior.
Ignorance is the bondage of saṃsāra; the person who does not know it is said to be transmigrating. Through knowledge, its cessation occurs, just as darkness ceases through light.
There is no knowledge higher than the knowledge of Śiva, nor is there any equal to it. O child, this knowledge is set forth in the *Suprabheda* for the purpose of destroying delusion.
The ladder of the paths leads to destruction and to the manifestation of Śiva.
Ignorance is said to be like darkness, while knowledge is said to be like a lamp;
the object of knowledge is declared to be like the sun; therefore, knowledge is preeminent.
(From the Sūta-saṃhitā)
One’s supreme power over the self is attained through knowledge alone, not through ritual action.
As stated in the Śaiva Purāṇa:
"Liberation arises from knowledge alone; it cannot be achieved otherwise, even by tens of millions of ritual acts. (7th line)
That knowledge of Śiva which is known through the grace of Śambhu and the grace of the Guru is not known otherwise; this is declared as the truth.
Just as a sun-crystal, when in proximity to the sun and impelled by its rays,
[releases fire], so too does knowledge, when in proximity to the Teacher, arise and become established within the self alone.
In the *Suprabheda*,
all principles and beings are seen as indeed the Self alone; this is to be contemplated.
He who is the witness of pleasures and pains in this world regarding all things— he who is subtler than the subtle, greater than the great, and higher than the highest.
In Pauṣkara,
when the mud of karma and impurity has been destroyed and the auxiliary conditions have ceased,
the power that unfolds, which consists of grace, descends.
As soon as she had fallen upon it, she became the regulator even of impurity.
When the power of the Great-Souled One has ceased, it ceases;
or else, the Supreme Lord purifies that person by means of his authority.
Just as [the power] which takes the form of grace acts as an obstruction to the course of [other] powers.
The power of impurity is destroyed; that is initiation, the ritual action of Śambhu.
In the *Kiraṇa*: "By the falling of intense power," and so forth. In the *Dharmottara*:
"He does not hear, nor does he smell, nor does he taste, nor does he see. (3rd line)
Nor does it perceive touch; the mind does not even form such a conceptualization.
He does not conceive of anything, nor does he perceive anything, remaining like a log of wood;
thus absorbed in the Lord, he is proclaimed to be established in samādhi.
(Suprabheda)
One who is liberated through the knowledge of the intrinsic nature of reality is indeed liberated while living;
he possesses equanimity toward pleasure and pain, and is the same toward the liked and the disliked.
O Goddess, in the Kālottara it is said:
"Toward friend and foe alike, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal—
in whatever state one may be, in that very state one should remember Śiva."
In that state, one should awaken the mind from sleep and again tolerate its distraction;
having abandoned both sides, one should move [the mind] only when it has attained [stability].
The mind that is always without support, devoid of all objects of perception,
and liberated from the states of the mental faculty— this should be known as the characteristic of liberation.
For in the ocean of consciousness— vast, profound, and stainless— the jewels of the Threefold Refuge likewise dissolve into their own self; indeed, the yogins of Śiva are blessed.
In the *Śivadharmottara*: "By the cord of dharma one goes upward; by the cord of sin one goes downward.
Having severed both with the sword of knowledge, one attains the peace that is bodiless."
He by whom the nectar-essence of knowledge has been tasted even once,
having abandoned all other activities, runs toward that alone.

For the yogin who is satisfied by the nectar of knowledge and has accomplished all that was to be done, there remains nothing whatsoever to be done; if there were anything left to be done, he would not be a knower of reality.
In all the three worlds, there is nothing whatsoever left for him to do;
even here, he would be liberated, for he possesses the vision of complete equality.
(Devīmata)
Just as a lamp is clearly seen from all sides when its jar has been broken,
so too does the Self shine everywhere and at all times upon the fall of the body.
In the Mataṅga [Tantra],
for the manifestation of knowledge, each principle (*tattva*) is clearly explained with respect to the individual soul (*aṇu*). In the Niśvāsa [Tantra]...
Endowed with immeasurable qualities, truly omniscient at all times,
the creator of all and lord of all worlds, he shines forth like Śiva.
In the Mataṅga [Tantra], it is said:
"When this [self] is manifested, it shines like Śiva; indeed, upon the dissolution of the body, it is Śiva himself.
(Śivadharmottara).
Omniscient, perfect, pure, all-pervading, and sovereign,
he becomes liberated from the ocean of worldly existence and is equal to Śiva.
In that very place,
at the end of the dissolution, having abandoned the body, he abides in his own self alone.
(From the *Sarvajñānottara*)
For him, there is no fruit of merit or demerit, especially regarding worldly conduct;
he has no fixed rule, nor any fasts or vows.
Both conceptualization and discursive thought— these are the family traits [of the ignorant],
which do not exist for children, the insane, and others who lack such differentiation.
Without the all-pervasive nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), there is no supreme liberation through these [means].
As stated in the venerable *Mataṅga*:
"By mere play, as the self is perfectly liberated while wandering about, by whom can it be restrained? (6th line)
In the *Sarvajñānottara*,
[it is said]: "Whether moving, standing, sleeping, waking, eating, or even drinking, those who possess the connection of direction, place, and birth, as well as caste and stage of life,"
At all times, during the performance of one's duties, in wind, cold, and heat,
in the occurrence of fear and poverty, and in states of dullness, fever, and the like.
While it appears, the wise person should abandon those [appearances] and contemplate non-existence.
Just as the wind, though extremely swift, does not go anywhere upon leaving the sky when exhaled. (8th line)
But one whose mind is cast upon the object of knowledge, while remaining within the sensory domain, is liberated.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"He who perceives me as all-pervading and everything as established within me... (9th line)
I am eternally established within him, and he is eternally established within me.
By the instruction of the true guru, through one's own self-luminosity,
[one realizes] that which is beyond the five states beginning with waking— namely, the state of consciousness within the universe of the conceivable (*cintyaviśva*).
It is being revealed through the instruction of the true guru; of this there is no doubt.
Having understood this, the wise one should especially practice meditative absorption (*samādhi*),
having established the mind in purity, which is indeed the very characteristic of Śiva. One should always practice the yoga of Śiva, which is the bliss that is the enjoyment of Śiva.
In the *Samayācārapaddhati* of the *Cintyaviśva*:
"The veil of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*) is thus; above that, however, it is unobstructed (*nirāvṛta*).
[Therein are] the Bindu, the Nāda, the Śakti, the Para, and the Parātpara."
The method for attaining Brahman and the bliss of the joy of the Self—
this very state, free from all veils, is remembered as the division of Śaivism.
(From the *Sarvajñānottara*)
In the state of barren wakefulness, one restrains all the senses;
endowed with the qualities of the fourth state (turya), it does not undergo the condition of being "burnt" (kṣāra).
In the same way, the knower is not defiled by the waters of the objects such as sound and the rest.
Purify the mind with that one [means]; what is the use of other external purifications?
In the *Suprabheda*,
it is stated that all [of this] is equal through pleasure and pain, as well as through the liked and the disliked;
indeed, it is experienced by oneself alone, like a wolf within its own body.
In the *Viṃśatikā* (Twenty Verses), regarding that which is to be contemplated (*cintya*), the characteristic of bliss (*ānandalakṣaṇa*) is explained:
"Form (*rūpa*) and the form of the cloth (*vasrarūpa*)—bliss is remembered as being threefold.
Form is manifold meditation (*dhyāna*), as well as color-form (*varṇarūpa*) and conceptualization (*kalpanā*). (7th line)
Form and formlessness are not considered to be bliss, nor are they devoid of conceptualization.
That which is eternal, yet devoid of the fourth state (turiya), is supreme bliss, the highest state.
Indeed, upon attaining this very state, there is liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Having understood this, the wise one should especially practice meditative concentration.
In the *Suprabheda*,
it is stated that although the nature of crystal exists within a crystal gem due to its association with dark blue and other colors,
one should diligently discard these [colors] and bring forth the pure crystal.
In the venerable *Raurava*:
"Having become Śiva within the divided body and being endowed with the Śiva-dharma,
one attains the bliss of Śiva and is rendered fit for manifestation."
Just as a river carrying its waters in a purified state, upon reaching the ocean, attains the state of salty water through the flow of the great sea; so it is here.
Thus, indeed, when the body has been dissolved, one attains the state of Śiva;
just as there is no longer any distinction between a river and the ocean once they have merged.
Regarding exhalation (*niśvāsa*), he provides an illustration: Just as fire, though pure and residing within wood, when stirred by friction,
enters again into the fire-drill (*araṇi*) once it has reached a state of complete stillness.
Just as that which has attained the state of clarified butter cannot become black water again,
so too, having realized perfect knowledge, one does not become a bound soul (paśu) ever again.
In that regard,
[the powers] are sung everywhere in Śivā solely on account of qualities such as omniscience,
according to the secret of the Siddhānta.
He is self-luminous consciousness, known as the embodiment of existence, consciousness, and bliss;
all those qualities which belong to Śiva, he possesses them in their entirety.

Those whose eyes have been illuminated by the rays of the Supreme Lord-Sun do not perceive Śambhu as they perceive with their physical eyes; rather, they know Him through the eye of Śiva. Just as milk poured into milk is undifferentiated, yet appears distinct to the sight of those with impaired vision.
The state of equilibrium between Śiva and the self is manifested through the balance of the qualities (guṇas).
He swiftly attains the peaceful state that has obtained the boon of knowledge;
then, indeed, there arises for him that which removes the miseries of *śiva*.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"As long as knowledge does not arise, one wanders through the power of karma;
for the embodied soul who observes the vow of ignorance is overwhelmed by suffering and grief. (7th line)
[The eighth sūtra is completed.]
In the *Śivajñānabodha*,
having abandoned the flickering ray of mental activity by beholding the Lord through the light of consciousness,
the wise one, having attained the shadow of the state of Śiva, should meditate upon the five-syllabled mantra.
In the Svāyambhuva [Tantra], liberation up to the end of the knowledge of the bonds (pāśa-jñāna) occurs, as does the knowledge of the bound soul (paśu-jñāna);
for liberation from everything is attained through the knowledge of the Lord (pati-jñāna).
Through the complete awakening to the reality of the world, ignorance is eliminated.
One should know that liberation is the five-syllable [mantra], and supreme increase is the six-syllable [mantra].
O fair-faced one, the various nets of scriptures are the knowledge of bonds that do not lead to liberation;
they are called the "knowledge of the bound" because they fall short of the sequence of instruction [leading to] the supreme state.
Likewise, in the exhalation (niśvāsa),
the Veda, Sāṃkhya, Buddhism, Jainism, Mukula,
and whatever other scriptures there may be— all have issued forth from the Bindu.
If liberation occurs for those born from eggs who are included therein through the destruction of the instruments [of perception],
then it indeed exists through inquiry, arising from the pain of knowledge.
That which exists through the state of non-perception is called *sāyujya* (union).
When [the cause]—
by means of the self alone and through knowledge itself— the body is understood from every side.
In that very extraction of mantras,
[he is] devoid of the expressed and the expresser, beyond the sphere of speech and mind;
endowed with qualities such as omniscience, the Lord is the abode of all principles.
Like space, the principles are all-pervading and stainless;
having abandoned the contemplation of space, one should contemplate the nature of Śiva.
In the Vāyavyasaṃhitā:
He sees the body, yet he does not see that very body;
some other person sees both of them, but they do not see him.
In the *Kālottara*, one should perceive the state of being a benefactor to Śiva; then one should perceive [the self] as having emerged.
In the *Śivadharmottara*... (6th line)
The Lord is pleased with that yogin who, possessing the sovereign powers of the qualities such as *aṇimā* and attaining omniscience,
renounces everything like a blade of grass.
Then, when the Lord of Devas is propitiated, the intellect proceeds from sattva;
endowed with the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest, that lord may renounce [the world] like Śiva.
(From the *Sarvajñānottara*)
Whether the attainment of qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest occurs or does not occur,
nevertheless, the embodied soul is liberated by realizing the stainless Lord—
[the Lord] who is the form of consciousness, free from all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and eternal.
Having realized "I am that Śiva," one should abandon all states of worldly existence.
Likewise, in the Vātula [Tantra]:
"Just as oil resides within sesame seeds and fragrance is inherent in flowers,
so does [the Self] abide within this body of a person, both externally and internally."
In the *Sarvajñānottara*, one should always meditate on the state devoid of [external] deities, thinking: "That which is Śiva is indeed myself.
Thus liberated from all fetters, there is the destruction of poison through the meditation on Garuḍa.
Through supreme meditation on the bliss of Śiva, he attains the highest goal.
This sequence, proclaimed in the Vedānta as "That thou art," is explained in the *Siddhāntasaṃbodhikā*:
having united [the self] with the nature of Śiva, the final determination is "I am Śiva."

"I am Śiva" is the established conclusion; in Vedānta, however, "I am He. Just as a pot, while conceiving itself to have arisen from the space within it, [is actually nothing but that space]. (3rd line)
Just as that jar is carried to the northeast, so too is the soul, which is like space.
Just as when a jar is broken, the space within it attains the nature of universal space, so too,
when the material body is dissolved, the self merges into the Supreme Self.
In this manner, through such metaphorical designation, the wise one should meditate upon the deity;
then, being completely liberated from all afflictions, he shall become composed of bliss.
Thus, the bliss of one's own self that has attained the bliss of Śiva is described here;
therein,
the impurity called *tirodhāna* is said to be of the nature of the power of the Self, which is essentially Śiva.
O Goddess, this five-syllabled mantra is a secret; it is not to be disclosed.

Having performed the placement [of mantras] from the thumb to the little finger and likewise for the six limbs of those two hands with the root mantra, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*). (6th line) [This is from] the *Raurava-mantraśuddhyavatāra*.
One should recite all mantras with neither fewer nor more syllables; for if there be a deficiency of syllables, death will occur, and if there be an excess, sorrow and disease will follow.
If the vowels are deficient, there will be misfortune; one should destroy it with that mantra.
In the *Kiraṇa*, worship is prescribed for the heart, and one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) at the navel.
Likewise, one should meditate upon the Lord Īśvara, the omnipresent Master, between the eyebrows.
In the *Suprabheda* (8th line): "The great channel named Kuṇḍalī is proclaimed to be situated below the navel;
it is eight-fold and circular, like a sleeping serpent."
Above the navel there is a lotus, known to be like a lotus in a pond;
situated in its center is the individual soul (jīva), possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns— thus it should be meditated upon.
In the presence of the Sun there, it should be like the sight of a king;
one should understand that the five-syllabled [mantra] is the vision of Śiva within oneself.
(Kāmika)
Alternatively, one should perform the mental sacrifice with devotion in detail,
[visualizing] one's own self as consisting of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Śiva and ending with the earth.
In the *Suprabheda*,
[it is said that] the bulb (*kanda*) consists of the egg of the earth (*pārthivāṇḍa*) and extends as far as water,
while the stalk (*nāla*) likewise extends as far as the principle of primordial matter (*pradhāna-tattva*), being joined with both the stalk and the bulb.
In the breath,
the heart of all embodied beings resembles a kadali flower;
it measures eight finger-breadths and is situated above the navel.
The lotus stalk has nine openings and is surrounded on all sides by thorns;
in its center stands an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.
The heart is one *vitasti* in measure, and the lotus is four *aṅgulas*.
In the *Kālottara*,
the supreme seed-syllable (*bīja*) is fifty [units], the source of the universe, higher than the highest.
It is equal in size to a thumb-joint and endowed with a pericarp and filaments.
In the Bhīmasaṃhitā:
"On the first [petal], on those eight petals, one should place the eight-syllable mantra in sequence from Indra to Īśāna, beginning with *oṃ śivāya namo namaḥ*."
In the exhalation (–), Viṣṇu resides in the pericarp; the knot is proclaimed to be Māyā.
In the pericarp there would be the Sun, and in its center is the Moon.
Within the moon there is fire, and within the fire is Maheśvara. Within his ray are the digits whose essence is mantra, and those mantras have Śiva as their essence.
Having fashioned for them a great white body for the pure path (śuddhādhvan), they [bestowed it].
In the *Niśvāsa*,
Sadāśiva is [the form] of Maheśa, and beyond even him is Śiva. In that very same [text]:
Above that is the Great-Souled Sadāśiva, higher than the highest,
stainless as the moon, the supreme Śiva who is beyond the reach of the senses.
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
Because it is characterized primarily by the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), it bestows liberation even for those who have fallen [from their practice].
At that time, that very ignorance is removed by knowledge alone, and not by ritual actions (*karman*).
In the *Suprabheda*,
it is proclaimed that the power of self-creation is conjoined with the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*).
In the *Vātula*—
Non-violence is the first flower; the restraint of the senses is a flower;
the flower of patience, the flower of compassion, and beyond that, the flower of knowledge.
The flower of austerity, the flower of truth, and the flower of intention—these are the eight flowers here; the flower is the very nature of Dharma.
[From] Mohaśūrottara.
"Agni is the breath, the mind, the vessel, filled with the crest of camphor incense"—
this and more is stated in the *Pūjāstava*.
Likewise:
And having thoroughly bathed that *liṅga* with nectar-like water,
[one should worship it] with detachment, sandalwood, the nine new flowers, and non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth.
He who is capable [of this] by means of the incense-rite arising from breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), by the offering of the lamp of consciousness,
by the oblation of the moon consisting of withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), and by the recitation pertaining to the *suṣumṇā* channel;
and by various concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) which serve as ornaments arising from pure meditation (*dhyāna*).
By offering even a tiny portion of that equality, the fortunate one worships him who is indeed the Fire itself.
In the *Suprabheda*,
the wise one should likewise imagine all the seats and so forth, as well as the enclosures, within the heart-lotus, exactly as described and in their proper sequence.
One should worship by mentally imagining offerings such as perfumes and the like;
in the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*,
mental worship is declared to be beyond the reach of Brahmā and the other gods.
In this case, however, since the external [rite] is not the primary element, one should therefore perform the internal sacrifice.
In the *Śivadharmottara*: Just as a mirror being constantly polished becomes stainless,
so too does the intellect of men become stainless through the practice of knowledge.
In the *Devīkālottara*:
"If worship is to be performed with flowers that have fallen of their own accord...
In the *Śivatantrarahasyasāra* (line 7):
When external worship of Śiva is not as stable as one's internal disposition,
then that [external] worship should be preceded by meditation, in accordance with one's meditative state.
Therefore, the external rite must always be performed preceded by the purification of the elements;
and one should personally perform the Vāruṇa rite once the latent impressions have matured, as stated in the Cintyaviśva.
The intellect consists of dharma and adharma, as do the karmas and their latent impressions (vāsanās).
There is no doubt that [evil] is destroyed simply by the worship of the Śivaliṅga.
To Parāśara,
Śiva appears as the Supreme Reality, accompanied by Ambā and possessing a body composed of Śakti.
One should, however, maintain the vision of Śiva toward all living beings everywhere.

Just as clarified butter pervades milk, and just as oil resides within sesame seeds, so too does the All-pervading Lord abide in the *Āgneya Purāṇa*— as the fragrance of oil and ghee exists in sesame, milk, and flowers.
Like fire within wood, that Śiva shines as the subtle essence, being identical with it.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Just as ghee exists within milk through the non-differentiation of its nature as knowledge,
so too is that Blessed One all-pervasive, immeasurable, and indeed incomparable."
In the Vātula,
it is said that the individual soul and Śiva merge together like a sacrificial fire.
In the Sarvajñānottara— (3rd line)
Thus, for that yogin who abides in a single self-nature and is free from conceptual construction, omniscience comes forth.
[The ninth sūtra is completed.]
In the awakening of the knowledge of Śiva,
he has attained oneness with Śiva; his own activity is dependent upon that [Śiva],
he is untouched by impurity (*mala*), *māyā*, and the rest, and he possesses his own direct experience.
In the *Devīkālottara*,
it is said that upon seeing such a man of knowledge, kings worship him;
yet through praise, blame, or commendation, one incurs merit or sin.
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Since the food is consumed by the yogi while meditating upon Śiva, that meal becomes as if eaten by Śiva himself directly. (6th line)
In the Kālottara [Tantra] it is said:
"Sufferings and pleasures arise and attend upon one as they have been accepted;
since he is the cause of them, he is afflicted by egoism."
In the *Kiraṇa*, it was stated that "the definition of the reason (*hetu*) has been explained"; now that which has been explained is being restated:
"Just as there is suffering when a domestic cock is eaten by a cat."
Such [power] is not found in a parrot, a sparrow, or a mouse;
as stated in the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Just as a great, blazing fire would burn even dry wood alone. (8th line)
In the same way, it instantly consumes the good and evil karma of those possessing knowledge.
In Mataṅga, the state consisting of the yogi and *lākṣā* exists as "mine" (*mamatva*) within the self;
it is the sprout of the seed known as ignorance (*avidyā*), the cause for the arising of *saṃsāra*. (9th line)
In the Śivadharmottara:
Therefore, the wise man who is capable, an ascetic with conquered senses,
and who strives to contemplate the true nature of the knowledge of Śiva— (P41a, 1st line).
Just as one playing is not smeared by fear, so too [the yogin] is not smeared by the five sense-faculties;
just as a lotus leaf is not smeared by water, even when it is touched by them.
One who knows reality is not defiled by the waters of objects such as sound;
having realized that this [world] is not a stain upon Śiva, the Supreme Self, through the compendium of the awakening of the knowledge of Śiva— (Śivajñānabodhasaṃgraha, 2nd line).
He who understands it as power (śakti) is therefore said to be purified.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*, it is said:
"The Self alone is established as the peaceful Self, satisfied and unwavering;
'I have not come, nor have I gone, nor shall I come, nor shall I go.'"
I have not existed, nor shall I exist, for my nature is established in the law of permanence;
yet actions are inherent in nature, and beings arise from the actions of nature.
The knower of reality, being disciplined, thinks, "I do nothing at all";
since there is no longer any obstruction, he is called "liberated."
The serpent is intent on bathing his fish-like body in air; the ram subsists on leaves;
the *cātaka* bird has no hope for water; yet the mouse does not enter this hole every day. (5th line)
The crane was indeed intent on smearing himself with ashes and devoted to the meditation on a donkey;
what fruit did that yield for them? Is austerity now primarily characterized by knowledge?
Therein, the Vedic scriptures and sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees do not exist; rather,
relying upon the stainless, all-pervading self-knowledge,
there is the absence of bondage for the Power whose nature is supreme consciousness.
Only the Supreme shines forth, showing no regard for liberated souls. Just as the burning power of fire is quickly neutralized by a mantra, so too [is the world-illusion suppressed].
In the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Just as poison that has been consumed is digested by the power of mantras and medicines, so too all karmas are digested in an instant by those possessed of knowledge. (8th line)
In the *Suprabheda*, it is said that when asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) is discarded, the fragrance in that vessel does not perish; [likewise],
through the experience of commenced karma (*prārabdhakarman*), one is purified by the fire of knowledge (*jñānavahni*).
Just as a potter’s wheel continues to spin even after the work is finished,
so too do all actions persist until their destruction at the end of the body.
Likewise, as it is said in the *Kiraṇa*:
"Just as when a jar has been produced,
the wheel continues to spin due to the perfection of prior momentum (*pūrvasaṃskāra*), so too does the body remain [in existence]."

Karma that was to manifest in many future states has been burnt away by subtle [flames], like a seed; even that which was yet to come is obstructed by him through whom this present body was begun. (The tenth Sūtra is completed.)
In the *Śivajñānabodha*,
it is stated that just as the Self is the one who causes the vision for the eyes, Śiva is the one who causes the vision for that [individual soul].
Therefore, one who seeks his own benefit should practice supreme devotion toward Him.
Untouched by impurity, māyā, and the rest, he possesses his own direct experience;
in the *Suprabheda*,
it is said that one who is freed from impurity is then called "pure" by the wise.
In time, through the remembrance of the Lord, one becomes stainless upon the destruction of impurities.
Therefore, having remembered the Lord, I subsequently attained identity with Him.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"He who is unaware is indeed a bound soul (*paśu*), for he is dependent upon the nature of emanation."
He who is known is eternal, pure, and auspicious; of this there is no doubt.
That which is born of yoga is the secret more secret than the secret; it is realized through one's own direct experience.
Thus, in the Sūta-saṃhitā:
If one perceives with firm conviction that the form consisting of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is [identical] to Śiva,
then the pure-souled one always performs the play of delight within his own self alone. Where people are perpetually asleep, there the seeker of union is ever awake.
O Keśava, where the wise are awakened, there the ignorant are in deep sleep.
In the *Śivadharmottara*: Knowledge that is full of conceptual construction and defiled by passion and other afflictions [is not true knowledge].
Knowledge that reveals Śiva is [true] knowledge; yoga therein is one-pointedness of mind.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*,
through the division of the higher and the lower, there is the division of the gross and the subtle;
the higher is supreme nirvāṇa, devoid of the creation of the other.
It is said to consist of gross power and to have subtle knowledge as its sole support;
thus has the knowledge of the Self been described in brief.
Or rather, O Six-faced One, by the speech uttered by Vāhuṇa— which is poorly expressed, characterized by various mental constructions, and causing delusion to the mind— (9th line).
One should conceive that all phenomena have the nature of the self;
it is born of yoga,
devoid of the signified and the signifier, and its sphere transcends speech and mind.
Śiva is declared to be pure, formless, imperishable, and the Lord.
In the state of contemplation,
that supreme state is devoid of the knower, the act of knowing, and the object of knowledge;
it is without differentiation.
O child, knowledge proceeds for the sake of destroying delusion,
for the destruction of the fetters of the paths, and for the manifestation of Śiva.
Ignorance is said to be like darkness, while knowledge is like a lamp;
the object of knowledge is declared to be like the sun; therefore, knowledge is preeminent. (From the *Mṛgendra*)
Neither through direct perception, nor through its inferential mark,
nor even through the word of Śaṅkara does that stainless knowledge shine forth at all times regarding all things.
In the *Cintya*,
it is stated that the exhaustion of karma is not possible for embodied beings because of the arising of the body; yet,
apart from the body, karma is never found to exist independently.
Although these two are eternally joined and exist in mutual dependence,
nevertheless, he again effects the destruction of karma through his body.
In that very place, the body of embodied beings is again commenced through merit and demerit,
just as one, having cast off worn-out garments, puts on a new garment.
In this way, having abandoned one body, one attains another;
thus do beings sink into the ocean of existence, burdened by merit and demerit.
Having boarded the ship of knowledge, living beings do not sink;
for in that state where all is conceivable, they perceive themselves as well as the impurity that is the cause of bondage and birth.

Liberation occurs through the destruction of the very latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of impurities; of this there is no doubt. In the *Suprabheda*, it is said that one who is liberated through the knowledge of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is indeed liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
He is called liberated while living; at the end of the body, he is said to be liberated.
Just as the potency associated with poison is restrained by mantras,
yet that poison is not thereby destroyed, so too is the destruction of the impurity of the person [not the destruction of the self].

The fruit of the *kataka* tree, when thrown into turbid water, effects the obstruction of its power; does it cast that power elsewhere from the water? In the same way, the knowledge of Śiva brings about the obstruction of his [the individual soul's] power.
In that regard, [an objection:
"From that, through the destruction of impurity (*mala*), there would also be the destruction of the person (*puruṣa*). The reply is:
Just as the redness of copper is not destroyed by its simultaneous presence with time, nor is that [time] destroyed,
so too would be the destruction of the impurity of the person (pums).
In the *Suprabheda*,
it is stated that one who is freed from impurities is certainly called "pure" with respect to the self;
[this is taught] in the *Raurava*.
Just as darkness quickly perishes upon the rising of the sun,
and just as the sprout of husks and chaff [is destroyed] by the great rays [of fire], so too is there the destruction of a person's impurity.
"How could that which is known as eternal and beginningless [be so] for Maheśvara? The answer:
"For him who possesses pure eyes, let there be no [beginning]; and likewise for one whose self is pure."
For those whose selves are bound [to it], there is never any destruction.
Furthermore, in that [system],
Śiva alone is said to be the life-force (*prāṇa*) of all beings, both moving and unmoving;
without him as the impeller, there would be no phonemes, just as there is no letter *a*.
In the Śivadharmottara:
One who lacks the eye of knowledge does not perceive Śaṅkara, who is peaceful and present everywhere, just as a blind man does not see the risen sun. (5th line)
O Mataṅga, just as every lotus becomes manifest through contact with the rays of the sun,
so too does his stainless power become manifest through contact with him.
That very [power] is said to be the bestowing of the Lord; it is not manifested by the individual soul (*paśu*) himself.
What is called "bestowing" is that [power] which, being inherent in oneself, consists of knowledge and action.
(From the *Niśvāsa*)
Just as the state of being gold remains latent within ore,
so too should the state of Śiva be known as latent within the individual soul (*pudgala*).
Just as copper, when processed with mercury, attains the state of gold,
so too does one attain the state of Śiva through union with the knowledge of the Self.
Just as base metals, when heated and touched by the contact of *kālikā*,
attain the state of gold through union with the fire of *hārītā*.
All yogins likewise attain equality through higher knowledge;
even those who have reached that state by means of the yoga of Śaiva practice become [equal] to the Lord of Beasts.
Having attained this supreme bliss that culminates in stability, they go to the highest state.
And they do not perform creation and so forth, because they are intent solely upon their own purpose;
thus, in the presentation of all doctrines,
Śiva alone is indeed the creator of the entire universe.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*, it is said:
"Having drunk the nectar of Śiva’s knowledge, he indeed wanders about by himself;
eternally pure like Śiva, he is devoid of the laws of emanation."
In the Śivadharmottara (2nd line),
having stated that [the soul] does not [remain] at the end of the dissolution, it remains within its own self; in the Raurava (–).
Upon the fall of the body, one attains the bliss of consciousness and becomes of the same essence as Śiva.
Therein,
although his nature is being and consciousness, he is distinguished by the state of agency [arising] from [the power of] knowledge.

Therefore, even a single [deity] is said to be worthy of worship, for he is the source of all benefits. In the *Mṛgendra*, it is taught that his sovereignty, consisting of vision and action, is preceded by the act of bestowing it.
He, the Lord, the Master endowed with two powers, is to be understood as being present here.
In the *Kiraṇa*,
the junction (*saṃdhi*) between that [deity] and Śiva is said to be like iron and copper;
[this is stated] in the *Vātula*.
The Puruṣa and Śiva merge together like salt and fire;
just as ancient copper ore, when freed from impurities, is perfected through smelting.
In that same way, when the self is dissolved into Śiva like salt in water, it becomes indistinguishable; so too does the self [merge] into the Supreme Self.
Thus has the nectar of Śiva been proclaimed; this must not be disclosed, O Guha.
[The eleventh sūtra is completed. (In the *Śivajñānabodha*)
Having attained liberation, they shall reach the abode of Śiva;
likewise,
those who are devoted even to the Teacher Mataṅga are also freed from suffering.
Even the celestial nymphs, with their minds uplifted, constantly sport there while observing their vows.
Furthermore, those men who with devotion and salutation worship the Liṅga of Maheśvara,
they too become perfected lords of the Gaṇas;
having attained the abode of Umāpati, they rejoice in various enjoyments.
When the auspicious installation of the Śiva-liṅga in the sanctuary had been completed with devotion, he—
Having attained the state of Śrīkaṇṭha, one obtains most wonderful happiness;
thus, for him, there is always devotion neither toward the division [of the scriptures] nor toward the *liṅga*.
Those perfected ones, the best of men, also worship Mahādeva;
those who desire Śiva should behold the devotees of Śiva at Mataṅga as if they were Śiva himself.
And the qualities were consecrated with auspicious mantras by the one whose form is Śiva.
All possess equal qualities; nevertheless, this rule is stated:
even among those who are equal in virtue, the mind of the elder sons alone [is to be honored].
Just as there is service according to seniority, as well as salutation and other such rites, so too is the sacrifice.
They performed their duties, rejoicing together, out of the teacher's sight.
In the *Cintyaviśva*, [it is taught] that the arising of knowledge of the true path occurs through the austerities of other people;
and in the *Mataṅga*... (4th line).
Due to the conjunction with the city-of-eight (*puryaṣṭaka*) in the person, according to their karma,
[they attain] Śiva— who is indeed eternal, constant, and whose nature consists of knowledge and bliss— as described in the *Kāmika*.
It is all-pervading among all principles, immeasurable, and incomparable.
One should specifically manifest that which is devoid of the signified and the signifier, beyond the sphere of speech and mind, partless within the whole.
In the Śaiva Purāṇa:
"That Brahman which is existence-consciousness-bliss, eternally perfect,
and is everywhere perceived as the object of the senses through that very [means]."
In the *Kālottara*, one should abandon the ordinary state and contemplate, "I am Śiva. In the *Niśvāsa* [it is said]: [...]
Śiva, residing within the body of the teacher, bestows grace;
he grants various supernatural powers and leads the bound soul to liberation.
One should protect the devotees of Śiva no differently than one’s own body.
In the *Aṃśumatī*,
it is said that the body is the *prasāda* and the embodied being (*dehin*) is remembered as the *liṅga*.
There is no difference between the two; therefore, one should cultivate this realization in such a manner.
Alternatively, in another manner, the best of divine disciples should contemplate Sadāśiva in the external linga and Śiva in the internal linga; thus,
through the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader, the linga itself is the temple.
The golden [image] up to the pinnacle is traditionally held to be the form of Śiva;
thus the Lord is worshipped within all limbs and bodies.
Or else, the Blessed Lord Śiva should be worshipped in a linga or in another auspicious place.
Invocation is meditation, which is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind;
through union with Śiva, one should contemplate with the mind and the intellect.
Thus it is stated in the Parākhya [Tantra].
The peaceful one is worshipped by those seeking the fruits of supernatural powers and liberation;
that very same Supreme Śiva, residing within the body of mantra, is worshipped.
Just as fire residing within wood is manifested through friction and other means,
so too is Śiva manifested through the power of mantra and through devotion.
Just as the milk flows from all the limbs of a cow, so this form consisting of the *liṅga* ascends toward all desired objects. (4th line) In the *Kiraṇa*.
O Lord, by Your grace, let those who are established here in whatever way they may be—
some of whom are fit for ritual action— be so indeed for the sake of the devotee.
Some are fit for knowledge (*jñāna-yogya*), while others are likewise fit for conduct (*caryā-yogya*);
thus, one should unite them with liberation according to what is appropriate for each.
The state of Sadāśiva is attained through yoga, or through ritual conduct, or through initiation;
it is reached by means of the fourfold methods for attaining liberation, according to the distinctions of the mind.
Likewise, in the northwest,
O Sovereign of the Gods, knowledge, action, conduct,
and yoga are proclaimed as the fourfold eternal Dharma and Adharma.

The knowledge of the Lord of Creatures (Paśu), the fetters (Pāśa), and the Lord (Patī) is designated as "knowledge" (jñāna). Performing the purification of the six paths (ṣaḍadhva) according to the prescribed rule is called "action" (kriyā).
By means of the very path described by me, one who has established the mind upon Me and restrained all other mental modifications— this is proclaimed as Yoga.
In the *Kālottara*, O Six-faced One, eternal knowledge is obtained through the mouth of the Guru—
[namely] restraint (*yama*), observance (*niyama*), posture (*āsana*), and likewise breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). (9th line)
Withdrawal, concentration, meditative absorption, and meditation—
O Six-faced One, one obtains this divine yoga through the grace of the Guru.

The attainment of various forms, as well as entering the body of another, and indeed becoming a mind-born being— all this is obtained by a person through the grace of the Guru. So too are the powers of atomization (*aṇimā*), levitation (*laghimā*), magnification (*mahimā*), and heaviness (*garimā*).
The eight siddhis— attainment (*prāpti*), the power of irresistible will (*prākāmya*), sovereignty (*īśitva*), and mastery (*vaśitva*)—
he obtains through the grace of the Guru, [becoming] free from death and old age.
In the *Viśvasārottara*:
The Supreme Brahman is the form of the Guru; the Supreme Śiva is the form of the Guru;
supreme knowledge is the form of the Guru; that which is higher than the highest is the form of the Guru. (3rd line)
Therefore, with every effort, one should always remember the form of the Guru.
Likewise, by means of seeing, meditating upon, and touching [the Guru], [devotees become] like fish, tortoises, and birds.
They nourish their own sons; in that same way, those whose conduct is wise [act].
O fair-faced one, reveal this knowledge to my devotees when you are exhaling.
It must be guarded with great effort, just as wealth is protected from thieves.
As stated in the *Devīkālottara*:
"One should not give such a true essence of knowledge to just anyone."
Having initiated the Great Goddess, [the gift] should be given after careful examination.
In the Kālottara,
it is stated that this [teaching] should never be given to a mere disciple nor even to a son; rather,
it should be given to one who is devoted to the Guru, the Deity, and the Fire, and who is free from envy.
This knowledge should be bestowed; one should not cause it to be given to others. [The twelfth sūtra is completed.]
[The Śivajñānasiddhi treatise is completed.]
Salutation to the two lotus feet of Śiva and Śivā.
(P45a, 1st line) (P45b(śrīsarasvatībhyāṃ namaḥ| samānasandhi|),
1st line) Homage to the illustrious Dakṣiṇāmūrti!
