[An explanation of the *samānasandhi* (vowel coalescence), not of the *vyakti* (manifestation) nor of that which has *t* as its following limit (*tapara*), is being composed by Mallāyārya under the title *Padadarpaṇa*.]

In this regard, first of all, for the sake of completion through the continuous practice inherited from the tradition of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), preceded by auspicious conduct (*maṅgalācāra*), and following the sequence of the phonemes beginning with *a*, I shall here characterize the words according to their order: those words whose *visarga* is elided at the time of *saṃhitā*, those words ending in *e* or *ai*, and those words ending in *t*.
First, the words containing *visarga* will be treated by means of the treatise known as *Samānasandhi*.

He promises to define [the cases]: "Now" (*atha*). Now, we shall explain those words in the *Yajurveda-saṃhitā* in which the *visarjanīya* is elided when it is preceded by a protracted *ā*-vowel (*ākāra-pluta-pūrva*), followed by a voiced consonant (*ghoṣavat-vyañjana-uttara*), and further followed by the letter *śa* (*sakāra-para*). Here, this word *atha* is for the purpose of auspicious invocation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*). Thus it has been said by the followers of the *Śikṣā*: "The syllable *oṃ* and the word *atha*—these two emerged from the throat of Brahmā in the beginning; therefore, both are auspicious. "Preceded by a protracted *ā*-vowel" means: the *ā*-vowel and the protracted [vowel].

The two [consonants] followed by the protracted vowel *ā* are so described because they precede it. They are followed by a voiced consonant (*ghoṣavat*) and the letter *s*. Those which have consonants following them are "consonant-final" (*vyañjanottarau*).

That *ś* and that *k* are "followed by *ś* and *k*" (*saśakāraparau*), and they are also "consonant-final" (*vyañjanottarau*); thus they are so described. Being both voiced (*ghoṣavant*) and followed by *ś* and *k*, they are "voiced-consonant-and-ś-k-followed" (*ghoṣavadvyañjana-saśakārapara*).

[Those words] followed by *t*, *tara*, *sa*, or *śa*; that which has these [sounds] as subsequent is so described—meaning either after an *ā* or a protracted (*pluta*) vowel, or after voiced consonants (*ghoṣavat*), or after a consonant followed by *śa*, or before a *śa*. In such cases, the *visarjanīya* is elided in those words within the Yajurvedic *saṃhitā*; it is not perceived. Those words we shall explain in detail. [End of second line] Provide your translation in English:

We shall explain [this]. In the phrase "in the Yajurveda-saṃhitā," the term *yajus* is employed for the purpose of excluding the *ṛc* and other [Vedic meters]. By the word *saṃhitā*, the Saṃhitā belonging to the Taittirīya branch is understood. Furthermore, by the word *saṃhitā* alone, the *Ākarṣa-saṃhitā* is also included. Otherwise, [the following forms would not be accounted for]: *viṣvak-ulkā* and *ulkā viṣvak* become *viṣvagulkāḥ*; *bṛhat-bhā* and *bhā bṛhat* become *bṛhadbhāḥ*; *varcasā gadhā* and *agadhā varcasā* become *varcasāgadhāḥ*. In the case of *yonau*... [etc.]

*mahiṣā mahiṣā yaunau yonau mahiṣāḥ |* *mahiṣā ahinvannahilvanmahiṣā mahiṣā ahinvan |* *me tanu vātastanu vāme me tanu vāḥ |* *suvo ruhāṇā ruhāṇāḥ suvaḥ suvoruhāṇāḥ |* In such passages from the *Pauruṣa-saṃhitā*, because of the subsequent presence of sonant consonants (*ghoṣavat*), there would be a subsequent application [of the rule]. And not [so] in *tthāsthi*. Therefore, by the word "saṃhitā," the forms within the *ākara-saṃhitās* are intended. Now, what is a protracted vowel (*pluta*)? They would say: "It consists of three morae (*trimātra*). Thus it has been stated by the authors of the *Śikṣās*: "One mora... [and so on].

A short vowel is said to have two mātrās, a long one is said to have three, and a protracted (*pluta*) one should be known as having four; a consonant, however, has half a mātrā. An example is: *vicityāḥ somā na vicityā* (the eighth line), and so forth; the syllable (*akṣara*) is indeed well-known. Furthermore, among the five groups beginning with *ka*, the voiced consonants are the third, fourth, and fifth [of each group], as well as *ya, ra, la, va, ha,* and *ha*.

Thus, we say that these vowels are designated as "voiced" (*ghoṣa*). The remainder of the consonants (*vyañjana*) are "possessing voice. We call those consonants the phonemes distinct from the vowels. As it has been said: "...the consonants. And likewise it is said: "The *hal* [consonants] are the consonants. But what is the *visarjanīya*? It is remembered as the *visarga* being like a horn, like the pair of breasts of a young girl, and like the eye of a black serpent.

Regarding the phrase "preceded by a long vowel (ākāra-pluta-pūrva)": what is an example? *bhrarathadhvajan*, *amutrabhrayād atha yadyamasya*, *bhrātravyamasya yajñasya*, *adhā asmerā asyā anāgāḥ*. This is because [the rule] to be stated hereafter would otherwise apply. Regarding the phrase "followed by a consonant with the letter *s* (vyañjanottara-sakāra)": what is an example? *ūrdhvā śukrā śocīṃṣi*, *pṛthivyā saṃbhava*, *śaptyāḥ śuddhāḥ śukrāḥ*, *pṛthivyā naiva*. This is because [the rule] to be stated hereafter would otherwise apply. [The rule applies when followed by] a sonant consonant (*ghoṣivat-vyañjana*).

Why should "having a *sa* or *śa* as a subsequent sound" not be considered a single definition? Do not say so; for it would lead to the absurdity of [the terms] *aghnīyāḥ* and *ayakṣmāḥ* being redundant, since those [words] lack the property of having a *sa* or *śa* as a subsequent sound following a sonant consonant (*ghoṣavad-vyañjana*). However, by means of *tantra* (simultaneous application), there will be both "having a sonant as a subsequent sound" and "having a *sa* or *śa* as a subsequent sound following a sonant consonant. This is because in the rule *halantyam*, one says *hal-hal-antyam*.

If you say this, it is not so; for there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of the definition in cases such as *iḍāsthamadhukṛtaḥ* and *yāstrayaḥ samanasaḥ*, because those [words] do not have a *sa* or *śa* following a consonant that is itself preceded by a sonant (*ghoṣavat*) consonant. Therefore, it should be explained as: "followed by a sonant" and "followed by a *sa* or *śa* that follows a consonant. In this definition, where there is no counting of multiple words within a single compound word (*iṅgyapada*), there is no plurality of words (*nānāpada*) among the *iṅgyapadas*. In this definition, among the *iṅgyapadas*... [there is no plurality of words].

You [assert that] *nānāpadānām bhāvaḥ* is the state of being multiple words (*nānāpadatvam*), which brings about the reality of distinct words (*bhinnapadatattvam*). Why [is it said] "the state of being multiple words in the domain of non-enumeration" (*asaṃkhyānaviṣaye nānāpadatvam*)? Because in cases such as *atiriktā vā eṣā sahasrasya*, since the definition applies—that "an excess (*atiriktā*) is not faulty"—it was not so [in the case of the *nānāpada*]. Why "in the domain of non-enumeration"? He will say later: "not from this" (*naitasmāt*). [This is illustrated by examples where] the definition does apply, such as *prajā vā uttarā devayajyā paśavaḥ*.

We say [it is] for that purpose. Of those, the preceding word is the *avagraha*. For those *iṅgya* words, the preceding word is designated as the *avagraha*; this is stated in the singular number with reference to the genus (*jāti*). The purpose of the technical term *avagraha* [is as follows]: he will state later that the *avagraha* and the prefix (*upasarga*) [are treated similarly]. Because the *pada* and the *avagraha* possess fixed genders, their mutual connection is possible. Thus it has been said: "In the enumeration of various *iṅgya* words, its [the *iṅgya*'] preceding... (3rd line).

"Regarding the rule *padam avagrahaḥ*: examine that treatise by which you previously asserted that words with elided visargas are to be identified by means of a specific connection. [The examples are: *ahi(hī)yāḥ*, *ayakṣmāḥ*, *agrāḥ*, *aprāḥ*, *asurāḥ*, *apraṇāḥ*, *ajāyadhāḥ* (4th line), *aśvāḥ*;
*ahṛṇīyyamānāḥ*, *athāḥ*, *asmerāḥ*, *aniṣṭhāḥ*, *anāḥ*, *agrahītāḥ*, *adhvantavyāḥ*, *akāmāḥ*, *akliptāḥ*, *apuṣpāḥ*, *asyāḥ*, *anāgāḥ*, *etyamedhyāḥ*, *atiriktāḥ* (5th line)."

Of this *apasyā*, the *asapannāḥ*, *anvakāḥ*, *ajaniṣṭhāḥ*, *ahatāḥ*, *avocadhāḥ*, *antamāḥ*, *atiṣṭhipāḥ*, *anabhyaktāḥ*, *anhiyāḥ*, *bastena*, *ajāḥ*, *anīkāḥ*, and *ardhāḥ*—in these words, at the time of word-division (*padakāla*), a *visarjanīya* that is followed by a voiced consonant (*saghoṣavat*) or by a *śa* or *sa* followed by a consonant (*vyañjanottara-saśakāra-paro*), is elided at the time of continuous recitation (*saṃhitākāla*). For example: (*asnigdhā*).

The portion of the gods; may you, whose eyelashes are not [closed], protect us. A prayer with a bright beginning, a prayer—may it reach heaven and earth. Those Soma-libations which belong to the gods; reaching both worlds, being born without a rival.

Obeisance to the vigor of those who are showerers of rain. O gods, you are the sacrificer, the sacrificial strew. Thus, those who are being led away as the food of the voracious ones. "Enough," thus [it is said] regarding Viṣṇu. Toward him, the young maidens look with smiling faces. Or indeed, that which is unoffered to the gods.

(…) | The vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are indeed the kinsmen; it is the vital breaths that these [grains] have grasped. The *droṇakalaśa* vessel is the Adhvaryu’s path; these gods are well-disposed toward you.

May their desire be for this [kingdom] whose sovereignty is unimpaired. And from those that are flowerless, [may they obtain] the flowering ones. The wild beast is within his mouth. Through the sinlessness of Aditi, may there be no transgressions. He desires this; beans are indeed impure. This is the one who has gone away. (2nd line)

[They] diminish the pairs [of enemies]. Whatever of that [world] is worthy of sacrifice—[it is] the thunderbolt, for water is indeed the thunderbolt; by means of the thunderbolt itself [he acts]. These are the bricks of those who have no rivals. With the *śarotaka* and the branch of the *vetasa* tree, he drives away [the enemy].

"May you stand firm; may we live long, free from injury. Indeed, in a difficult place, [he is] the slayer; do not deliver us to the end. You have established the sacrifice. The plants do not cry out against one another. Against what [do they cry]? Against honey.

[The words] *samiktā*, *viśvaiḥ*, *tiro*, *ahiyāmāsu*, and *hutāḥ* [are examples]. [The word] *bastena* [is used before] *ajā* and *vṛṣṇinā*; [the word] *avīḥ* [is used before] *bastena*. Why [mention] *bastena*? [Because it occurs] in *yad ajā vaśā*. These nights are indeed two-fold (*dvyanikā*); they possess half-wool (*ardhāvayāvatīḥ*). (5th line) Others say that [the rule applies] when *vadantīm* is followed by *saṃyatanāḥ*; others say [it applies] when *saṃyatanāḥ* follows *vadantīm*. Thus, in this context of the preceding [word], the *visarjanīya*—being as previously described—is elided in *saṃhitā* when followed by [a sibilant]. (6th line)

For example: *pravadantī manyā vācaḥ samanyāyanti anāyatanā anyāyā āghāravatīḥ*. Why "as before" (*pūrva*)? [Examples include: *anyā vo anyām avatu*, *ghorānyā śivānyāyat*, and *(7th line) ariṣṭāḥ syāparaḥ*. In the word *ariṣṭāḥ*, the *ā* of the visarga is elided. For example: *ariṣṭā syāma tanuvā suvīrāḥ*. Why "syāpara"? [Example: *ojori*(8th line).

[The *visarjanīya*] is elided in all [these cases]. Why [is it said] "provided they are unimpaired" (*ariṣṭā*)? [Because] if it were bound (*baddhā*), it would not be so. For example: *āyudhāḥ*, *ānaśānāḥ*, *ātānāḥ*, *āraṇyāḥ*, *āgneyāḥ*, *ādyāḥ*, *āsīnāḥ*, *ādityāḥ*. In these instances, the *visarjanīya* is elided according to the aforementioned rule in *saṃhitā*. As in: *digmāyudhā rakṣase*; *suvarānaśānasviṣṭir naḥ*; *abhyātā*.

The *vaiśvadeva* verses are not [to be used]; nor are those belonging to the wild (*āraṇya*), such as the *śakvarī* meters. Therefore, those that are *triṣṭubh* meters are *āgneya*. Here, it should be understood that the word *āgneya* is accepted in its *saṃhitā* form without the doubling of the *y* sound (*dvitva*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the rule applying to cases such as "the *ṛc*s addressed to Agni" (*āgneyyā ṛcaḥ*) or "the *gāyatrī* addressed to Agni" (*āgneyyā gāyatryā*). Therefore, the word *āgneya* is taken here with the *y* sound alone in its *saṃhitā* form. Those who know thus are the first. With five [verses], they sit for the human world.

Regarding the example *kam* [in the phrase] *yathādityā vasubhiḥ*: the prohibition "one should not insert [the *n*]" refers to the case where it is said "one should insert" [the *n*] when the word *ādityāḥ* precedes. In that word (*ādityāḥ*), the *visarjanīya*, being followed by the aforementioned [vowel], is not elided in its own form within the *saṃhitā*. This means that in this word, there is no *visarjanīya* [to be elided]. In all counter-examples, it should be understood in exactly the same way. By proximity, the word *ādityāḥ* is obtained as the object of this prohibition.

The *visarga* in the word *āśāḥ*—as in the phrase *nirdahedādityā vai āśāḥ* (*nirdahedādityā vai āśāḥ*)—is elided in *saṃhitā* when followed by the aforementioned [vowels]. *Āśāḥ* means the quarters (*diśaḥ*). [Example: *ā praṇa*. Then follows [the next rule]: because of proximity, the word *āśāḥ* is understood [from the previous rule]. In this word *āśāḥ*, the *visarga* is elided provided that a *ja* or *pa* sound follows. Yielding desires, bestowing skill upon themselves—bestowing skill upon themselves, thus the former [words]. O you who are to be wiped, you are divine; o you who are to be wiped, thus the former [words], "divine. In these cases, the *visarjanīya* [is treated] as follows: "May the dwellings of heaven and earth be made firm";

"O gods who know the way"; "O you of good skill, sons of Dakṣa"; "Given by us among the gods"; "Bestower of life, this one"; "These are indeed the messengers of the gods"; "From the intermediate direction, from all directions, let the rain be driven away, having been cast out, free from harm. (Fifth line)

What is the purpose of the term *avāntara*? [Examples: *jyotiḥ pradiśā diśantā*; *devikā nirvapet*; *ādadānā vimatthnānāḥ*; *anupañcadohāgām*; *grāvāṇodantāmukham*; *ekapātrā dvidevatyā gṛhyante*. (6th line) What is the purpose of the term *dvi*? [Example: *bhrātṛvyadevatyā vai praśnayaḥ kāmadughāḥ*. What is the purpose of the term *kāma*? [Examples: *suvarvartī sudughānaḥ*; *dakṣandadhānā janayantīragnim*; *ātmaṃ dadhānā vāṇaḥ*. Why is it said "in this manner, as before"? (7th line)

*todadhānā vīraṃ videya* | *tuvimrakṣāso divyā navaśvāḥ* | *te divyā dyāvāpṛthivyāśvavit* | What is meant by "thus the preceding"? It refers to that which is *divyā vṛṣṭiḥ* (divine rain). Regarding the word *devatāḥ*: the visarga in the word *devatāḥ* is as previously stated. (8th line) *prajāpatiḥ sarvā devatā devatāsu* | *na kṣepiṣṭhai tasya pūrvaḥ* | *kṣepiṣṭhā etasya* | Thus, in the case of *devatā*, when the visarga follows the aforementioned sounds in *saṃhitā*, (9th line) [it remains].

It is elided; the meaning is that the *visarjanīya* does not exist. For example: *kṣepiṣṭhā devatā vāyum*, *aśvinā vetasya genakā yaḥ*. This is understood as "those whose presence is prohibited. [Examples include:

*yaktā gamayet*, *gamayati*, *niyante*, *vibhajati*, *brāhmaṇam*. When these words are present, the *visarjanīya* in the word *dakṣiṇā* is elided in *saṃhitā*. [Examples include: *dakṣiṇāyuktā yajñam*, *dakṣiṇāgamayedā de*.

[The word *dakṣiṇā*] is [substituted for *devatā*] when followed by *vat*, but not when followed by *devatā*. At the *savana* (pressing), the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are led forth; [the word *dakṣiṇā*] distributes the sacrificial fees among the deities. To what extent does "distributes" (*bhajati*) apply? [Example: *dakṣiṇāvīhi svāhā*; *yad dakṣiṇā brāhmaṇam*. Why is it specified as "followed by another word" (*para*)? [Counter-example: *śyāmo dakṣiṇā bārhaspatyam*; *dhenur dakṣiṇā ye pratyañcaḥ*. Here too, the rule is that [the substitution occurs] when followed by *nākasat*. And [it applies] when preceded by *candra*. The particle *ca* (and) refers back to the word *dakṣiṇā*. [That is,] *candra* is that which precedes the word *dakṣiṇā* in this context.

The *visarjanīya* is elided in a *saṃhitā* when it follows [the word] *yathā* as specified above. For example: *candra-dakṣiṇā-yajñasya pathā*. Why [is it said] "after *candra*"? [Counter-example: *śūrṇo dakṣiṇā vaiṣṇavam*. [The following words are listed: *vidhṛtāḥ*, *dhāyāḥ*, *dhiṣṇiyāḥ*, *dhīrāḥ*, *dhāyāḥ*, *dhānāḥ*, *dhuvānāḥ*, *dhiṣyāḥ*, *vai*, *dhiṣaṇāḥ*, *dhāḥ*. In these cases, the *visarjanīya* is [elided] according to the rule. For example: *manuṣyā vidhṛtā brahmavādino vadanti*. Why [is it said] "after *vi*"? [Counter-example: *vācā vadati dhṛtā manasā*. When... (6th line).

To the left-hand son, you have spoken boldly to the gods who are wise among the gods through their desire for favor. The all-sustaining [goddess] is the weapon against every sorcerer. Like winds that flow together, they are invincible as a firm foundation. (7th line) Knowledge indeed is the *dhiṣaṇā*; by means of knowledges, what does she go? Causing me to enter, the *dhiṣaṇā* has brought me forth. Holding strength, like one who previously possessed faith (*śrad-dhā*), [she is] faith (*śrat*). "Vi" and "it"—thus, in the word *dhā*, the *visarjanīya* occurs as previously stated. (8th line)

When followed by the aforementioned sounds, the *visarjanīya* is elided in *saṃhitā*. This means that the *visarjanīya* does not exist [there]. Water (*āpaḥ*) is indeed faith (*śraddhā*). It is ordained (*vidhīyate*) as a support (*vidhā*). Regarding the word *dharāḥ*: when the *visarjanīya* follows the word *dhāraḥ* and is followed by the aforementioned sounds, it is elided in *saṃhitā*. For example: *madhordhārā vyānaśuḥ*. [In the case of] *aneṣāpūrvaḥ*, the word *dhāraḥ* is understood by proximity. The word *eṣaḥ* [is used] in the sense of "only this" (*eṣāpūrvaḥ*) regarding the flow (*dhārā*).

The *visarjanīya* is not elided. "This one has Viṣṇu as its support" (*tasyaiṣādhārā viṣṇuḥ*). Why say "preceded by *aneṣā*"? [Example: *prate dhārā madhuścutaḥ*. "That which has *eṣā* as the preceding word"—from what follows after this, it is "preceded by *eṣā*" (*eṣāpūrvaḥ*). That does not occur; thus it is "not preceded by *eṣā*" (*aneṣāpūrvaḥ*). [Examples: *netroḥ*, *namasyāḥ*, *na vedāḥ*, *navaśvāḥ*, *nabhāḥ*. In these cases, the *visarjanīya* remains as it is. [Examples: *agninetrā dakṣiṇasadaḥ*, *pitaro namasyā devā yajñiyāḥ*, *na vedā yaśasvatīḥ*, *divyā na*.

They cause it to flow down; for him [it is] with uplifted smoke. Purūravas, drinks, those who are pleased, offspring, men, fivefold [offerings], lords, paths, nourishments, ancient things, covered things, born things.

(4th line) Feet, principal things. Cities of the gods, vessels, sacrificial cakes, purifying things, beginnings, things pertaining to the foot—among these, the *visarjanīya* [is treated] as follows: *purūravā ghṛtena*, *tanūpā hy eṣaḥ*, *te 'smai*. (5th line)

May they be pleased as before. May those thoughts which Pārī joined together be fulfilled. May we be possessed of good offspring and heroic sons—whether they be cattle or men; for cattle are fivefold (*pāṅktāḥ*). Cattle indeed belong to Prajāpati.

(6th line) May the paths leading to the gods belong to the sacrificer, along with the increase of wealth—those that were here of old and those that are new. Enveloped in mist and by the heat of the sun, born of *ṛta* in fortune, [may they be] the feet of the self. (7th line)

[The words] *jātāḥ*, *vāḥ*, *viśvāyuḥ*, *śarma*, *sa*, *pradhā*, *namaḥ*, and *pūtā* [are followed by a vowel]. *Devalokaṃ* [is followed by a vowel]. *Devapurā* [is followed by a vowel]; [the word] *deva* [is used here for the sake of illustration]. Why [mention *deva*]? As in *etasya purā brāhmaṇāḥ*. *Ekapātrā* and *dvidevatyāḥ* [are followed by a vowel]. (8th line) *Anusavanaṃ puroḍāśāḥ* is prescribed; *pavamānāḥ* and *brahmavarcasaṃ* [are followed by a vowel]. *Tat* [is followed by a vowel]. Sacrifices (*yajñāḥ*) beginning with the *agniṣṭoma*; *daśapadyā* [is followed by a vowel], as is the case with *yāvān* [followed by a vowel]. *Pṛthivyāḥ*; in this case, the *visarjanīya* [is treated as a vowel], as in *pṛthivyāḥ*. (9th line)

"In *devayajanaṃ pṛthivyā viśve*," the word *eva pūrvaḥ* [is used]; because of its proximity to "of the earth" (*pṛthivyāḥ*), it is understood as "thus indeed the former. Thus, in the expression *eva pūrvaḥ pṛthivyāḥ*, the word *pūrvaḥ* does not have a dropped visarga; the meaning is that there is no *visarjanīya*. For example: *vācaiva pṛthivyā yajñam*; *ime alajayośca*. The particle *ca* negates the word "of the earth" (*pṛthivyāḥ*) and performs the action of excluding it. *Ime vai sahāstām*. (Second line)

In these two sections, "alaja āntarikṣaḥ" and "pṛthivyā," the *visarjanīya* following "pṛthivyāḥ"—though it would normally be elided according to the rules—is not dropped in *saṃhitā*. This means that the *visarjanīya* is not absent; it remains as it is, just as in the case of "ime. Therefore, in "pṛthivyā yat somaḥ," it is just as in "alaja. And in "dyāvā pṛthivyā śvāvit," the *visarjanīya* following "pratanāḥ" when followed by a *ja*-sound is dropped in *saṃhitā*. As in: "agninā devena pratanājayāmi."

What is the meaning of *japara*? [Example: *pracarṣaṇībhyaḥ pratanā haveṣu*. Why *pratanā*? [Example: *pūrva-juhoti*. Regarding *priyāḥ māsma paraḥ*: the *visarjanīya* in the word *priyāḥ* should not [be elided] when followed by *māsma paraḥ*; being thus followed, it is elided in *saṃhitā*. For example: *priyāmānastanuvaḥ*, *vipriyāsmo yānata imāḥ*. What is the meaning of "followed by such" (*evaṃ para*)? [Example: *priyā vo nāma huveturāṇām*, *saṃpriyā hṛdayāni vaḥ*. [Regarding] *phālāḥ phalā...* [text fragment].

The *visarjanīya* is elided in *saṃhitā* [as follows]: *śunaṃ naḥ phālā vitudantu bhūmim* ("May the ploughshares furrow the earth for our welfare"). Regarding the *brāhmaṇāḥ* and *bāhyāḥ*, the *visarjanīya* occurs as follows: *brāhmaṇā vai chandāṃsi | te ye bāhyā dṛśīkavaḥ* ("The *brāhmaṇas* are indeed the meters; those who are outsiders are the *dṛśīkas*"). In these cases—the words *bhāmāḥ*, *bhārāḥ*, *bharatāḥ*, *bhakṣāḥ*, *bhūyāḥ*, *bhūmyāḥ*, *vitthā*, *bhadrāḥ*, *bhrātṛvyāḥ*, *bhaktāḥ*, *bhūyiṣṭhāḥ*, and *bhāgāḥ*—the *visarjanīya* occurs as follows: *bhāmān avavarjante* ("They avoid the *bhāmas*").

The *yajus* for the withdrawal: "O Bharatas, this is your king. May we, long-lived, partake together. Among the gods, may there be splendor. Having encompassed the earth, speak the path. Do not be terrified; do not be harmed. Here are your auspicious reins. When [the offering] belongs to Agni’s rival, it is not [offered] to Agni; therefore, they are born divided. For the abundance of cattle, [there is] the threefold *upāṃśu*. Those who are the divine divisions, those who are not preceded by clarified butter (*ājya*), [are called] "portions" because of their presence.

It is obtained [that] the word *ājyapūrvabhāgāḥ* does not have its visarga elided. For example: *sarasvatyā ājyabhāgā syāt*. Why "preceded by *ājya*"? The aforementioned example [is given]. That which has the word *ājya* before it is *ājyapūrvaḥ*. That which is not *ājyapūrvaḥ*—meaning it does not have its visarga elided—is as follows: *tamāḥ mandrāḥ mitrāḥ manasyamānāḥ manuṣyāḥ mukhāḥ manāḥ sumedhāḥ māndāḥ māsāḥ muñcamānāḥ ca māyāḥ mudāḥ matthnānāḥ miśrāḥ meghyāḥ muṣkarāḥ medhyāḥ*.

The *marutvatīya* verses are primarily unmeasured (*niḥparimitāḥ*). Those measured (*mitāḥ*) are as follows: in these words, the *visarjanīya* [is treated] as follows: *madhumattamā mandrādhanasya tamāḥ*. Why "tamāḥ"? [As in: *mandrā svarvācyaditih*, *sumitrā na āpaḥ*, *sumanasyamānāviyac ca yayā manuṣyā jīvanti*, *viṣṇumukhā vai devāḥ*, *pratinaḥ sumanasā bhava*, *sumedhā svāhā*. Why "svāhā"? [As in: *yam medhā nopanamet*. *māndā vāśāḥ śuddhyūrajirāḥ*—thus he recites. *mā...* (fifth line).

She indeed releases those which are the illusions (*māyā*) of the illusionists of the world—what is this? You have been made by *svadhā* out of the demonic illusion (*āsurī-māyā*). With joy, you crush the Apsarases of the world; he who gives various [gifts]. Having gone to the back of heaven, having reached the celestial realm, you are mingled with the gods. The voices of the lightning-flashes are worthy of sacrifice (*medhyā*); the cattle belonging to Indra are for the one with testicles. Those which are indeed worthy of sacrifice and fit for the ritual, the cups dedicated to the Maruts are drawn at the proper seasons. Therefore, they are known as... (line 7).

From the beginning: these *sāmidhenī* verses are "constructed" (*nirmitā*). Or rather, the *ṛc* verses are "limited" (*parimitā*). Why not "equal" (*sammitā*)? Because [the verse] "that which is the corner-stone of the fire-altar" (*yad agniṣṭhām aśrim*) is measured. [If one objects: "It would be 'unlimited' (*aparimitā*)," [we reply: there would be no elision of the visarga (*avisargaḥ*) because of the word *pari* preceding it. If you say this is so because of the word *pari*, do not say so. (8th line) [Because...

since the intention is to express the word *pari* as preceding, in the phrase "it becomes unlimited" (*aparimitā bhavati*), there is no occasion for the elision of the visarga because the word is not preceded by *pari*. Sacrifices (*yajñāḥ*), diseases (*yakṣmāḥ*), worthy of sacrifice (*yajñiyāḥ*), offerings (*yājāḥ*), fame (*yaśāḥ*), sacrificers (*yajamānāḥ*), yoked ones (*yuktāḥ*)—(9th line).

The *yājyās* of the *prāyaṇīya* are [those] that are regulated; among these, the *visarjanīya* is as follows. These are the sacrifices performed in conjunction (*samṛtayajñāḥ*). These diseases do not find him. The deities worthy of sacrifice are the gods. The *anūyāja*s are born. Having performed the *prayāja*s...

(P55a, 1st line) ...together with glory, she is glorious. May the sacrificers go to heaven with well-being. Those [verses] joined with sacrificial fees burn the sacrifice. Those which are the regulated *yājyās* of the *prāyaṇīya*. What about those of the *ayanīya*? A *yājyā* having a mark above will be born. (2nd line)

"Only [the] honors, for they are not extended; therefore they say: 'O gods, women have indeed become dear to you; the *ṛc*s are yours, not these sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). These ten [fingers], which are beyond the gods—women indeed, O gods, have become dear to you. (Third line) To you, O gods, the *ṛc*s, the sacrificial fees—not these ten, while these gods are beyond—in this [phrase], the *visarjanīya* is not elided. As in the *saṃhitā*: 'The women who are of one mind, of the sense-organ... (Fourth line)

By which indeed there is the non-destruction of vigor; by which the beloved bodies [are formed]; what is the purpose? "The two paths (*yāvaḥ*) provide protection for the one who exerts himself. "The plants that have been born"; what is the purpose? "Of every one being sacrificed. "The two paths, O gods, which are splendors in the sun, the splendors which are in the cows and in the horses"; what is the purpose? "The two paths provide protection for the one who exerts himself; the splendors which are in the cows and in the horses; with those which are the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*); these which are our beloveds."

"O gods, now for you—what are these? Or those who go to the house? Those which consist of ten syllables each; those which have placed their bodies among the gods—let them depart, having been anointed. May he, possessing good seed, be established in seed. I loosen [the bond] from the one who is released (7th line). [The bond] of the rays, as of the reins. What is it that I bind? The girdle of all the plants. He is the man who rejoices in death. Like birds protecting their young, they speak. Cattle indeed belong to Rudra: the silver ones, the tawny ones, and the lead ones (8th line)."

That which is black in the night [is the form]; the *uparavas* and the *āhavanīya* are the *navasā*. Because of their proximity, they are understood as "forms" (*rūpāḥ*). The word *vaśā* does not have its visarga elided, because it is followed by the word *rūpāḥ*.

(Line 9) The meaning is that there is no *visarjanīya*. For example: *sā dvirūpā vaśā bhavat* ("She became a two-formed cow"). *Rudrāḥ anūṅgyantaḥ agnīṃ gyānto rudrāḥ*—this word *rudrāḥ*, being followed by the aforementioned [word], has its [visarga] elided in *saṃhitā*. (P55b, 11a, Line 1)

It is prescribed as follows: *rudrā vasavaḥ samiddhatām*. Why [is it said] "not ending in an *īṅgya*"? [As in: *somā rudrā vivṛhatam*. That which has an *īṅgya* at its end is called *īṅgyānta*; that which does not have such an end is *anīṅgyānta*. Regarding the *visarjanīya* of these two [words], as in *limpāḥ lokāḥ*: "The worlds named Salila-Nilimpa praise these. [Why is it] "not after" (*na paścāt*) [the word] "prior" (*pūrvaḥ*)? By proximity (*sānnidhyāt*), the word "worlds" (*lokāḥ*) is understood. Because the word "after" (*paścāt*) is prior to it, the word "worlds" (*lokāḥ*) is not [the subsequent element].

"Subsequent to 'pūrvaḥ' [comes] 'paścāt': in the phrase *paścāt pūrvo lokāḥ*, the *visarga* does not occur; that is to say, there is no *visarga*. [Examples include: *paścāllokāḥ*, *vā*, *eṣā*, *prācī*, *valaśāḥ*, *vitthāḥ*, *viprāḥ*, *vedāḥ*, *vayāḥ*, *vīrāḥ*, *vrātāḥ*, *vasavyāḥ*, *varcāḥ*, *vasiṣṭhāḥ*, *vyacāḥ*, *vaiśvānarāḥ*, *veśāḥ*, *varatrāḥ*, *vātāḥ*, *vidānāḥ*, *savratāḥ*, *vidyāḥ*, *vaiṣṇavāḥ*, *vayasyāḥ*, *ekavṛtāḥ*. In these cases, the *visarjanīya* remains as it is, as in *sahasra*. (5th line)

O bark, do not tremble; do not be pierced; do not [harm] you. May the inspired ones [be inspired] by the inspired one’s prayer, by the wise one. May the all-knowing, radiant drops [flow]. O wide-striding, all-conquering, noble hero—may we live long.

The hosts of Varuṇa have come together—the divine Vasus, the gods. With good luster, with excellent luster—may you be the most excellent among them. Vāta, the Gandharva of all-pervading reach; may the Vaiśvānara gods fumigate [the sacrifice].

We have heard the neighboring dwellings in the measure; establish them from the even path. The great winds, seeking protection, are in agreement upon the back of the firmament for the sake of the rite, O Agnis. What is that? My devoted followers, longing for the head. Wisdom is indeed the *dhiṣaṇā*; [it is] by means of wisdoms.

(8th line) The trees belong to Viṣṇu; the animals are of various kinships, having diverse minds; the Asuras have a single vow, as do the gods. What is "evā" (thus)? All follow his vows. For he who is beyond the world, all the offerings are well-established. (9th line)

These words are so designated because of the word *viśvā*. Thus, the subsequent word *viśvā*—in those instances where its visarga is elided—is [treated as such]. From *ubhau indrāgnī* up to *agnir vṛtrāṇi*, the section consisting of questions and answers is called the *anuvāka*; this is referred to as the *saṃhitā-yājyā*. As it has been stated: "Now, the *agni-yājyā*. In that regard, for example: *viśvā yaś carṣaṇīḥ*, *viśvā hi māyā avasi*, *viśvā bhuvo abhavat*.

What is the meaning of "evaṃ para" (and so on)? [Examples: *śośucāno viśvād dveṣāṃsi*, *viśvā bhuvanāny anyā*. Why say "in the *yājyā*s"? [Counter-examples: *viśvā hy agne duritā saha svādhā*; *śuddhāḥ śukrāḥ śravāḥ śuṣkāḥ śarmaṇyāḥ kaviśastāḥ* (3rd line);

*ślokāḥ śaphāḥ śubhrāḥ śreṣṭhāḥ śarāḥ*—in these cases, the visarga remains as it is. [Examples: *kasyāścid abhiśastyā avīta hotram*; *śuddhā yūyaṃ devā udhvam*; *tava śukrā bhrājanta īrate*; *saṃśravāha*; *apaśuṣkāviḍa* (4th line).

The boiling of the sacrificial animal; O gods who grant protection, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Aryaman—let the delightful ones, praised by the seers, carry you hither. What is the purpose of the syllable *ka*? It is for the non-slaughter of the horse. They cry out in all directions like travelers on a path. The sacrificial hearths are the hooves; their name is *yajūṃṣi*. Like bright children, they are like calves; our blessings are most excellent. For the one whose arrows are straight, there is a quiver made of reeds. Serpents, makers of what is done, hundreds and thousands of them, gentle, seated, wearing garments of woven cloth. He... (line 6).

*spiñjarāḥ*, *sikatāḥ*, *sīsāḥ*, *sthitāḥ*, *syandamānāḥ*, *somāḥ*, *ūṣatyāḥ*, *āha*, *saumyāḥ*, *sthāvarāḥ*, *sparaṇāḥ*, *sṛṣṭāḥ*, *stutāḥ*, *somāḥ*, *somapīthāḥ*—in these [cases], the *visarjanīya* [is elided]. For example: *sarpā vai jīryanto manyante*. *madhukṛtas tyonāmā viśaterāmadaḥ*. Why [is it] said "when [the word] is formed"? [As in: *suśevāsyonāmā viśa*. *sahasrasāḥ śatasā arvā praṇaktu mitadrava*. (8th line).

"May they be winners of a thousand through wisdom. What is the purpose of "sahasra"? [As in: "May she be all-living, may she be all-pervading. "I gratify the seasons, the Sāmans. "Go forth, O Soma-loving Fathers, with your deep [songs]. Or: "Those who have entered into the realm (*rajasi*). What is the purpose of *ni*? [As in: "(9th line) May your attendants increase. "May our blessings be true for you. What is the purpose of *va*? [As in: "May the form of my mind be true. "Those who are thieves and robbers; those who are yellowish among the trees. (P56b[12a], 1st line)

He scatters sand for the sake of completeness. Yoke-horses made of lead are yoked; these two are not firmly established, flowing according to their will. Those rising [waters] are the glory of Soma. The gods are thirsty for three days. What about "three"? The form of the one with true mind. (Second line) For he [is] through the deity... He says "āha"—what is it? "Soma indeed... Varuṇa is the seizer; whatever is stationary... and these are for the protection of the self. The seasons, once created, did not turn back. Having been consecrated, they attained the Virāj. (Third line)

The *vicatya* [rule] applies to *soma*, *ina*, and *trīmatra*. What is the purpose of pronouncing [the word] *uccāraṇena*? [Examples: *agniṣomau ha viṣaḥ*; *agnīṣomo brahmaṇā*. This is indeed for the sake of covering the *kloma* at this time. Regarding *sthāḥ*: in this case, the *visarjanīya* is as follows:

*prastareṣṭhā* (4th line), and *barhiṣadaśca*. It is not preceded by *prati*. Because of proximity (*sānnidhyāt*), the word *sthā* is obtained. The word *sthā* preceded by *prati* does not have its *visarga* elided. The meaning is that there is no *visarga*. For example: *pratiṣṭhāya* (5th line). Thus.

The word *sthirāḥ* [is subject to elision] when not preceded by *ava*. That which has *ava* before it is "preceded by *ava*" (*avapūrva*). That which does not have this is "not preceded by *ava*" (*anavapūrva*). Thus, the word *anavapūrvasthirāḥ* does not undergo the elision of the visarga. For example: (line 6) *jayatā narasthitāvaḥ santu*. Why say "not preceded by *ava*"? [Consider: *avasthirāmaghavadatyaḥ*. In the case of the word *sarvāḥ*, when the visarga follows what has been previously described, it is elided in *saṃhitā*. For example: (line 7)

"Prajāpati is all the deities. [In this case,] because of the presence of "vai," the word "paraḥ" is not [required]; thus, it is understood that they are "all" due to proximity. When "vai" follows "paraḥ," the word *sarvāhuti* does not have its visarga elided. The meaning is that the *visarjanīya* exists after the letter "n. (8th line) "This [is] for all the birds. Regarding "sādhyāḥ": when the word *sādhyāḥ* occurs in places other than those containing the word "ṛkṣu"—that is, excluding verses (*ṛc*)—the aforementioned *paraḥ* is elided in *saṃhitā*. For example: *sādhyā* (9th line).

Indeed, the gods [are thus]. Why [is it said] *anṛkṣu*? For those Sādhyas who have eaten the oblation (*haviradantu*). [The following words apply: *himāḥ*, *hotavyāḥ*, *hāyāḥ*, *hāyanāḥ*, *hārukāḥ*, *hotrāḥ*. In these words, in the *saṃhitā* (continuous text), the *visarjanīya* at the end of a word is elided when followed by a sonant consonant or by a vowel other than *śa*. For example: *śataṃ himā adyumantaḥ*; *ete hotavyā jayaty eva*; *yad vihāyā dhātā vidhātā*; therefore, this is known.

When followed by *manuṣyāḥ*, [the visarga] remains as *āpaḥ* before *agniṃ*. It is precisely in this way that the *hotrāḥ* are the protectors (*varūtrayaḥ*). It is not something else. By virtue of proximity, it is understood as "the *hotrāḥ*. In the expression *deparo hotrāḥ*, there is no elision of the visarga. The meaning is that there is never an absence of the visarga. When followed by *makāra* (m), [the visarga] follows *hutāḥ*. In the word *hutāḥ*, the visarga, being followed by *makāra*, is elided in *saṃhitā*. For example: *upahutāmanuṣyā ityāha*. Why say "followed by *makāra*"? [Consider: *upahutā dhenuḥ*.

[Thus ends the commentary on the *Samānasandhi* composed by Mallayārya]. May there be auspiciousness! Having prostrated before Bhāratī, and having prostrated before Nārāyaṇa—the sole mother of all the worlds—so that this treatise on *lakṣaṇa* which is to be transgressed may be completed without interruption, he makes it known: "I shall now declare the steps to be transgressed. That knowledge, which consists of the form of the *lakṣaṇa*-treatise about to be commenced, is that [which is to be transgressed].

The statement that the subject matter, purpose, and connection—characterized by the nature of being the means of instruction—are indicated right here constitutes the proposition (*pratijñā*) formed by the sentence. He explains the qualifier "to be bypassed" (*vilaṅghyāni*) with the words: "the phonemes *e* and *ai*" (*ekāraikāravarṇau*). (7th line) The term *ekāraikāravarṇau* means "the phoneme *e* and the phoneme *ai*"; these two phonemes are those which undergo modification in *saṃhitā*. In the domain of *saṃhitā*, this [phoneme] *e* is to be elided. (8th line)

The meaning is that these [words] ending in the vowels *e* and *ai*—which possess modifications (*vikāra*) at the time of the Pada-text according to the rules "varṇam apūrvo" and "yavakārau," and which are seen to undergo modification in cases such as *agre vāre*—are to be passed over by those most learned in the Veda. Why mention the vowels *e* and *ai*? [Consider: *kiṃ śatakṛtā vudvaṃśamiva yemire surabhāvuloke*. Why mention "those which undergo modification"? [Consider: *āre asme ca*.

They choose [thee] for stability, not for misfortune. Why [is it said] "those ending in -t"? As in *paitṛvājīkanikṛt*. "Those of the Rudras, Soma-Indra, the tawny-marked ones. But surely, in the case of *somendrāḥ*, there is no modification; for in the *saṃhitā*—[both lines omitted]—in both instances, the single *e*-vowel is directly perceived. It is replied: Now, regarding "one" and "both," under the heading "now the phonemes," by the rule *ekāram ekārapade ekāyam*, the *ā*-vowel and the *e*-vowel are common [to both].

Because the single vowel *e* is prescribed [only] in that specific context, there is no such reversal in the *saṃhitā*. To exclude that possibility, it is stated "ending in those" (*tadantāni*). If this were so, then even at the end of a word—as in *vanaspate vasrjā rarāṇaḥ*—since the *e* and *ā* are common [to both], the *ā* would also have to be marked in that way [with a vertical stroke]. It is not so; it is not so deleted. By the rule "preceded by *t*, *e*, or *o*," it is specifically the *o* mentioned after the *ā* that is obtained.

It is said [that the definition is] "because of the state of the letter *e* remaining as it was," since its very nature (*svarūpa*) has already been established by the ancient authors themselves. Anticipating the objection that [the mention of] "the beginning of the vowel *ṛ*" (*vṛṣaṇārambhe*) would be redundant, he refutes it with the words "distinct from the ancient" (*purātanetiriktam*).

The meaning is that the ancient definition is to be rejected because of its superfluous statements and omissions; having abandoned that, other faultless definitions are being formulated. Now, the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*)...

He performs [the operation]. Regarding the rule "that which is a word containing a *iṅ* vowel," here in this definition, it is intended that the effect applies even when there is a state of multiple words where there are actually identical words. The purpose of that is stated as follows: by means of a simple expedient, linguistic usage is maintained; otherwise, in the case of *ekadhanavinda*, both *ekadhanavinda* and *ekadhanavida* would be possible according to the two rules (*pate*). Consequently, there would be prolixity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, in the case of *uttha utthe soma indram mamāda*, regarding the preceding and following segments...

It would follow that even what ought to be excluded [would be included]. That has already been defined by the first half [of the verse]; by the second half, something else remains. In that regard, whatever phoneme or cluster is indicated as being non-pada (anīṅgya), it must be understood as consisting of a *pada* itself. For instance, in examples such as *ekājagme*, *mamāraraṇyā*, and *evaṃ vidvāṃsava*, the word *eka* is taken as consisting of a *pada*; or in *ekāṣṭakāndīkṣante*, this word *eka* is taken as consisting of a *pada*. Furthermore, there is that which does not consist of a *pada*.

That which was stated as "one part" (*ekadeśa*), he begins to define it with the words "at the front" (*agre*). [The examples are: *agre guvo 'gram imam*; *pakṣmabhyaḥ svāhā pāra ikṣavaḥ*; *yac chūdre yad asya enaḥ*. Why [is it] "belly" (*udarya*)? [As in: *agne viśvāny arya ā*.

(3rd line) Regarding that, he said, "having approached her. Just as for the guest who has arrived. This person offers the *niṣṭāka* oblation. "O ageless Dawn, you have come! Furthermore, he establishes the out-breath (*prāṇa*) within the in-breath (*apāna*). Why [is it] "thus" (*eva*)? [As in: *astaprāṇa āyata*. With the right hand, food is eaten. (4th line)

The *ojastranayas*. [The word] "sāhna" [is used] for him; [the word] "sāhna"—why? Because "the *ājya* belongs to the middle day. [In the mantra: "May the lower ones rise up, and the higher ones... Why [the word] "udīratām avare"? [As in: "Manojavā was the lower one, O Indra. [In the mantra: "He has attained the mind, the wide mid-air (*urvantarikṣam*). [In the mantra: "It was recited: 'Both have conquered'"; thus he strides across the mid-air itself. He places [the brick] on the right shoulder. Gold is indeed immortality; [he places it] in immortality itself. He expiates this direction [with the mantras]: "O Iḍā! O Aditi! Come here! O Agni! O Ocean! Why [the word] "anīṅyam"? [As in: "The Āgneya..."

The *aindrāgna*, the *āśvina*, that whose departure others have followed, the one who is being enjoined, the *arka* alone, those for Agni Āyuṣmat, and the *traiṃśika*—what is meant by "the *traiṃśika*"? There are two *traiṃśika*s; these constitute the *agnikāṇḍa*. Regarding "with which word," there are three, excluding ten. (7th line) In that case, its state of being delayed would not occur. For example: "Let the fires proceed with this," "for him," "to him let there be great heroism," "by means of the *samaṣṭi* [the deities are below]," "he says after having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*," and "of the ocean's firmness. (8th line)

"In the upward movement"; "the oblation is for the one who does not deceive. By descending, [he reaches] downward. For non-violence, [there is] the Audumbara [wood]. With light, he overcomes darkness. "That which is prior"—what is it? One should not eat its food. For that [deity], there is the Āhavanīya fire. (9th line) They proceed with the subsequent days for the sake of safety. For this [earth] is, as it were, seated. He invokes [the gods] toward him; he places the *āvya* [ghee] in him. He pours together from the *upabhṛt* [ladle]. They offered to Indra for themselves. The latter [verse] is for themselves. Therefore, the Adhvaryu [acts] for himself alone. (P58b(14a), 1st line)

What is that? It is the sacrifice itself belonging to the Self. What is "Indra, O God, that supreme"? Prajāpati [offered] a bull and a cow from his own self. He himself performed the oblation of clarified butter on an *aśvattha* tree. He measured out the offering on an *audumbara* [vessel]. "He turns back," so he said; for he is indeed the Sun. They returned to the world of the gods by means of one [verse]. They remained in these worlds, taking hold [of them]. When the year had come around, they [performed] with these [verses]. "Both are to be slain," they say. He places [it] between for the sake of separation; he anoints it. "Following him, together, let us begin," [they say].

By the attainment of the fourfold turning, it becomes one. As many as we are, so are these two. He takes the sacrificial grass (*barhis*); he desires this. They speak the truth; seek this. "By fire is fire kindled," he says. It is indeed kindled in him. What is the *samit*? "Among the gods," he says. He places [the fuel] upon the Āgnīdhra. Why "Āgnīdhra"? Because he does not place the fuel-sticks [there]. These gods are indeed sacrificed to; he places this in the kindled [fire]. "O heads, be gracious; O *iḍ*, come. What is "be gracious"? The enclosing stick is praised by the *iḍ*. He places [the brick] on its own dug-out depression (*iriṇa*).

They indeed kindle [the fires] with the consecrations (*dīkṣā*). The Āgnīdhra causes [the sacrificer] to fast. He shakes off evil for him. "Not so," he says; "further," he says. "What is this? "We shall go according to the manner of the Aṅgirases," he says. It is in the power and vigor of Tvaṣṭṛ. "What is 'Tvaṣṭṛ'? "A man endowed with a hundred powers in his lifespan. "The gods have come to the end of the sacrifice," he says. "We implore that," he says, referring to the filter (*pavitra*). "They do not have mastery over that," he said. They did not look toward what was to be eaten. Thus they awaited what was coming. "Arise, arise! Grant us a share! "Agni is being praised," he says.

"The Āgrayaṇa is set out. He places it while the [verse] is being recited. "It shines near at hand. "The vessels are being cleansed," he says. "With help from the lips," [he says]. "This [earth] is strewn around. "She was deprived of her virility; he begat her," [it is said]. One should place one [verse] on the half-verse. What about the other? "Yonder [sky] is indeed the half-verse, this [earth] is the half-verse. One should also place oneself for Nīrṛti. "May I prosper myself," [he thinks]. What about that? "In the lap of Nīrṛti. "May I prosper my offspring."

"May these be successful for us, for Indra who possesses fury (*manyumat*). What does 'beyond that' mean? It means from the mouth of the sacrifice, from Agni. These gods have followed after them. For Indra who possesses vigor (*ojasvat*), this one [is offered]. 'Thee for the sky (*vyoman*) of Truth'—what does 'for enjoyment' mean? 'Swell through the ritual act. Make yourselves non-departing, O you who are piled with bricks. Even in the mouth of the thicket, he is invited at the preparation of the oblation. Now, which are these gods? Those for whom these [acts] are performed; they are self-made."

One should settle [the fire] on barren ground. Why say "self-made"? [It refers to] fuel made by oneself. Why say "what is its cruel [aspect] immediately following"? [It refers to] the gruel as the cruel [portion]. "It is drawn away by its brilliance"—thus I am indeed the Soma-purchaser. "In every section, in every section, him [he purifies]. (3rd line) "He strides along after; this one indeed purchases spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*)," so they say. "He prepares it; while preparing it, they act thus. "Why shall we seize this? [They reply: "Let us purchase food and vigor. Having performed the *svagā*-offering, [he places it] below. (4th line)

By advancing, one [cup] is for me; by arrangement, it is below. Bring security both in rest and in exertion. The eastern lip wastes away from the truth; therefore, they are dug to the depth of an arm. This is indeed for manifestation.

At the end of the branch, these worlds are taken. The bright [cup] is taken from the Āgrayaṇa; the bull is taken for the Rājanya. May she bear Agni as her embryo; may she bear the first embryo—what? The embryo of the world, across the two worlds.

It is indeed accepted for him; one should announce it to him as he accepts it. He places the donkey down; he performs the *svāhā*-utterance, [thinking] "in heaven itself. Therefore they say, "The domestic rites (*gṛhya*) are at the end," for the sake of protection. Indeed, they say below that these two are not to be taken together with the *gāyatrī*. This belongs to the *gaṇyā* for the gods: "For Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, thee! Why is this so? Because his [offering] is indeed for the slayer of Vṛtra. One who piles the fire-altar is liable [to harm]; the fire is moved by means of the *pāvamānī* verses: "O thou who art seen by all" (*viśvacarṣaṇi*).

"By these [bricks], the fire is piled," they say. "The eyes of Varuṇa," he says; that is indeed the divine procreation. It is consciousness itself, for the sake of consciousness. "They shall be born," [he says] at the beginning. "For life, live! (9th line).

"In whom, when born, this..."—"In whom, when born"—what does this mean? One who is already born. "They are born after him," [he says] as he extends further. "O wife, come! "Of the light of Truth," he says. "Of your light"—what does this mean? Of universal light.

"Placing [the bricks], let us be born," he says with desire for them. "May we live through her, through Agni’s wisdom, and may we be born through offspring"—by this very means he goes forth by means of the Jagatī. Why? For the overcoming by the Jagatī. "Those two wives of ours, having conquered both worlds, do not go beyond"—why say this? They say it is for the sake of total victory: "Let us conquer right here. Through procreation, there is no intermediate defeat among the sovereigns; thus he protects him for Indra. It is at the very ford.

They consume [the portions]. This Agni belongs to *tejas* (splendor). "The dog that stands in the second place is not yours"—[this is said] for Indra, the subduer of Vṛtra (*vṛtratūḥ*). Why [is it said] "for Indra, the subduer"? He says, "O powerful one, for Indra, the subduer of Vṛtra. This is seized for the sake of *tejas*. They approach the middle; they approach the highest. Why "the highest"? [Because] this is the highest. They bring them forward. Indeed, they stand near the *iḍā*. Thus he says, "for the *triṣṭubh* meters. Why does he say [this]? "The summer [season] is for the *triṣṭubh* meters as fuel; the *triṣṭubh* is strength in the higher [region]. Why [does he say] "up" (*ud*)? (Fifth line)

"Whoever is more skilled than we, [let him] go up. Why "up" (*upa*)? [As in: "The plants rise up after him. "To him may you go with zeal. "For the continuity [of the sacrifice], [may there be] destruction of the *rakṣases*. [The two ends] of that [sacrifice] are cut off from within.

(6th line) He cooked the *brahmaudana*; they gave him the remnants thereof. Why "cooked before this" (*itaḥ apacat pūrva*)? [As in: "The *māruka* [demon] is in the waters of her who bathes. "He took the food; here I [take it]. "Svarāt, Indra, come hither; let all beings enter. (7th line)

Why "indródame"? Because this [cup] is indeed his *dama* (subduer). "I take up the arm of Indra"—this is for him on the gambling-ground itself. "The milch-cow of the Veda indeed"—this is for her. "Where first the waters were held firm"—this is for the *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial gift) as they are being set down. "Give us Soma, O Āgrāviṇas!"—this is for food that is unscarred and fit for sight. That very *prāṇa* (vital breath) is in the consecrated one (*dīkṣita*). "Placing the self in these"—these are indeed beneficial for cattle. Therefore, they enjoy strength from [the navel] upwards. Having taken hold, they are consecrated; he who is afflicted... him [they heal].

He offers to the deity while standing. Why [is it said] "to this other one"? Because there are eight [verses] beginning with "who has come from the deity Agni" and ending with "he who establishes the fire. He says, "of you who stand in the ordinance. They are being placed down; [he says] "you are the seat. He places [the brick] on the *dhiṣṇya* of the Hotṛ. Just as one who is yoked is driven, so [it is]. This is the black husk; they drive it away for the support of the sacrifice, indeed with a focused mind. With the last [verse], he places it here on the altar. It is led southward.

The *niṣkāsa* is for the *udayanīya* offering. "With the Aindra sacrifice, drive [the enemy] away," he says. "From the dwelling of the ocean, lift [the ladle]," he says. "For the *tanūnaptra*," he says. "For me, through the bowing down, for such-and-such [deity]. Thus, purify Agni, your own self. One who is ill should press [the soma]. With barley-meal, they act out of compassion. He is nourished along with the *āgnāvaiṣṇava* offering. With barley-grass, speed forth vigor. Abundant nourishment, both by itself and by its essence. Truly, he who pours into the full—what is meant by "full"? For Prajāpati is indeed like the full. The dust is full of nourishment (*irāvatī*).

He places [the brick] on the right wing with the verse beginning "gātumitamanasaspata imam. Regarding the rule concerning what is preceded by *ati*: [it applies to] *indrāyāgnaye pūṣṇoṣadhībhyaḥ prajābhyaḥ* and *agnaye pūṣṇa*. Why [is this said]? [To exclude cases such as] *pūṣṇa ādhipatyam*. Regarding the rule concerning what is preceded by *pra*: [it applies to] *ikṣavo vāryebhyaḥ*. (5th line) Regarding the rule concerning what is preceded by *anu*: [it applies to] *yadajuṣanta pūrvṛksāmābhyām*. Why [is this said]? [To exclude cases such as] *abhipūrva uddhrīyate*, *prarodhanaṃ pūrva udayanam*, and *ūrjannodhehi dvipade catuṣpada ityāha*. Why [is this said]? (6th line)

The *yājyā* verses consist of four feet; [this is] for the sake of the four-footed [animals]. If one were to scatter [the grains] upon the *gārhapatya* fire, [it would be done] under the sovereignty of Dhātṛ, with the result that life would be diminished. Why [is it said], "Life is supreme"? It is because the *gārhapatya* is established for this world [of ours]. [The verse] "Mayu is the offspring of Prajāpati" and "He chooses splendor, O Puṣya," he says; "For the path of the lord of the sacrifice," he says. Why [is it said], "Supreme"? [It is because] "Indra is the sovereign lord of weapons. "For the protection of the wife," he says; thus [it is] for the wife.

"What is the meaning of this? [The response is: "O most pervasive one, [place] darkness upon the earth, O you who are to be held. Why does it say "darkness upon the earth"? [It says] "far from the earth, O Agni, with a thousand eyes," he says. He offers it to the Brahman priest in a single portion. [He offers] to the Brahman priest.

What does this mean? [He says: "Brahmā brought forth Brahmā. He restrains with the mind; he performs both. "For Sūrya, thee, for brilliance—this is thine. Indra has two shares, Viṣṇu the third. What does "two shares" mean? "This is thy Gāyatra share," so it is said to me. [Regarding] thee who art established... do not fall away from the sacrifice; "O Āśrāvaya! We would be possessed of the portion born of Truth. They enjoy through both; they indeed enjoy of life on the northern half. "He enjoys of life"—so it is said.

"What? He who knows thus—these two consume him. This [earth] out of fear from us [consumes] the other. That thunderbolt kindles him through service. 'May you enjoy by means of both,' [he says]. Thus he makes the *brahman* at the very mouth of the sacrifice. It is kindled as the highest. They purified this with the formula:

(3rd line) 'For Indra accompanied by the Maruts, for thee—this one. At the midday pressing itself, for the sake of sovereignty over the great *kṣatra*. 'For the sake of sovereignty over the great'—what does that mean? 'We have meditated upon the name of the Great Truth. It was placed of its own accord in the clarified butter on the *aśvattha* wood. Indra made that exhilaration of Soma. (4th line)

[The word *pūrṇamāsa* occurs] in the *āmāvāsyā* [passage]. Why [is this restriction stated]? Because they say, "There is a thirteenth month. [Examples follow: *namo mahimna uta cakṣuṣe te*; *agniśca me indraśca me*; *adite maha o khāndadhātu*; *anute dāyi maha indriyāya*. Why [is it said that *maha* occurs before *indriyāya*]? Because [in the following case it does not]: *āte maha indro'tyugra*. [Also: *vardhamānaṃ maha ā ca puṣkaram*; *anāmrata evāgniṃ cinute*; *namaste rudra manyava uto*; *ya ukhāṃ*.

"Release the animals toward the north," he says; this is for the bamboo. "We fix the praise for Agni," he says; he thus fixes it for him. Just as a son who is born dies, so too [is the offering]; "May the thousand-eyed one protect my wealth," he says, for they consider the milk-mixture (*āśira*) to be like something already lost. They approach the central [fire]. There is an eleven-potherd cake for Indra; for the ram and the ewe, "O Mother, what [is] yours? [he says]; these are the secondary offerings for Anumati. By means of release, he releases himself from evil.

"The sacrificer sacrifices"—this [is said] at the place of *iḍā* in the sacrifice to the gods. "He who, indeed, when the sacrifice has arrived for its performance..."—thus he says; verily, at every performance, he [secures] it for him. Or, "he who, when the sacrifice has arrived for its performance, [offers] to Agni..."—why [say] "Agni first at the performance"? His *iṣṭi* is indeed at the performance. "We who shall sacrifice" (*ye yajāmahe*) consists of five syllables. One should offer [an animal] to Vāyu accompanied by his team (*niyutvat*).

The sacrificer alone takes hold of the life-span; the sacrificer alone bestows splendor. In this pressing sacrificer, there are blessings. [Question: What about "blessings"? [Answer: This the sacrificer receives. [Question: Why "life-span" and "blessings" specifically? [Answer: For that very reason, the sacrificer prospers. He says, "This sacrificer is invited. If he does not lead this one forward at the beginning of the sacrifice, it would be a defect in the sacrifice. [Question: What about that? [Answer: The sacrificer himself should pile that very altar. The sacrificer secures the blessings of the sacrifice.

"From that [side], drive him away with the left," he says. What does "drive him away" mean? It refers to that which one offers as the *upayāja* oblations. Those who undergo initiation (*dīkṣante*) on the Ekāṣṭakā day; those who have come here to this Soma-pressing (*savana*). What does "who have come" mean? It refers to those who have poured out [the libations]. Those who have attained this sacrifice; those who consume this sacrifice with their own inherent power (*svadhā*). Those wild animals that are not domestic cattle. He who, knowing thus, performs the Ṣaḍrātra rite. What does "knowing thus" mean? It means he who knows in this manner. Those drops (*indavaḥ*) which are the sacrificial victims (*paśavaḥ*); those which are their cattle. What does "those which are their cattle" mean? It refers to those which are theirs... [fifth line].

[The examples are: *bhṛtyām*, *ya udyantastomāḥ*. Why [is it specified] "beginning with *udyan*"? [As in: *ya unmādyet*. [Also: *ya etāvantaśca*. Why [is it specified] "referring to the subsequent [portion] beginning with *ekājagme*"? [As in: *mahām indro yojasā*. Or, others [hold that it applies] to the remote (*parokṣa*). [Examples of the remote: *ya eva devāḥ*; *navo navo bhavati*; *ye antarikṣe ya upadyaviṣṭha*; *uśantastvā havāmahe*; *asuṃ ya īyuḥ*; *yevājinam*; *yaṃ īmāhuḥ*; *yeva...* Why [is it specified] "for the sake of clarity"? [As in: *vispaṣṭārthaḥ*.

He performs the *samidh* offerings. [This refers to] those paths which lead to the gods (*devayāna*). Why "the *samidh*s"? [To ensure it does not apply] in cases such as *saṃpaśyāmi saṃśrava*. Or rather, these [offerings] are for heaven; for those who undertake the *upasads*, these are offered for the sake of the heavenly world, for the divine chariot, or for their own world. This is for the purpose of including even these two [terms], *sarjanāni* and so forth. Thus, the prohibition "having gone beyond, one should not go further" is set aside. [This is] the prohibition.

Do not have confidence in this [word] *bhakṣe* when it stands in these worlds; there is the *uttaravedi*. The *uttaravedi* belongs to those gods who have come into being. It belongs to those who are in these worlds—what does "in these" mean? It means "in these two. (P61b, 1st line) Regarding "those who give self, who give strength": why say "beyond the diversion"? It is because in these sections (*anuvākas*), there would be no skipping over the subsequent [section]. For example: *teṣām ayane yate*; *prayājānām mithu*. (2nd line)

He who knows thus: "O gods, a formidable sacrifice is being performed; the sacrifice itself is established in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Therefore, in this sacrifice, you must call upon [the gods]; you must extend [the sacrifice] toward them. Why [is it said], "toward the sacrifice, the *hotṛ*-priestesses approach"? Because it is indeed a formidable [act]. Why [is it said], "you must call upon the supreme"? For water is indeed the sacrifice, and water is immortality (*amṛta*); thus his sacrifice prospers. Why [is it said], "not before them"? Because the sacrifice itself belongs to them. When the battle is joined, [he is endowed] with power (*indriya*).

Therefore, among the teams (*yūdh*), he is the bull of the teams. These broad ones are seized as sacrificial posts (*yūpa*); they are called "the yoked" (*prayuj*), for they are indeed the two eyes. They are yoked to this very [sacrifice]. In his own abode, power (*indriya*) belongs to him who, having said "I shall sacrifice," then yokes [the teams]. "The divine waters... Just as one who is yoked is placed upon the nose-rope (*nasi*), so [it is with] "The winds are honeyed for the one who follows the Law (*ṛtāyan*). What does "for the one who follows the Law" mean? It means "we know this fountain from which [the fragrance] flows. For him who is beyond sight, these [verses] are for the rising of the fire.

Vomit indeed is the sacrifice to the gods; the *rakṣas* has been shaken off. By means of this very [rite], one should sacrifice with a motive. Truly, he drives away the *rakṣases* from himself; they are cast right here. "I take hold of the sacrifice from the wind," he says. "O pure ones, you shine when offered. It is as if it truly shines. Thus he secures it. "Kindling you... This is the redundant [verse] for the redundant [purpose]. What is beyond? They secure it by scattering [the earth] from the high altar (*uttaravedi*). "Along the earth and the wide dawns... In the kingdom itself, following the reed...
He binds. The twenty-one-night sacrifice indeed shines forth. He begins directly with these two; he prospers. "Etaśa’s gift for men, O Āyu, in the heat;
the black antelope for King Yama, the R̥śya [deer] for King Yama"—why does it say "for King Yama"?

[It is to exclude] "of King Varuṇa, of the Ādityas," "of Pūṣan, the swift one, of the Waters. "Come here, seize them, O carriers! he says. This is for the attainment of food. "Below, for the attainment of food"—why does it say "below, for the attainment of food"? [It is to exclude] "wild animals for the attainment [of food]."

They say: "Animals are sacrificed; indeed, both domestic ones are sacrificed. He sacrifices at the junction for the sake of both. They remain here in this world, and there in yonder world. [But] he remains in the world of men alone. "What does 'This cow was formerly his' mean? [The answer is: "He conquered this very world by means of the *rathantara* chant. "But its world is the heavenly world (*suvarga*). "What does 'The cow was formerly his' mean? [It means that] "In this very world, Indra slew Vṛtra. This is so that there may be no occasion for the prohibition [of the sacrifice] in this context. "Why shall we sacrifice this one? [It is for] Pūṣan.

Indra and Vāyu were also chosen; Indra is for you, the knower of the *ekadhana* [soma-vessels], for the sake of life and for one who stands up. He upon whom all wait—may he increase your long life, O herb! From the earth, from the sky, from the highest realm—what is this? One should say, "This is the boon. Regarding "offspring and food" (line 4): indeed, the plants are truly [the source]. "Come, you of beautiful form and rain-like color! He says, "O Agni, come for the feast! He says, "We choose Agni as the messenger. He alone is the one who possesses constant wealth. He approaches him with reverence; thus he chooses the deity. Him—(line 5).

One chooses the *ārṣeya*; one chooses [the *ārṣeya*]. Regarding "having placed the weapon on the highest tree": why does it say "on the tree" (*vṛkṣe*)? [Because of the example: "What tree was the *kamaṣa*? [And: "For Indra, [the soma] possessing power; for Indra, [the hymn] possessing splendor. [And: "For Indra, who possesses the Ādityas, thee! [And: "Agni saw the oblation for [Indra] possessing the *nīka*. Regarding "for Indra, preceded by the *ādityanīka*": why [is this restriction applied]? [Because of the counter-examples: "From afar he has come"; "from the beyond"; "may I go up from the downward slope and up from the upward slope"; "of that which is drunk by Indra, [the soma] accompanied by the bay horses (*hari*).
