[omitted] ... (7th line

Your mind is like the wind, moving restlessly; mount the aerial path like a horse. He who does not speak excessively is called "one who does not over-speak. When he brings [the gift] for him, thinking, "He will say a thousand," he is struck down at the point where there is no further speech. In the second year, [there is] an offering to Agni. During that year, they created one cow; thus he finds firm support in the year itself. Why is there only one offering to Agni? Because the year swells [with abundance]. Let this not be the limit for him; rather, let the year itself [be his support]. In the ninth line...

(…) “Let them pluck [the wool] for success. Day by day they bestow vigor upon the wind. What is this? That Agni is the thunderbolt (*vajra*), and there are eleven fires. Of the piercing ones, he says, “May he be easy to cross, like a ford. It is indeed a ford. As for the bull being like a ram—Śalu indeed spoke thus: “I shall choose a boon; let me be the one who turns toward [them] and becomes victorious. “Let us two choose a boon: may we be the favorites among the gods. “Let us choose a boon according to the season; may the clans dwell here in their own world.”

Or rather, [it is] water; therefore he places [the brick] for the sake of rain itself. Why "even further"? For Vāyu indeed rules over rain. Just as one who is worse [seeks] from one who is better—when [he says] "to Agni Śuci," it is for the sake of life itself. Thus he invokes this [brick]. "The ladle you heat in your mouth"—whatever portion of *vyaṃśas* there is, it is for the sake of power (*indriya*) itself. "Homage to thee, O bearer of flame, with thy glow," he says. Why "without flickering"? [It is said] "of him who is invoked, possessing bright glow. He [Agni] established himself as the preeminence among those born. But he said, "It does not rest within me. (Fourth line)

He lies to the south of himself while he is being cooked by the waters; this indeed is his solitary reclining. He lies around himself—his very self around himself. What does "low" mean? It means lying below, like one who is without cattle. Because he lies down to the south, he lies in a place of rest;

he releases [the animal] for the sake of peace and to prevent burning. "Open wide like doors for the prize, through hearing, O waters; sharpen the bones," with these words he scatters [the ashes] for the sake of purification. "The roar of Indra for you!"—this is the womb of the *ṣoḍaśin*. 6th line.

"O pleasant one, strew the *āhavanīya* fire; strew it as a rival for Indra and Agni. Thus he creates them; he approaches him. He should offer at a difficult place; [the word] "end of the sacrifice" (*igyāntam*). "May we be able to [serve] Agni in his dwelling place"—why does it say "end of the sacrifice"? [As in: "O stallions, you are in the lap; you are wide. Why does it say "not the *yājyā*"? [As in:

"In whose lap is the wide mid-air," or "he desires to please in his own life. Why does it say "not" followed by "further"? [As in: "Do not strike us; protect us. "O giver of strength, bestow strength. "Let all those accompanied by Indra rejoice in the invocation. "Thirty-three sit for a day."

"Let all indeed be present"—why [is this said]? "Whoever sacrifices with the Aśvamedha, for him all indeed..."—[the chariot is] clearly visible. "At the impulse of Savitṛ," [with these words] he takes up the wooden sword (*sphya*). Why [is it said] "furthermore"? "This impulse of strength has come forth; therefore, O Indra, at this impulse, by this [verse]... "To the one who carries a quiver, to the one who possesses a bow-case, grant a thousandfold wealth. "Flow on for the winning of strength"—by this, they are indeed *anuṣṭubh* verses. Why [is it said] "they are indeed *stu* (praises)"? "He piles them with *anuṣṭubh*s. "Be gracious, O son..."

"May the benevolent ones come with their mouths. At the morning pressing, he should place [the *ātman*] within himself. Having placed it, he then departs; furthermore, this is the *stoma* itself. What about "downward first"? It is the *stoma* of those rising up. The *cākṣuṣa-stoma* is the *ātman*. For well-being, the *āsurī-māyā*. The sacrificers create this very thing.

(2nd line) Indeed, at the beginning of the *savitṛ-ṛc*, with the meter, he who [performs] in the *bahiṣpavamāna*—if it has not been chanted, the *āgnīdhra* says: "The *pavamāna* has been chanted. Why does he say this? He says, "It has been chanted by Indra. In the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), he approaches the *soma*. Why does he say "previously unchanted"? "The *soma* has been pressed, according to the *ṛta*, not in vain... (3rd line)

"By means of two foundations, O Agni, let us fill the pit," he says; "for prosperity, for good crops, thee! [This refers to] the offerings to Sinīvālī, Anadvāhas, and Agnāvaiṣṇavas. He takes up the wooden sword (*sphya*) for the sake of impulsion, for the Aśvins, for mindfulness, so that there may be no harm. For the creation of progeny, Agni [is taken] from the gods. It is double-edged for the perfection of form. "The two vessels are invoked"—this is the invocation. "No," says the other; what then? "They are invoked," he says. Progeny indeed [is meant]. "Having sacrificed here to him... (fifth line).

The Āhavanīya fire becomes like that of a village. Why is it said, "The Āhavanīya belongs to Indra," and not, "The Āhavanīya is the heavenly world" or "The Āhavanīya is its foundation"? If one were to place [the fire] after it has been offered, the Agnihotra would go out. "We invoke the Indra who is worthy of sacrifice for food. The sacrificer has struck away [the enemy]; Indra slew Vṛtra. Having placed it in his hand like an Aṅgiras. Why is it said, "He shall not move to the end," and not, "With hands on all sides and feet on all sides"? [They] carry it around.

[The cups] beginning with the Aśvins. He invokes them: "O Agni, protect him; do not abandon him. As he draws [the Soma], it is indeed diminished. For you, the oblation is offered as food, for the removal of foul odor, for Agni. "Slay the Rakṣas! "Let us bring the portion! "Let us bring the all-encompassing portion! "Draw out the draft of the animal! "Thou art fuel for concealment from Varuṇa; for thy stability and safety. [Thus the explanation, having leaped over [the text], is completed. May there be auspiciousness! Salutations to the lotus-feet of the Guru Dakṣiṇāmūrti. Hariḥ Om.

The lineage of these [verses] is as follows: "Having first paid homage, I shall compose a new definition (*lakṣaṇa*) that is supreme, ninth, and most excellent, which brings about all prosperity for the goddess Rāyaṇī"—this is the connection. Having stated, "I shall compose a new definition," he now speaks in order to justify the work being undertaken by demonstrating the abundance of defects in the ancient treatises on definitions, saying: "It is difficult to know" (*durjñānam*). It is "difficult to know," meaning impossible to understand, due to ignorance regarding the composition of the texts; this is said with reference to those [ancient works] that are dependent [on others].

Because it was difficult to read due to the obscurity of its phrasing, because it was impossible to recite due to the lack of coherence in its composition, because it was dependent [on external aids] due to being an incomplete instruction, and because it was disordered—lacking the proper sequence beginning with the letter 'A'—that [text] has been set aside and rejected. Having discarded it, this [work] has been composed with a commentary, arranged according to the sequence of letters starting from 'A', complete and full. This is what is meant: since the ancient version was difficult to understand and observed here to contain many external defects, it has been rejected; and for the sake of easy comprehension by the teachers and students of the Taittirīya Veda, this summary has been provided.

In the form of Vyāsa, there is both a refutation and an illustration; ancient knowledge is another characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). This connects with the phrase "I shall do. It was urged that the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is not to be commenced. However, he speaks in order to establish that it *is* to be commenced, together with an explanation. [He states: "The verse concerning the non-commencement of the *Kṛmikṛśla*. By which they urge that this is not to be commenced; thus, even though one's own position is established, the words of the Veda are of a single form.

He thus states another reason for what was said regarding "the well-known study": therein, one who is an expert in sentences (*vākya-kovida*) becomes [one who knows] all words and word-meanings for the purpose of maintaining the continuity of the Vedic words. And that has been shown in the *Prātiśākhya* by the sūtra beginning with: "The letter *ha* preceded by the first [vowel], its position as the fourth [consonant], belongs to the Plākṣis, Kāṇḍins, Gautamas, Pauṣkarasādins, and so forth. What [is the point of] this? Again, he who... [repeats the phrase].

[He is] very generous. Because it is so, from what is it inferred? By certain skillful great souls (*mahātman*), it is determined that [this is] among those renowned in the Vedas. By certain great souls such as Vyāsa and others, who know subtle reality, through words composed of praise and meanings arising from their own great soul, there is a cognition produced by a single, constant mode of application which is always and everywhere non-deviant; just as the former teacher was, so too is the latter, difficult to comprehend by opponents.

Since even in the Taittirīya Veda, certain letters become great "sanadehakas" (those that possess a body) due to the similarity in form between the *takāra*—which is accepted as the subject of the definition of the Veda—and the two *ratnas* (jewels) in the *saṃhitā*, it must be determined by some rule (*lakṣaṇa*) without which the reading of the well-known *salabdhi* [text], which has the *nakāra* ending in *takāra* (3rd line), cannot be established. A rule exists for the sake of its object; why then would it not be determined by those who, having heard every word, are forgetful and lack discernment? Therefore, there must be a rule. (4th line)

It must be explained: with reference to what object does that definition (*lakṣaṇa*) operate? What is its subject matter (*abhidheya*), what is its purpose (*prayojana*), and what is the doubt (*saṃdeha*), and how does it arise? To one who raises such questions, [the author] now states that very same point in summary form by means of two verses, expanding upon the scope of the response, the object, the subject matter, the purpose, and the manner of the doubt. Therein, [the letters] *la*, *ca*, *ka*, *pha*, *ja*, *ta*, *da*, *dha*, *na*, *ma*, and *la*— [End of excerpt]

This is the designation beginning with *ca*. In that regard, when followed by a word beginning with *ca* and so on, the final *n* at the end of a modified word undergoes change in *saṃhitā*. Likewise, when followed by a word beginning with *ta*, the final *t* at the end of a modified word undergoes change in *saṃhitā*. These two—the *t* and the *n*—are indeed the objects of this rule (*lakṣaṇa*). That which is to be expressed through their modification is the knowledge of the *t* and the *n*; thus, it has already been stated that the purpose of this [work] is precisely the knowledge of the *t* and the *n*. He clarifies this very point with the two verses beginning with "In the case of *ca*, *cha*, and *ja*" (*cachajeṣu*) and "In the case of *ca*, *cha*, and *ja*" (*cachajeṣu*).

When the letter *n* at the end of a word precedes the letters *c*, *ch*, or *j*, it becomes *t* in *saṃhitā*; having understood this, it attains its true form (*tatvam*). The same applies to the letter *m* at the end of a word. In that case, when *m* is followed by a nasalized stop (*sparśa*), [the rule] "it becomes a nasal" (*manunāsikam*) applies; thus it attains its true form. In *saṃhitā*, these two are known to have a single form. When the four letters of the *ta*-group are present, excluding the letter *dh*, they become their respective members of the *ta*-group when combined with the letter *dh*.

When followed by the four sounds *ta*, *da*, *dha*, and *na*, a final *n* becomes *ṇ* in *saṃhitā*. Where [the rule] applies, the place of articulation is nasal. But this does not occur here. Here too, the *e*-vowel is the *saṃhitā* even when followed by *m*; furthermore, a final *n* undergoes the *saṃhitā* operation even here, as a final *m* at the end of a word is "highest" (*uttama*) with respect to its own class (*savarṇa*). [This is] the highest of its own class...

By that [rule], it attains the state of *natva* (the substitution of *na*). Here too, in the five beginning with *tad*, one should not suspect a change in the nature of the letter *na* due to the absence of any alteration in its essential form (*svarūpa*) within the *saṃhitā*. This is because, at the time of the final pause (*avasāna*), there is the instruction regarding the dental quality (*dantardūlatva*) according to the rule "the dentals (*tavargīya*) are optionally [so] at the end or beginning, and when followed by *ṛ*, *u*, *la*, or *j*" (4th line), since the *saṃhitā* has also taught the non-inclusion of those endings. [Objection: "If there is a difference in place of articulation (*sthāna*), there is a difference in the phoneme (*varṇa*)," because some modification is present. [Response: When *la* follows, the *ta* at the end of the word [remains as such]. (5th line)

Regarding the rule *nakāro lakāram*: in *saṃhitā*, [the nasal] becomes *lakāra* with *anunāsika*. Regarding the rule *makāro'pyantasthā paraśca savarṇamanunāsikam*: in *saṃhitā*, it becomes *lakāra* with *anunāsika*. Here too, there is a *saṃhitā* of multiple forms for these two. When *nakāra* follows, the final *nakāra* undergoes some modification, yet it is said to remain *nakāra* itself. Here too, the final *makāra* is followed by a *sparśa* consonant.

It has been stated that due to the combination (*saṃhitā*), the position (*saṃsthāna*), and the nasality (*anunāsikatā*), it is indeed the letter *m*. However, here [in the following case], the *t* at the end of the word is followed by an "uttama" (the last letter of its class). According to the rule "when followed by an uttama, it becomes the uttama of its own class," it becomes the letter *n*, as it is the uttama of its class. Here, there is a single form of *saṃhitā* for the three letters *n*, *m*, and *t*. If, in all these cases, even when obstructed by a *dvandva* compound, the example is not always of the *t* at the end of the word, then in the presence of letters other than *m* such as *ca* and so on, the final *m* [becomes *n*]. [This applies to] the end of the word...

Where this *m* is connected with its counterpart (*pratiyogin*), the *m* following a *n* becomes a *t*, and the counterpart also [becomes a *t*]. For example: *nanu śatatadāṃs traṃ hanti*. But how is there a resolution for a *n* at the end of a word in this case, in that case, and elsewhere?

"Not acute" refers to that which is an acute vowel in the *padapāṭha* (word-text), but becomes acute upon entering into *saṃhitā* (continuous text). The meaning is as follows: That vowel which, in the recitation of individual words (*padapāṭha*), is neither acute (*udātta*) nor circumflex (*svarita*), nor is it a *pracaya* [vowel], provided that in the *saṃhitā-pāṭha* it follows an acute vowel—of that vowel, one should understand that the vowel at the beginning of the following word is not elided (*na stri*). For example: *uddhṛto hute 'gnihotre*, *adhvaryo ver apāḥ*, *subheṣajaṃ yathā sati*, *bhrātrvyo yajamāno yajamānasya*. And whatever is acute in the *padapāṭha* becomes circumflex upon entering the *saṃhitā*; the completion of the sentence is as before. By this, the sense is as follows: (line 8).

By that, they do not obtain it; he does not reach the further [stage]. [Examples: *śatāyudhāya yajñāyudhāni*; *āśīrāhavanīyyāgneyāgnāmuṣyāyaṇaśrutiḥ*; *satyāśīr ityā...* (7th line).

Regarding the *havīṃṣi* for Vītra: after offering the cake on eight potsherds to Agni in the *āhavanīya* fire, one offers with the oblation to Agni-Viṣṇu, [reciting]: "This I [take] from the self of such-and-such a descendant. They have come to the den of the wild beast, where the chariot of Manu was fashioned. Having offered the five [oblations], he offers: "Consciousness, the fashioned, and intention. (5th line)

"With the desert" (*dhanvanā*)... [7th line].

For the sake of radiance and for the sake of fervor; seized for the sake of non-attainment. Having made [it] like the earth; having taken what was first desired, likewise the eating and the burning. Having gathered and having taken—thus it was not desired. Not to be eaten by Prajāpati; both the eaters and those to be eaten. Or the destruction of the sacrifice and the speaking together. (10th line)

The *ādhāna* (establishment), the *adhimādhīta*, the *ādhipatya*, as well as the *ādhayas*; the *hastādānas* and the *puruṣas*. *Svāhā* to the *adhimādhīta*; *svāhā* to the *adhīta*, to the mind, and to the sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) of Varuṇa. To that [belong] the *ādhayas*... the *ādhāna*, and also the *āpyāntyāyana*, and also the *ānujāvara*.

The placing of the *tūṣa* grass for the fire; [the fire] is behind and as far as the end. One should take [it]; the younger brother (*anujāva*)—[the Aśvins are indeed...]—"the younger" (*jāvara*)—what does this mean? The younger brother by birth (*anupitā*), the younger brother by age (*anubhrātā*). And regarding the *anṛcu* [verse], it is through the *anuṣṭubh* meter; likewise, speech (*vāk*) and water (*āpa*)... [the *anṛcu* which is... ...and through the *anuṣṭubh* meter, speech... [for the sake of power (*inasāyaṃ*) in the evening].

"O Agni, you shall obtain [them] for yourself. For the sake of attainment (*āpti*), having attained, and likewise having attained through attainment, [there is] the *apasvār* at the very end. Through the attainment of the fourfold revolving, it is unified. Having attained the *iṣṭakā* within day and night—this is their attainment. That [attainment] turned back toward the one standing in the front. "O divine waters, from the *svār*"—what [is meant by this]? "The waters have spread with light. Behold the one who causes to attain, the one who causes to flee, and the subsequent one. Behold the auspicious one. Why "behold"? [Because of the verse: "The waters have spread with light. The Hotṛ is the one who causes the waters to attain that.

“Svāhā to him who has fled, svāhā!”—what is the purpose of the word “uttara” (further)? [The answer is: “Svāhā to him who is about to flee, svāhā to him who has fled. From the point where one begins to obtain [the goal] by means of a *yajus* up until the *avagraha*, these [two formulas] do not serve to obtain anything; they say they are for obtaining cattle. Why does it say “by means of a *yajus*”? Because he says “to obtain,” he obtains that very thing by means of these two [formulas]. He obtains these very worlds by means of these two. Why does it say “until the *avagraha*”? [Because of the example: “By means of the *ṛc* and the *sāman*, by means of the *yajus*. The recitation of the *āmbā* names [is performed].

[The offering] for one suffering from consumption is made with parched grain (*saktūn*). For those suffering from truth-ailment (*satyāmayin*), [the offering is] a sacrificial pap (*caru*) of *āmba* grains. "Svāhā! To the mind! And what indeed is the name? For one suffering from fever (*gratāmayin*), [the offering is] with curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*). For one suffering from consumption, they approach with curd-mixture; likewise for one approaching [death]. With the *maitrāvaruṇī* curd-mixture, for whomsoever there is suffering, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are seized. They approach while bowing down to the aged and the increasing [deities]. Why "approach" (*upāyanti*)? [Because in other cases they] "go along the river" (*anudhanvanāyanti*). Like a cow coming toward them, [they approach]. In these [verses], "sināya sūryaḥ pṛthivyāḥ," it is not "going" (*cāyate*). "To the white one (*sitāya*) svāhā! To the white one svāhā! (8th line).

Sūrya is the god among the gods. Svāhā to the earth! Svāhā to the atmosphere! In these sections (*anuvākas*), there is no [fixed] position for the word *āyate*. Svāhā to him who goes away! His descent is here. Svāhā to him who comes! Svāhā! (9th line) To the one coming to the gods, to the sacrificer, be protection! Svāhā to him who comes with a cry! To Āyāsa, to Āyata, to Āyas, to Ārti, to the seasons (*ṛtūn*). Svāhā to Prayāsa, svāhā to Yāsa! As he encounters [them] through his striving (*yathāyatayā*). (10th line)

[He who is] cool-bodied, [and whose] mind is free from affliction; the seasons were released as [they flow] onward. [By means of] both [hands], the self was seen in the midst of the [world]. There is no affliction in his purposes. He indeed [performed] the sacrifice for the sake of this [world] and that [world]. Thus he protected [it]. So [it is]. (P73b, 29a, 1st line)

They honor with the *pītha*; the deity is the moist constellation. He does not meet with distress. In the five seasons, indeed, in the seasonal [periods]... it is commenced from... [he is] released from distress... Tvaṣṭṛ... from our [domain]... he who... (second line).

[The word *alābhyā*] is used [in the sense of] distress regarding a sacrifice, or for one's own pleasure, or when causing affliction to offspring; [it is used] from afar, [and] after what has been obtained and not obtained, [it is used] repeatedly. [It is used] with the mind, [and] for one who is to be approached and for one who is to be brought near. *Svāhā* [is uttered] for what is obtained, *svāhā* for what is not obtained. That very thing which is not obtained—what is "repeatedly"? It is that which is not obtained. Both *alabhe* and *tāpyālabhata* have the acute accent (*udātta*) on the first syllable. When one obtains cattle, thus he obtains them by means of the former [formula]. Why specify "with the acute accent"? [Because in other cases, such as] *ardharcam ālabheta*, [the accentuation differs]. Having brought [them] under control, he obtains them. *Ābraścanāt*.

*dhāvitam* and *āvirāviddham* [are examples]. Or, that which emerges from a cutting tool [is so called]. *Prācīnāvītam* belongs to the ancestors (*pitṛ*). "Sūryo nāvirbhavati"—why [is there] *na*? [Because in the following: "sā kṛṣṇā virabhavat" [it occurs without *na*]. Like a pierced [object] being cut out. From the point where the pause (*avagraha*) begins, it is *āvya*; up to the preceding [pause], it is *āvṛtaḥ*. "asāvāvadadhīdevāḥ. Why [is there] *na avagrahāt*? [Because in: "prajāvadasme draviṇāyajasva," one does not take hold of the *nāvya*. "svāhā vallate svāhā. Why [is there] *pūrva*? [Because in: "svāhā parevalgate svāhā."

The months turn toward the south. By the turning of the *āvāpa*, he entered the root with an acute accent (*udātta*). The dice were in the house of the *āvāpa*. For the sake of the vow of the one who knows, he entered the worlds. Why "with an acute accent"? [As in: "The face of Agni has entered the waters. Likewise: "He turns back; thus the hunters have settled upon the *āśira* mixture. The high altar (*uttaravedi*) turns back. He becomes a hunter. It is covered with a turban (*uṣṇīṣa*). That indeed is for the head. From the fire, having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, [the response is] "O you who are eager to hear! Not thus, nor "and that. That is prior to the fire, in the essence.

Having taken hold [of the sacrificer], one should cause the *āśrāvaṇa* to be uttered: "The deity, the best of stars; svāhā to the white one, svāhā! The two, the dwelling-place of the fly and the sun; Āśā by name, and Śumāśya—one should cause the *āśrāvaṇa* to be uttered even with an acute accent. For those standing nearby, [the formula] is "mitravada astvojaḥ" (O Mitra-like one, may there be strength for you). [The word] "girāśuñjayantam" (conquering quickly with song). (9th line) There is no elision of the *niryāsa* (resin/exudation). One should cause the *āśrāvaṇa* to be uttered without taking hold [of the sacrificer]. Why say "with an acute accent"? Because one should cause the *āśrāvaṇa* to be uttered while standing. Likewise: "āśurathāvasya tvāsannāstvāmupāsmahe" (We worship you, the protector of the swift chariot, who are near); "āśuṣeṇāya cāśurathāya ca" (To him of the swift army and the swift chariot); "viśvadāvasya tvā" (Of Viśvadāva, you...). (10th line)

I sacrifice together (*sañjuhomi*). May there be strength for you (*sahāstānte*). We worship the form of light (*jyotirūpāsmahe*). "May you sit" (*āsītāste*); likewise, "may she sit for you" (*tathā sā te āsīnaśca asurastathā*). He should not sit together with him (*na sahāsīta*). "May you release" (*pratimucyāste*). "And may the more wicked one sit" (*pāpīyyāścāsāte*). Sitting, he sustained [them] with his vital breaths (*prāṇairdadhārā sīnaḥ*). The Asura was named Āsīt. Regarding "tvāparannāsate": it would mean "he will eat you" (*dhāsyādāsiṣyata iti trayam*). "His bay horses sit on the bank" (*tasyāsate harayaḥ saptatīre*). Why "tvāparanneti"? [Examples: *sate*, *tvāsate*, *tvā*. So that it might be "swallowed" (*grasitam*). Why "yayeti"? [Example: *yagno patramā*.

There should be compassion. *Āsiṣyate svāhā*, *sīnāya svāhā*, *sitāya*. We have sat down, and we shall also cause you to sit with our mouth upon the Asura. This earth was indeed hairless, as much as we have occupied. He desired: "May I be seated. [With the verse] "From Agni’s... [and] "The eagle... [he places it]. Both of these are for the Asura. He places it, and likewise he raises it for that which has been placed. He also places the sprinkling waters (*prokṣaṇī*). Why [does he say] "having raised"? With a verse addressed to Varuṇa he places it. For the sake of the offering that has been placed, [he says] "the one who stands" and "the one who has stood," having released the call from the *āhāva* at the place of offering.

"Stand! Be firm! Your place is here; the praise is near; the jar is set down; the pit is prepared. Having brought [the earth] from elsewhere, one should place it there. "The invocation has been smelled. They carry it with a small [vessel]; there should be a carrying-vessel and a carrying-pole. They carry it with a small [vessel]. Why does it say "with a small [vessel]"? [Because it says: "He carries the head. And [it says] "and the carrying-pole and the carrying-yoke. "A little bird is the yoke," so it is said.

"With the season, having struck us, forward, away—having caused [the announcement], with the invitatory verse. He says "first," they say "and"—this is the well-established rule. With the season, *sna*, having struck, forward, away, having caused the announcement, with the invitatory verse—thus it is.

The former says: "As for example: 'twice he said again'; 'Aruṇa said to him'; 'having approached, for the sake of the Lord of the Forest'; 'having brought it, he said'; 'he spoke of himself'; 'having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he said to the gods'; 'he spoke with the *puro'nuvākyā*. What is this 'the former'? By this much one becomes possessed of sin. They say the ocean is together with the *rasā*. [The explanation of *avarṇya* and *avarṇayoḥ* is completed. Hariḥ Om. May there be auspiciousness.
To the one who is devoid of the three qualities (*guṇa*) and the ordainer of the three sacrifices, the Śruti...

Having paid homage to the Lord of the Three-Eyed One—who is eternally present within the three sons—and to the instructor of the destroyers of obstacles, he teaches [this work]. With these three verses beginning with “The word that is a locus of doubt because of its similarity to an immovable thing,” while performing an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*) for the unimpeded completion of this treatise, he pays homage to his chosen deity and reveals the subject matter. He says, “the immovable word is taught. By “immovable word” (*aniṅgyapada*), what is meant is a word that is indivisible (*avibhāgapada*), and not a compound word (*samāsapada*), even though...

In the case of a compound such as *śacīpati-bṛhaspati*, because it lacks a nominal suffix (*niṅg*), its status as a compound is understood through etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*); furthermore, its possession of multiple udātta accents is also understood through derivation. Even when such [words] exist as compounds, they are appropriately applied directly (*añjasā*). The original text... (P74b, 30a, 1st line).

(…) because of the impossibility of [its] arising in those cases. Otherwise, having stated only "an unaccented word [is treated as such] with the exception of one [vowel]," there would be an error. Because of the protection of the unity of vowels, and because of the prescription of the udātta [accent] for those [vowels], and because of the repetition, it is indeed a portion of that.

It is appropriate [to say] "that which is not to be moved" (*aniṅgyam*). Instruction (*anuśāsana*) means teaching, such as "this should be employed in this manner. However, in this case, lest there be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because there is no instruction regarding the category of words that are not to be moved in the context of *kṛsara*, he specifies the scope. No; for "not to be moved" (*aniṅgya*) is used because of its similarity to what is to be moved (*iṅgya*), in order to avoid ambiguity.

"Spadaṃ padam" (the word *pada* [is used] where there is doubt). That word which is doubted because it serves as the cause for uncertainty due to its similarity with other words (*iṅgyasādṛśya*) is precisely what is being defined here. The application of the definition is for the purpose of dispelling doubt; thus, "that which is the locus of doubt. Regarding the phrase "its essence fell away" (*tasyai rasaḥ parā patat*), the second instance where it says "fell away" (*parā patat*)—in the analysis of forms such as *parāpatat* and so on—a dual form arises from the word *pada*, but this does not fall within the scope of the present subject matter. Example: "Speech, when articulated, is raised" (*vyākṛtā vāgudyate*).

What is the purpose of [specifying] "anudātta" (unaccented)? [Consider: *udyate svāhā* ("Hail to that which is being raised!"). There is a double mention of the form *udita* because it is both the past participle and the verbal noun; as in *uditau*, *uditaye*—here [the intention was] "may there be desire"—and *uditau sūryasya*, *uditāya svāhā*. The Vedic revelation (*śruti*) says: "One should say *eta śai*"; thus [it becomes] *etodveta*. [And]: *vātaśena*. *Eta*... (second line).

vya- | etāvān | etāvatī | etāvantam | etadum | ekādaśa | ekādaśanīm | The word *udumbara* is understood [here]. The word *udumbara* is mentioned again because there might be a suspicion of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) regarding the suffixes (*madānām*) when a modification occurs at the beginning or end. *gopam*, *gopārtauḥ*, not a form of *vit*.

The inclusion [of these words]: lest there be doubt regarding the two terms "gopā" and "gopa," thinking that they might mean "herdsman"; yet, as for the term "gopa," since it is also seen in a low (non-Vedic) sense, it should not be rejected. Furthermore, the term "cikittu" was accepted on the grounds that it occurs in the *Niyukta* recension; and "madintama" was accepted on the grounds that it is not unconnected [to the context]. [He is] the most exhilarating (*madintamaḥ*), the most pervasive (*vyaciṣṭham*)—[4th line].

The word *udāttam* is understood [as meaning "high-pitched"] so that there may be no suspicion that it refers to a prefix (*upasarga*), as in the case of *vyaciṣṭham*. The word *pravatvatī* is understood as being used even when low-pitched, as in *pravatvanī*. The phrase *bṛhaspate* is recited even when used in a low tone, as in *dhatta bṛhaspate vaiśvānara*. The word *samasya* is understood as referring to a verse (*ṛc*), so that there may be no suspicion that it refers to a conjunction (*saṃyukta*), as in *mā naḥ samasya*. By the word *hiraṇmayam*, only a mere indication of the direction has been shown for those things not explicitly mentioned in the detailed exposition; therefore, whatever else is unmentioned—

This [work] is to be inferred by the wise. Because the non-conjugational (aniṅgya) forms in this treatise are manifold and because speech is scattered, it is impossible for a single person to characterize them all; furthermore, there would be excessive bulk in the text if every word were explicitly provided. Therefore, only a mere indication of the direction has been shown, and it has been stated concisely. Consequently, whatever word not mentioned here that serves as a point of doubt must be inferred by the wise—the learned—meaning it is to be understood through usage. Thus, the path of these non-conjugational words has been demonstrated.

By this [phrase], it is shown that this treatise was composed with reference to the Taittirīya branch (*śākhā*) by the illustrious Śrīvatsāṅka, who was honored by the wise among the gods. By the word "teacher" (*śāstṛ*), there is no limitation of his lineage or fame. (9th line) (…) The *Niṅgyaparibhāṣā* is completed.
Now, [the examples] *anamitra*, *anyatara*, *ambarīṣa*, and *avadhiṣma* are cited; the meaning is that the actual forms of these *niṅga*-words are being stated.
Now: *anamitra*, *anyatara*, *ambarīṣa*. (P81b, 37a, first line)

(... ) are pronounced with the *atiśaya* accent. *avadhiṣma*, *aśvataraḥ*, *artavadyam*—these words are not subject to modification (*neṅgyāḥ*). *anamitram*, *anamitrāya suvadhvam*, *anyatarān*, *anyatarasya*, *ambarīṣāt*, *ambarīṣe*, *avadhisma rakṣam*, *aśvataraḥ* (...), *ana*(...)*pu*(... *yuvānaḥ*. (Second line)

With the *avākā* plant, he has pressed out the *kaṃ* [soma]; may he protect us with that which is most powerful, from the one who is not to be slain. These are the unyielding [verses]. With the *avākā* of the ocean... what *kaṃ*? What meter? He has pressed it out for the sacrifice... with the new [plant]. From the midst of darkness, the most powerful one; he has protected me from the measuring [of fate]; you have made him invulnerable. (Third line)

That which one might contend against with a covering—by means of that covering one approaches; the coverings of the worlds. The *droṇakalaśa* is not seized, he whose two seize-ers (*grahītṛ*) would encompass heaven and earth. O sinless one, then your greatness; your body is sinless. Even as they go forth, the *apsarases* [are] for him, the cattle-like ones, unswollen, flowing.

Thus is the impulsion of the approach. The plants are the *apsarases*. These two words: "for him" (*asya si*), "the cattle-like ones" (*apasyuvaḥ*). "Unswollen" (*anulbaṇaḥ*), "flowing" (*asravantīm*), "the two *apsarases*" (*apsarasau*). But that which is "wide-spreading" (*perum*), "for him" (*asya si*). Wearing the waters, weaving the water-woven [cloth] that is not coarse, may we ascend the flowing river. The sound of the whirlpool is the cattle; the sound of the calf is the horse... the sound of the wind. The sound of the seasons is the cattle; the sound of the non-cattle is the goat... the sound of the ram. That is Aditi. (6th line)

Yama has attained [it]. Not falling away from within, he has reached the end along the shore and has looked upon the ornament. Not falling away, the earth [has attained it]. "Apadya" is taken as a word ending in *m* so that there may be no suspicion that it is a preposition joined [to another word]. He causes [them] to drink from within. Both purifiers (*pavitrau*). Without a barrier, without an end. Standing along the shore (*anvīpam*). For the sake of the ornament, O Maruts, you have looked upon the ornament. With the *anuṣṭubh*, with the *niṣṭat*—for the *niṣṭaka* is indeed for the sake of protection—by means of these protections, for the sake of reaching. With the *anuṣṭubh*. (Line 8)

Do it! May your unpraised [deeds] increase. This is the one who has not praised; [let there be] extensive praises. For the sake of great favor, for the sake of praise, the fearless ones have found [it]. From all sides, through rain, for the destruction of the surrounding darkness. By this, she is not here; she is not a serpent-turning one, as heard from the sin of the thigh. Let him make me equal by this. Heaven and Earth, the blameless ones, today [make] me blameless. With good movement, free from sin. From those of good vows, free from sin. The lack of turning, the evil. That which was through the lack of turning. (Note: The provided text contains fragments of Vedic mantras and ritual formulas. The translation reflects the archaic, sacrificial context.)

"Va vo dadhāna," "sa moka sāvare paśau," and "eteṣām anyathāhutiḥ"—in all these [cases], the thumb [is used]. Regarding the *atīkāśas* for the *acchāvāka*: I have stated that the *ajiṣṭa* and *aniṣṭa* [verses] are not to be recited in a low tone (*aniṅgya*). For example: "alaja āntarikṣaḥ. He makes the *atīkāśas*. This [is the second line].

The Acchāvāka: "We have spoken to the Seer; may the unloved and unwished-for deities perish. I have not given away the bull, nor the goat, nor the horse—may the one who strikes [them] be struck down. These are the non-limbs. "The Seer struck [them]; he spoke when they were not praised; I gave [them]. (Third line)

Ah! The three eastern [days] are non-journey-days; I am the journey-day for the Agnīdh; the two Varuṇī [days] are non-journey-days. The word "ajagara" (serpent) should be uttered by Aramati; let it be uttered by the one who is free from desire. These are the non-removing, immovable [verses] of the serpent. With the serpent [he addresses] the serpents. O Mitra-mahas, may he be free from reproach; [may] Aramati [be free from reproach]. (Line 4)

Long-lived; he who is measured becomes youthful. He should not become aged; he offers the Soma and sets it down. Without cattle, without a well, without performing the *āśīr* (curd-mixture), [the offering is made] for each and every one. These are the non-obstructive ones. One who lacks cattle is [thus addressed]. They [made] the well for the sake of speech. They made it of iron with a sacrifice lacking *āśīr*. For each and every one, they struck down others. Without anger, O well-hearing one, the well was filled with cakes. [These are] the non-obstructive ones. Without anger in mind, the swift one is the lower; the lower one is surpassed by the others. Pour forth!

The great pit; those who are in the pits; the cake on the Ekāṣṭakā day; the five-leaved *aṅku* plant; the dustless ones, the *avaka* plants, the wolves, the followers of the dead, the dustless ones, the *vinata* birds; following the *avakā* plants; the *avuka* plants have not grown weary; for in the *avuka* plants [they are] obstructed.

Let them come down with their aid; with your aid, for the sake of those who have feet and those who move like the wind. As you provide clothing, so do you drive away the disease. You have made the remedy for this ailment; he makes it a remedy. [He drives away] the serpent from the one who presses Soma, who does not give, and who does not ask. (........ (8th line)

[May he] cause [the one] harming [us], the one who does not press [Soma], the non-sacrificer, and the one who does not wish to give, to be made to give. [May he grant] a bow with three arrows, unasked for, unhindered, and irresistible—[thus] the Atharvans. Come to this enclosure; [grant] the irresistible [and] auspicious [state]. The Atharvans are the Bhr̥gus. (9th line)

The guest has arrived. Just as for one who has come on a lunar day (*tithi*), so [have they come]. The Adhvaryus have stood within; free from disease (*ayakṣma*), like iron, sounding with a cry. The Adhvaryus have stood within; [they have placed] the most... within the limbs. And [he has made it] free from disease. He has protected [them] from disease. He has opened the iron [gate].

(…) smayyava-mādha | yuyavan-namīvāḥ | anamīvo bhavānaḥ | adhvaryor-abhīketa-uddhyarcitā-rokṣityā-aṃ(…)ra(…). t | ghṛtavatīm-adhva(…) iti (…)hīke | (2nd line) (…) smilingly, he has driven away diseases; may you be free from disease for us. At the presence of the Adhvaryu, having been praised, he shall ascend with radiance. (The vessel) full of ghee, the Adhva(…) thus (at the presence). (2nd line)

Those who honor [thee]... for imperishability, thee! Thou art Aṅghāri; O Aṅgāra, Baṃbhāra, O thou that art not subject to old age, [protect] the one being purified by fire, the lowest, the most lowly. "O thou that art not subject to old age, the bursting, the roaring..."—[the repetition of] "O thou that art not subject to old age" is for the purpose of ensuring there is no doubt regarding the division [of the mantra] at the word *aja*. Thus it is in such a case.

(... must be observed). From one who has sacrificed, [one should look] to one who has not sacrificed. From the lowest, the middle. He becomes the lowest. The *stomas* are indeed the lowest. By taking up the three forms—“the lowest,” “the lowest and the lowest,” and “the lowestest”—it is for the sake of the purpose [of the ritual]. In such a manner, this should be understood in the eight-fold [context]. [He is] approached by those who do not deceive. (4th line)

May he attain and may he pacify. With guileless [prayers], [he attains] the *kapiñjala* birds. That he might attain the greatness of the reins (*abhīśu*). The gods have attained peace. The secret woman among others, and among those who eat [the food], even among women... the *viś* is the meter. Who knows of these others? (5th line)

[The waters] touched [the world] with their empty dwellings—those which are visible in the distance. On the far shore, the wind blew forth; the waters surged with foam. On the far shore were the sugarcanes. Having crossed over, O Wind, [they] flowed away. With those [waters], be favorable to us. O you who possess no wealth, may my [sugarcanes] be small; on the far shore, [may] my self... (6th line).

The *āmikṣā* belongs to the lineage of such-and-such a seer (*ārṣeya*); there is a scriptural mention of Agni as the source of life (*āyuṣ*). [The word] *āmuṣyāyaṇam* [is used]. For the self is among those invoked. [It occurs] in a part of a word. [The suffix] *-ya* belongs to this. In this [verse], there is one born of such-and-such a lineage (*āmuṣyāyaṇa*). He strikes at the lineage of the seers (*ārṣeya*). ... [the four] ... of the *āmikṣā*.

Let it be addressed to Agni (*āgneyī*), in the *triṣṭubh* meter. It goes within the span of life (*āyuṣ*). Through life, [he makes] the long-lived. From the egg (*āṇḍa*)—O giver of hearing, O giver of wealth, from the wild [animal]—[it is] like the sun. Raw [meat] is well-cooked. *Svāhā* to the two eggs! With the bow (*dhanvanā*), let us conquer with the arrow (*jijñayā*). By means of ... [the eighth line].

In the *mājis* [verses]: *āṭṇāraḥ*, *kakṣīvān*, or *āraṇyam*. (*...*) *āraṇyāḥ*. *ādityaṃ garbham*. They offered into the vessel; you shall obtain it. O Āvirdhāvatharvaṇa, Cākha, Ākhara, Atithya, and Śarjava—O Āvirdha, Daddhya, and Ātharvaṇa, [grant] friendship. Marūkha goes forth. O Rudra, let the Ākha accept your hospitality. "Hospitality is being performed," [he says]. Āvinnā... [the tear].

The path of the waters; the end of the journey; Pūṣan has helped us; Mitra and Varuṇa have helped us; Vena has helped us; he has helped the gods; of the swift rice-grains; the quarters of space; he [is] the hope of the quarters of space; his first portion; the clarified butter of Prajāpati; the oblations of Agni; you are clarified butter.

When [the word] *ājyena* follows *somah* which has been taken from the Asuras, [the final syllable of *ājyena*] becomes unaccented (*anudātta*) if it occurs at the end of a sentence (*āntyāyana*). For example: *ājyam āntyāyana āyan antodāttam āsani*. This [term] *āntyāyana* refers to one who has reached the end. He, having attained the world, went toward godhood. Why [is it said] "ending with *anucchoda*"? As in: *vidadhātyāyan*. And if there is another accent... (4th line).

This is a refutation of that [previous statement]. He sits upon the three [seats]. Svāhā for the sake of eating! Therefore, it is to be excluded. They fall through desire... for the sake of... for the sake of... (5th line).

They say that [the gods] dwelt among the Akṣus. A pap of rice for the Āmbas; Indra and Agni for the Āṅgirasas. "We have indeed dwelt here," they said, "in whose directions... The non-injuring, the injurer, the one who causes to flow, he who is the protector of the living, for the sake of the living... they have called him [the one who] injures when [the time has come].
